20735-mrs-mary-eales-s-receipts-1733:
Mrs. Mary Eales gave her name to a famed book of receipts, an old word for recipes, dated 1733. One receipt tells how to boil stoned cherries until the juice is gone. Sugar, finely beaten, then goes in for two or three more boils before potting.

Confection work fills these pages, from preserves to sweets for a fine table. Eales cooked for royalty, and her book shows that craft in plain steps. Cooks and food historians can trace old tastes, weights, and methods here. The terse style trusts the reader to know the kitchen well already.
a-popular-history-of-ireland-from-the-ea: McGee's passionate history of Ireland appears here in another edition, carrying readers from legendary beginnings to the triumph of Catholic Emancipation. Written by an Irish nationalist who lived the cause, the narrative blends scholarship with love of country. It remains one of the most readable popular histories of the Irish people.
a-storehouse-of-physicall-and-philosophi: A Storehouse of Physical and Philosophical Secrets, 1633. The secrets' storehouse. This book preserves that book. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
alphabet-of-phrenology-a-short-sketch-of: Alphabet of Phrenology, 1833. The beginner's sketch. This book preserves that work. Future scholars will discover it. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
arxiv-2511-20533:
Cherkaoui and Dey pack post-quantum encryption onto a cheap microcontroller. Their 2025 paper builds isogeny cryptography from Engel expansions over p-adic series. Quantum computers threaten today's public-key systems broadly. Many post-quantum candidates need keys too large for tiny devices. Internet of Things nodes have kilobytes, not megabytes, to spare.

Isogeny systems are famous for small keys already. Engel coefficients compress the torsion data even further. Public keys land between about 1.1 and 16.9 kilobits. The arithmetic stays local with fixed-precision p-adic operations. A SIDH-style key encapsulation mechanism is built and proven out. Closure and isomorphism properties of Engel arithmetic are established. An ESP32 chip ran the full implementation for validation. Latency scaled linearly with message size as designed. Doubling clock speed cut encryption time by about half. Security rests on the supersingular isogeny decisional problem. A new Engel inversion problem adds quantum resistance.
arxiv-2511-20733:
Ali Madad builds in 2025 a pass-or-fail gate for AI systems that form caregiving-style relationships with users, where risks build over weeks of conversation. Single-turn safety tests cannot see those slow harms. InvisibleBench runs conversations of 3 to more than 20 turns and scores five dimensions: memory, safety, compliance, trauma-informed design, and belonging and cultural fitness. Certain failures end the test instantly, including missing a crisis, giving medical advice barred by Illinois's WOPR Act, or engineering emotional attachment.

Madad ran four frontier models through 17 scenarios, 68 conversations, across three complexity tiers. Every model showed critical safety gaps: crisis detection ranged only from 11.8 to 44.8 percent across the field, a spread Madad cites when urging fixed, rule-based crisis routing in production. DeepSeek Chat v3 scored highest overall at 75.9 percent, while GPT-4o Mini led on compliance at 88.2 percent and Claude Sonnet 4.5 detected crises best at 44.8 percent, still under half.
arxiv-2511-20833:
Ruyi Liu and colleagues propose in 2025 a calibrated Bayesian method for cluster-randomized trials, where whole groups, not individuals, get assigned to treatment. Standard Bayesian models report a treatment effect tied to the model itself, which can mislead when the model is wrong or group sizes carry information. Liu's procedure instead targets two plain quantities: the average effect per cluster and the average effect per individual. A calibration step then adjusts the summary so its intervals keep their promised coverage.

In simulations, the calibrated estimators showed negligible bias and hit nominal coverage where the model held. They stayed robust when the working model was misspecified, a setting where plain mixed models broke down. The paper also tests covariate adjustment and flexible tree-based models as working models. The aim is trial analysis whose conclusions survive imperfect assumptions.
arxiv-2511-20933:
Mootez Saad and colleagues probe in 2025 whether code language models truly grasp two pillars of software design. The pillars are cohesion, how well a module's parts belong together, and coupling, how strongly modules depend on each other. They generated flawed code fragments and tested DeepSeek-R1 models at 14, 32, and 70 billion parameters. Tasks ranged from verification to guided completion to open-ended analysis, with distractor elements injected as noise.

In ideal conditions the models looked solid: the 70B version scored an F1 of 0.899 on coupling and 0.825 on cohesion. Under noise and open-ended demands, coupling reasoning collapsed, with F1 scores dropping by over 50 percent in the hardest settings. Cohesion analysis resisted noise in guided tasks but also failed once guidance vanished. Reasoning traces showed shortcut-taking on coupling versus exhaustive but still failing analysis on cohesion. The models can assist with design review, but not reason alone in messy codebases.
arxiv-2511-21233:
Luca O. Trinchão and colleagues present in 2025 a way to measure how light modes overlap inside coupled microresonators, tiny rings that trap light and amplify nonlinear effects. When rings sit close together, their modes hybridise into supermodes spread across the chain, and the strength of nonlinear interactions depends on how much those supermodes overlap in space. That overlap was hard to measure, especially for longer chains.

Their pump-probe setup sends an intensity-modulated pump laser, at about 1546 nanometres and tuned to one supermode, into a three-ring device. Through Kerr and thermal cross-phase modulation, the pump imprints its pattern on a probe beam near 1542 nanometres, revealing it. Measured quality factors were 350,000 for the symmetric and antisymmetric supermodes and 200,000 for the centre mode. The experimental overlaps agreed well with theory. The authors note the technique generalises to more complex multimode systems, where unmeasured overlaps can cap efficiency.
arxiv-2511-21433:
Nicolas Crampé, Loïc Poulain d'Andecy, and Luc Vinet reveal a single algebraic origin for a whole zoo of special polynomials in 2025. The Askey scheme organizes dozens of polynomial families, Hahn, Racah, Krawtchouk, and their q-deformed cousins, used across physics and combinatorics. Clebsch-Gordan coefficients, the change-of-basis numbers that appear when two representations of an algebra combine, were already known to produce the dual Hahn family from the Lie algebra sl2.

Crampé and his coauthors reverse the viewpoint: every finite-dimensional family in the Askey scheme arises as Clebsch-Gordan coefficients of some algebra with a chosen coproduct, the rule for combining systems. Hahn polynomials come from the oscillator algebra, with Krawtchouk reached by a limit. Dual Hahn and Racah polynomials need sl2 with a generalized coproduct, and the q-versions attach to a q-deformed oscillator algebra and the quantum group Uq of sl2.
arxiv-2511-21733:
Dayan Pan and five coauthors propose RoSA, a fine-tuning method that spends its small trainable budget where a model actually needs it, in 2025. Full fine-tuning of large language models is prohibitively expensive, so parameter-efficient methods update only a fraction of weights. Existing methods, though, treat all components and layers as equally worth updating.

RoSA starts from an observation about rotary position embeddings, the mechanism that encodes word order in attention. These embeddings spark strong activations in low-frequency dimensions of attention states. The method's first module selectively boosts exactly those components. Its second piece, Dynamic Layer Selection, ranks layers by gradient norms and updates only the most critical ones. Tested on fifteen commonsense and arithmetic benchmarks, RoSA outperformed mainstream parameter-efficient methods given comparable trainable parameter counts. The authors release their code for reproducibility.
arxiv-2512-00133:
Designing soft, flexible structures that touch and press against themselves is a hard simulation problem. Andreas Henrik Frederiksen, Ole Sigmund, and Federico Ferrari present a Matlab code for it in 2025. The code handles analysis and topology optimization of hyperelastic structures, including contact.

Contact is modeled with the Third Medium Contact approach, which fills the void space with a weak dummy material. A regularization method limits skew distortion in the void regions, helping the nonlinear solver converge. Engineers get a documented, reusable code for optimizing rubber-like structures whose parts meet during use. Publishing the code itself, not just results, lets other groups build on it directly. That openness speeds up a niche but growing corner of computational mechanics.
arxiv-2512-00233:
Breaking a graph into its dense cores reveals cohesive groups and central nodes. Davide Rucci and co-authors investigate parallel k-core decomposition in a 2025 study, implemented as a Rust library. Sequential algorithms exist, but modern networks are too large for one processor.

The library is built for multicore and distributed use on large graphs. Core decomposition helps analysts assess node centrality and find tightly knit substructures in social, web, and infrastructure networks. A fast, shared implementation gives researchers a practical tool for graphs that no longer fit comfortably in a single machine's workflow. Rust's speed and safety guarantees suit a library meant for heavy graph workloads. Core decomposition is also a preprocessing step for many community detection methods.
arxiv-2512-00733:
Ho-Lin Chen and Pin-Ju Huang wrote a 2025 paper in game theory and scheduling. Factories and computing jobs often move through a fixed chain of stages, each on its own machine. When each job is run by a self-interested owner, choices at one stage affect everyone else.

The price of anarchy measures how much total performance is lost to such selfish play, compared with a perfect central plan. Chen and Huang extend that measure from single-stage scheduling games to the multi-stage case. Their results help show when pipelines and workflows can run themselves fairly well, and when rules or payments are needed.
arxiv-2512-00933:
Ginés Pérez Teruel wrote a 2025 paper on rules that may limit quantum gravity ideas. Many approaches to quantum gravity change the dispersion relation, the link between a particle's energy and momentum. These modified relations often take shapes that effective field theory, the usual low-energy framework, cannot easily handle.

Examples include logarithmic, exponential, and trigonometric forms from causal set theory, nonlocal gravity, and related models. Loop quantum gravity adds its own corrections of several kinds. Pérez Teruel uses a geometric framework to place constraints on such relations. Bounds like these help sort which quantum gravity proposals stay consistent.
arxiv-2512-01233:
Pratham Gupta, Aditya Gabani, Connor Nelson, and Yan Shoshitaishvili present the CTF Archive in a 2025 computing education paper. Capture the Flag competitions are a powerful hands-on approach in cybersecurity education, blending many concepts into interactive hacking challenges. Students learn by attacking and defending real systems.

The events are short, usually one to two days, and their infrastructure vanishes afterward. That ephemerality blocks sustained learning from a rich resource. The archive aims to capture, curate, and keep CTF challenges usable forever. Preserved challenges could let classes practice on real competition material long after the event ends.
arxiv-2512-01433:
Tristan Stevens and co-authors present a toolbox for smart ultrasound imaging. Ultrasound is cheap, safe, and live, so clinics use it a lot. It serves in pregnancy, heart, and belly care. Its images can be grainy and hard to read, though.

The toolbox, called zea, helps teams build new imaging methods. It supports work that thinks about how sound forms an image. Users can test ideas fast and share code. Open tools like this speed up trials of clearer, smarter scans that could help staff find disease sooner. Open code and docs come with the release, so teams can test the toolbox on their own scanners and probe types right away.
arxiv-2512-01733:
Heyang Li, Anthony Lin, and Domagoj Vrgoc add constraints to path queries over graphs. Path queries find routes that match a pattern. Constraints let users bound values along the route. Those values may range over an infinite domain, which makes checks hard.

Their language extends regular path queries with SMT constraints. Equality and linear real arithmetic bounds are supported. Users can ask for routes whose data obeys numeric rules. Such queries serve fraud hunts and network audits where both shape and values matter at once. SMT solvers do the heavy checks behind the scenes, so query writers state rules plainly while the engine proves each route fits.
arxiv-2512-02333:
Data in the real world will not sit still: tastes shift, sensors age, and yesterday's model quietly rots, a problem called concept drift. Wenzhang Du proposes in 2025 an online learning method that fights drift with a retrieval-augmented memory instead of forgetting the past or waiting for alarms.

Classical fixes slide a window over recent data or fade old examples, discarding patterns that later return, while drift detectors are fragile and often react late. A memory that can retrieve relevant old patterns when they recur promises steadier adaptation. The approach targets any streaming task, from recommendations to monitoring, where change is the norm.
arxiv-2512-02433:
A beam of charged bits has an edge, the outline of the bunch. That edge can go unstable in ways ruled by many linked laws. Ji Qiang studies this 3D edge instability in 2025. He uses automatic differentiation to pull fine facts out of his runs.

The full set of laws runs to twenty-one linked equations. No hand work can track how each knob steers the whole. But the code itself can yield exact rates of change for each knob. With those in hand, designers can see which knobs drive the wobble. Then they can shape the machine so strong beams hold their form.
arxiv-2512-02733:
Heavy neutral leptons, also called heavy sterile neutrinos, might hide in decays of B mesons and tau leptons. Modern flavor experiments can search for final states that include such a heavy neutrino. A joint study with the Belle II experiment sets constraints on one such decay channel.

The review also covers the theory status of how these heavy neutrinos themselves decay. Rates must be known well before a search can claim discovery or exclusion. Sharper predictions, including new quantum chromodynamics corrections, help experiments worldwide hunt for these possible new particles. Each rate set in print saves the next search team months of work when they plan where to point their gear.
arxiv-2512-03033:
Random tilings of a diamond shape show sudden order. Maurice Duits and Roger Van Peski introduce a new random version in this 2025 work. They place random weights, drawn from Gamma variables, on the edges of the Aztec diamond graph.

From those weights they study the random dimer measures, which describe pairing patterns. They prove there is no phase transition at the level of free energy. They prove several other results about the measures too. Such models help mathematicians understand how large random systems form patterns. Random dimer patterns model crystal surfaces, so their phases matter beyond pure math.
arxiv-2512-03133:
Dark matter may have frozen out of the hot early universe. Dan Hooper, Gordan Krnjaic, Tanner Trickle, and Isaac Wang survey that idea in this 2025 work. Freeze-out can set the amount of dark matter left today in a natural way.

The authors study many pairs of dark matter and mediator particles. The mediator links dark matter to quarks, the building blocks of normal matter. Their survey works like an encyclopedia of options that can fit the observed amount. It helps theorists see which models remain worth testing in labs. Model builders can scan the survey for gaps where no viable freeze-out pair exists.
arxiv-2512-03333:
Rebuilding a quantum state from few measures is a prized skill. Xun Tang, Haoxuan Chen, Yuehaw Khoo, and Lexing Ying present Sketch Tomography in this 2025 work. It builds on the classical shadow protocol used to estimate quantum observables.

Their procedure targets states that are matrix product states, a compact form common in one-dimensional systems. Combining shadows with that structure makes tomography efficient. Efficient state checks help verify quantum computers and simulators. They also reduce the lab time needed to certify devices. Matrix product structure keeps the method light enough for near-term quantum hardware.
arxiv-2512-03433:
The brightest quasars in the young universe deserve X-ray views. Xiangyu Jin and a large team present a deep Chandra survey in this 2025 work. They observed seven luminous quasars at very high redshift with the Chandra telescope.

Combined with archive data, the survey nearly completes X-ray coverage of known bright quasars at that era. X-rays reveal how fast their black holes feed and how much energy they emit. A complete sample avoids cherry-picking bright outliers. It gives a fair picture of black hole growth at cosmic dawn. Complete samples let scholars measure black hole feeding without brightness selection bias.
arxiv-2512-03533:
Outflows from a bright quasar carry several components at once. Misaki Mizumoto and a large team resolve those components in this 2025 work. They study PG 1211+143, a luminous nearby quasar shining near its Eddington limit.

Using the XRISM mission, they took the first high-resolution X-ray spectra of its iron absorption structure. Their aim is to characterize ultra-fast outflow features, a forest of them. Fast outflows can shape a galaxy by pushing gas out. This is the first paper in a planned series. A forest of absorption lines suggests many outflow speeds, each tracing a shell of gas leaving the quasar at a different rate.
arxiv-2512-04333:
Shreyas Shende and seven co-authors built a tool that hunts for gene markers of cancer in RNA data, aiming at earlier detection. Finding cancer early lifts survival odds, but RNA data carry thousands of gene readings at once. Plain statistics often miss the web of links between genes. Their 2025 arXiv paper joins feature choice and diagnosis in one pipeline.

The tool, called RGE-GCN, first builds a graph from gene activity profiles. A graph neural network then sorts samples into cancer and normal groups. A scoring method flags the genes that drive each call. The pipeline then drops the weakest genes and repeats, shrinking the set step by step. What remains is a compact marker set that stays accurate and easy to read. Tests covered made-up data plus real lung, kidney, and cervical cancer cohorts.
arxiv-2512-04533:
Haomiao Huang, Xuan Fang, Jorge Garcia-Rojas, and co-authors report deep spectra of three glowing gas clouds where two ways of weighing the elements refuse to agree. Planetary nebulae are shells shed by dying stars. One method reads abundances from bright collisionally excited lines; another reads faint recombination lines. The second often gives far higher values, a puzzle called the abundance discrepancy. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies three extreme cases with the Very Large Telescope.

The UVES spectrograph split each nebula's light into hundreds of emission lines, each carefully calibrated. Temperatures from the bright lines ran hotter than those from hydrogen jumps. Temperatures from oxygen and nitrogen recombination lines fell strikingly low, below two thousand kelvin. That cold reading points to hidden cold pockets inside the nebulae. The abundance gap may come from those pockets, which bright-line tools miss.
arxiv-2512-04633:
Katherina von Dichter and Mia Runge map exactly which values the diameter-to-width ratio can take for a class of flat shapes. The shapes are planar pseudo-complete sets: bodies whose width stays the same in every direction, measured against their longest span. Minkowski asymmetry gauges how far a centered shape sits from being mirror-symmetric. Their 2025 arXiv paper describes the full region of possible ratios as that asymmetry varies.

The route runs through containment inequalities between two derived bodies: the overlap of a shape with its mirror, and the averaged difference body. A factor the authors define measures the smallest rescaling that lets one body cover the other. They pin down that factor's full range in the plane, again as a function of asymmetry. Complete maps like this close off guesswork in convex geometry and feed work on shape covering and packing.
arxiv-2512-04833:
Benjamin Fritz and Waqquas Bukhsh build a way to explain power grid decisions by answering a pointed question: why was this generator not dispatched? Grid operators solve hard optimization problems to set output across plants, yet the reasons stay buried in the math. In markets, that opacity breeds distrust among participants. Their 2025 arXiv paper borrows counterfactual explanations, which find the smallest change to the inputs that would have flipped the answer.

The method covers two core problems: DC optimal power flow and unit commitment. For the first, demand patterns across places serve as the adjustable inputs. For the second, demand over time takes that role. Each explanation separates the real case from a near twin where the generator does run. Users can then see which differences truly drove the decision. Transparent dispatch reasons could help regulators, traders, and plant owners trust market outcomes.
arxiv-2512-04933:
Mathias Sonnleitner computes the next term in the growth of the volumes of Schatten balls, the unit balls of matrix spaces measured by singular-value norms. These volumes are known exactly only for two exponent values. For all others, even the leading growth was the frontier. His 2025 arXiv paper expands the logarithm of the volume one order deeper for general exponents above one.

The proof borrows asymptotics for the partition function of beta-ensembles, random matrix models solved by Leblé and Serfaty. In the complex case, the expansion runs one step finer still, to constant order, for every exponent from one upward. A parallel team reached part of the range independently at the same time. Such volume laws feed random matrix theory, quantum information, and the geometry of high-dimensional data, where how much room matrices have shapes what is typical.
arxiv-2512-05033:
Monishwaran Maheswaran and ten co-authors present Arbitrage, a way to make reasoning language models answer faster without getting dumber. The standard trick pairs a small, quick draft model with a large, careful one: the small model proposes, and the large one checks. Checking word by word rejects good steps over trivial mismatches, while checking whole steps wastes the large model's time redoing rejects that barely improve on what was drafted.

Arbitrage routes each step by predicted advantage. A lightweight router learns to guess when the big model would produce a meaningfully better step, and only then is the step sent its way. The router mimics an ideal judge that always picks the stronger draft. Across standard math reasoning tests, the method beat earlier step-level schemes and cut waiting time by up to about half at the same accuracy. It offers a practical route to cheaper, quicker machine reasoning.
arxiv-2512-05233: Berk Ceylan studies two ways of measuring distance on a surface: the intrinsic metric, which follows paths inside the surface, and the extrinsic one, which cuts straight through the surrounding space. Their ratio shows how much a surface folds back on itself. For certain surfaces inside the unit ball, he proves the ratio's maximum is bounded below by a quantity set by the area, so enough area forces sharp folding somewhere. Examples then show no such global bound holds in general.
arxiv-2512-05533:
Theocharis Tavantzis, Stefano Lambiase, Daniel Russo, and Robert Feldt argue that adopting AI in organizations is a behavioural problem dressed as a technical one. Prior work notes the human factors but stays technical, leaving team change and trust unexamined. The authors build a human-centric framework from organizational change literature and talks. It is organized into nine parts — from strategy design and evaluation to collaboration, governance, leadership, culture, and upskilling. Each part comes with concrete design principles and actions.

People working in the field then rated the framework: a survey of over a hundred respondents and two expert workshops. Upskilling and strategy design drew the highest perceived importance. The pattern is telling: firms now invest in the procedural elements of adoption while the human-centred guardrails lag behind. Workshop feedback backed the point. The framework is offered as a plain roadmap for the socio-technical complexity of AI adoption.
arxiv-2512-05633: Alex Citkin's paper sits in mathematical logic, where intermediate logics meet the algebra of Heyting algebras. Some of these logics are structurally complete: every rule that holds in all their models can already be derived inside the logic. The hereditary form is stronger, since the property must pass to every sublogic. On the algebra side, the same question asks whether a variety of Heyting algebras is primitive. Citkin gives an algebraic proof of the known test for when this hereditary property holds.
arxiv-2512-05933:
Xuanru Zhou, Jiachen Lian, Henry Hong, Xinyi Yang, and Gopala Anumanchipalli argue that speech understanding should show its reasoning, not hide it in one black box. Today's speech models bolt an encoder onto a language model. They grasp what was said, but reason weakly about the rest. The authors split the system into modules, tied together by a world model of latent states.

Speech understanding is factorized into four modules that pass messages along a causal graph, together defining a space of cognitive states to search. Search traces guide a language model that writes the causal analysis and the response. Because the graph is explicit, users can stage counterfactual interventions: change one factor and watch the conclusion move. The paper presents the design as a path toward speech systems that are transparent and controllable, able to explain how the hearing led where it did.
arxiv-2512-06133:
Melone Nyoba Tchonkeu, Soulaimane Berkane, and Tarek Hamel design an estimator that lets a drone know its speed through the air and its full heading when satellite navigation is gone. The aircraft navigates from an inertial unit, a pitot tube, a barometer, and a magnetometer. Whether those sensors suffice is not obvious; some motions may leave the state invisible to them.

An observability analysis establishes when the state is uniformly observable. A nonlinear observer fuses all the sensors in one framework. Simulations confirm robust convergence. Such observers are the mathematics of not getting lost.
arxiv-2512-06233:
Kai Qi, Qingzhi Zou, and Ignacio Pagonabarraga set out a recipe for measuring how tiny swimmers change the fluids they move through. Microbes swim in gels and mucus, not plain water, and their strokes bend the polymers around them. Those bends feed back on the swimmer, yet labs have lacked a shared way to measure that response.

Their recipe maps a swimmer's push onto a standard lab test in which a plate shakes a fluid back and forth. Swim speed and push become the shake rate and shake size of the plate test. Standard tools can then read out how stiff or runny the fluid acts. Computer simulations of a model swimmer in a polymer mix back the recipe up. It gives labs a common yardstick for active fluids, from microbe studies to new soft materials.
arxiv-2512-06333:
Roberto Onofrio, Alexander Smith, and Lorenza Viola propose a fresh way to test one of the base rules of physics: that all things fall alike. The weak equivalence rule says gravity pulls on every test mass in the same way, no matter what it is made of. Past tests used plain matter. This team asks how the rule fares when the test mass sits in a blend of energy states, which labs can now prepare.

Their model treats mass as a quantum quantity, and works out what a torsion balance should register. They show that both the average twist and its spread carry the signal of any breach, in a way that resists shot to shot noise. Since such blends fade fast, they also design a version with a shifting gravity field. The study maps a path to a new kind of gravity test.
arxiv-2512-06433:
Ziyang Xin, Zhaoli Guo, and Hudong Chen refine a kinetic model of turbulence, the chaotic swirling in fluid flow. Rather than track only big averaged quantities, kinetic theory follows the spread of particle speeds, which naturally captures effects that standard models miss. A recent model of this kind covered open flows without walls. Real flows, though, run past walls in pipes, wings, and engines, where behavior near the surface is crucial.

The authors rework the model's relaxation time so its flow traits line up better with established turbulence theory. Step by step expansion recovers the classic simple closure at first order, and richer nonlinear closures at second order, including a new formula for turbulent energy flux. They also add wall damping and surface rules so the model handles wall bounded flows, resolving the thin layer near the wall or using a wall function where fitting.
arxiv-2512-06833: Alex Degtyarev works in algebraic geometry on K3 surfaces, a special class of smooth shapes at the center of much modern geometry. Degtyarev looks at these surfaces over the real numbers and cuts them with flat hyperplanes. Some cuts break apart entirely into straight lines, and the question is how many such split cuts one surface can have. The paper sets upper limits on that count, shown in most cases to be the best possible. Most limits match the known complex-number results.
arxiv-2512-06933:
Zifan Peng and co-authors study why people approve Ethereum transactions they do not understand, a habit known as blind signing. Interviews with sixteen Web3 users showed what good explanations need: clear structure, warnings about risk, and detail down to each token movement. From those lessons the team defines a new task, TxSum, and builds a data set of complex transactions with flow-level notes and plain summaries.

Their system, MATEX, explains a transaction using several cooperating agents. It fetches outside knowledge only when unsure, then audits its own explanation against the raw transaction record to keep facts straight. In tests, MATEX gave the best overall explanations, strongest on fine detail and true intent. Users grasped complex transactions far better with its help. They also rejected malicious transactions far more often, while rarely turning away honest ones.
arxiv-2512-07333:
Oche D Ankeli and Marvin M Ogore present IyaCare, a proof-of-concept platform for maternal care where mothers die at the world's highest rates. In Sub-Saharan Africa the burden is severe. Digital health tools usually arrive one at a time: a prediction app here, a monitoring gadget there, records somewhere else. IyaCare converges three technologies into one system designed for scarce resources: risk prediction, continuous vital sign monitoring through connected devices, and health records secured on a blockchain.

The build pairs a web front end with a cloud back end, an Ethereum ledger for record integrity, and gradient boosting models trained on maternal health data. In feasibility testing the risk model flagged high-risk pregnancies with solid accuracy, and the ledger's integrity checks passed.
arxiv-2512-07433:
Yezi Liu and Mohsen Imani wrote this 2025 computing paper with William Youngwoo Chung, Yang Ni, and Hanning Chen. Their topic is fairness in graph hyperdimensional computing, a brain-like method that works with very long vectors. Such systems run fast and resist noise, yet nobody had checked whether they treat groups fairly.

The authors show how the way data is encoded can pass bias along or even grow it. A classifier that matches new items to stored class vectors can widen gaps between groups. To fight this, they build a training method called FairGHDC. It adds a fairness check based on demographic parity into the training loop itself. The fix works inside the vector space, with no change to the graph encoder and no backpropagation. On six test datasets it cuts fairness gaps sharply while keeping accuracy close to rival neural methods. It also trains far faster on graphics hardware.
arxiv-2512-07533:
Yuzhou Nie, Hongwei Li, Chengquan Guo, and five co-authors wrote this 2025 computer security paper. Finding flaws in code is slow work, and pattern matching tools miss deep bugs. The authors argue a model should reason about program states instead.

Their model, VulnLLM-R, is the first reasoning language model built just for this task. Reasoning, they say, helps the model generalize and blocks shortcut learning. Their training recipe selects data with care and generates worked reasoning examples. It then filters and corrects those examples before the final tuning stage. The finished model is modest in size beside giant closed rivals. Across datasets in Python, C, C++, and Java, it beats static analysis tools and large reasoning models. An agent scaffold built around it outperforms famous tools on real projects. The agent even found zero-day flaws in actively maintained code.
arxiv-2512-07633:
Eleftherios Politis, Antonis Tsapalis, and Fotios Diakonos wrote this 2025 physics paper on the hottest matter known. Quark-gluon plasma filled the early universe and is recreated briefly in colliders. The authors model how it cools and changes character with temperature.

Their tool combines a new quasi-particle model for gluons with a simple gas of quarks. Three quark flavours enter, matching the setup of large lattice simulations. The fermion masses are allowed to drift with temperature in the model. Above a critical temperature, the quark mass must plunge to fit the lattice energy data. That plunge marks the restoration of chiral symmetry in the system. A second signal moves in step: the gluon variance collapses across the transition. At high heat, the model's gluons behave like those of perturbative theory. Deconfinement and chiral restoration, the model suggests, are deeply interrelated.
arxiv-2512-07833:
Thao Nguyen and eight co-authors wrote this 2025 computer vision paper on a kind of similarity machines miss. People see not only matching traits but matching relations between things. An apple resembles a peach by color; Earth resembles a peach by layered structure.

Crust, mantle, and core map onto skin, flesh, and pit in that example. Popular metrics like LPIPS, CLIP, and DINO capture surface traits only. The authors define relational similarity as a measurable problem in its own right. Two images count as similar when their internal relations correspond, whatever their looks. They build a large dataset of images with anonymized captions. Those captions describe the scene's relational logic, not its visible content. A vision-language model is then fine-tuned on that material. It learns to pull relationally alike images closer in representation space. Existing models, they show, fail at this deeply human skill.
arxiv-2512-08033:
George G Pavlov, Vadim Abramkin, and B Posselt, astrophysicists, posted an observational study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is an isolated neutron star known as RX J2143.0 plus 0654, observed with the Hubble Space Telescope. They measured its spectrum from the ultraviolet through the near infrared, and combined it with X ray data taken at the same time.

A joint fit uses two blackbody components plus a power law for the optical light. The colder component dominates the ultraviolet, while a hotter, smaller region explains part of the X ray emission, matching earlier X ray work. Near infrared images may show faint extended emission around the star. Comparing positions fourteen years apart gives a slow proper motion across the sky. That motion fits the idea that the neutron star was born near the solar system about half a million years ago.
arxiv-2512-08133:
Mitchell Creelman, Kiran Jain, Niles Oien, John Britanik, and Thomas M Wentzel, solar physicists at the National Solar Observatory, posted a technical report on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is the observatory farside mapping pipeline, which tracks active regions on the far side of the Sun. Those regions are invisible from Earth, yet they matter for space weather forecasts that protect communications and other infrastructure.

The pipeline uses helioseismic holography on steady Doppler images of the visible face, reading the acoustic signatures of hidden regions. Data comes from the GONG network of telescopes. This report outlines noise reduction updates made to the pipeline. The changes produced more accurate and more consistent farside maps of active region size and location. Better maps strengthen both day to day forecasting and research use. The authors note that global helioseismic monitoring is still a young field, with methods and reliability still improving.
arxiv-2512-08233:
Timothy Chen, Marcus Dominguez Kuhne, and colleagues, roboticists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about teaching robots a human sense of risk. People judge risk as a graded feeling, not a simple safe or unsafe label. The team wants robots to learn that graded judgment from watching humans act safely.

Their framework builds risk maps with meaning built in, using a Bayesian recipe. A pretrained vision language model supplies a common sense prior about what looks risky. A learned vision transformer then adjusts that prior into pixel level risk values for a queried object. The output is a dense risk image that can guide robot planning or lift into three dimensions for path optimization. Because the model is Bayesian, new observations or rules update it fast. Tests show the maps line up with human preferences, and demos use them in real planning pipelines.
arxiv-2512-08433:
Michael Stefszky, Kai Hong Luo, Jan Lucas Eickmann, and a large team of quantum optics researchers in Germany posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They introduce the Paderborn Quantum Sampler, a platform for boson sampling, a photonic task proposed as a route to quantum advantage. The catch they address: many large experiments swapped hard to make single photons for easier Gaussian light, quietly giving up the non Gaussian resource that makes the task hard classically.

Their sampler runs eight different input states, Gaussian and non Gaussian, through one interferometer in a single run, so regimes can be compared side by side under identical conditions. A semi device independent test certifies that no classical model could fake the data, without trusting prior knowledge of the device. Applying that test, they observed clear performance gains from the non Gaussian inputs.
arxiv-2512-08633:
Chris Lambie Hanson and Pedro Marun continue work on higher dimensional walks on ordinals, a topic in set theory started recently by Bergfalk. Walks are a method to move between ordinals and extract functions that reveal structure. The authors look for natural coherence conditions on higher dimensional sequences that force the resulting higher rho functions to be coherent as well.

They also introduce higher square principles by adding nontriviality demands to those coherent sequences, and they study basic properties of the new principles. As in the classic case, the principles are shown to hold widely in the constructible universe, yet they can be forced to fail when large cardinals are assumed. Certain rho functions from square sequences are also shown to be nontrivial, which yields non vanishing cohomology groups for the cardinal with its order topology.
arxiv-2512-08733:
Kuniko Paxton and coauthors address fairness in skin lesion classification at the level of the individual person, not just broad groups. Fairness work in medical imaging often sorts skin tone into coarse categories. That grouping can hide bias faced by people who are outliers inside their own group.

The study treats skin tone as a continuous trait and models its distribution with density estimation. The team compares many statistical distance measures for gaps between tone distributions. They then propose a reweighting loss that corrects under representation of rare tones during training. Tests across convolutional and transformer models show that category based reweighting misses individual level gaps. Distribution based reweighting performs better, with several distance measures standing out. The method may also help for other continuous sensitive traits in medical imaging.
arxiv-2512-08833:
Jean Christoph Jung, Patrick Koopmann, and Matthias Knorr review interpolation in knowledge representation, a topic with many practical uses. Interpolation helps with explainability, forgetting irrelevant detail, splitting systems into modules, reuse, and even learning. Meanwhile, many formalisms used for knowledge representation do not support interpolation in general, and computing interpolants in practice is hard.

The authors focus on two prominent formalisms: description logics and logic programming. For each, they discuss what theory says about Craig interpolation and uniform interpolation, and what methods exist to compute interpolants when they are available. The review maps both the limits and the workable paths. Readers who build knowledge based systems get a clear picture of when interpolation can be relied on and how to obtain it, as well as where open difficulty remains.
arxiv-2512-08933:
Lixiang Yan and coauthors study how artificial intelligence agents, acting as undercover teammates, shape collaborative learning in student groups. Such agents are now placed in learning settings, yet their effect on how groups build knowledge through argument is not well understood. Theory suggests these agents have bounded autonomy and can act as participants, not just tools.

The study analyzes discussion data from just over two hundred human participants and several dozen agent participants. The groups worked in triads on a reasoning problem. Agents were given either supportive or confrontational personas. A four part method tracks participation, reasoning quality, argument structure, and social modes of knowledge construction. Supportive agents promoted participation and shared understanding, while confrontational agents provoked critical thinking and debate through conflict. Participation stayed balanced in both cases. Learning gains were predicted by the quality of reasoning, not by how much was said.
arxiv-2512-09133:
Swadeepan Nanda and Pavan Hosur study how tilt affects transport and spectra of two dimensional Dirac fermions under disorder. Dirac fermions appear across condensed matter, from topological phases to quantum critical points. In semimetals the cone is often tilted.

Spectral analysis always matches the expected random matrix ensembles, which suggests delocalization. Conductivity scaling tells a richer story. For a single Dirac node, conductivity grows with the log of system size, with a tilt dependent coefficient that spikes at the boundary between two cone regimes when tilt and transport align. For two nodes with time reversal symmetry, scaling follows a power law with log corrections. Tilt along transport can flip the sign of the exponent, hinting at a localization transition, while tilt across transport always implies localization. That tension between spectral and transport views is a central finding.
arxiv-2512-09233:
Alan T. Sherman leads a team auditing SecureDNA, a system that lets DNA synthesis machines screen orders against a database of biological hazards. The system uses new cryptography so that neither the customer's order nor the hazard list is revealed. The authors examined its design, engineering, and code, and formally checked its key protocols.

Their main finding is a structural flaw that needs no broken cryptography. The system's custom authentication protocol, SCEP, authenticates only one way: the hazard database and key servers never learn who is talking to them. That weakness breaks defense in depth and could let an attacker dodge the rate limits that protect the hazard list, if a synthesizer connects to a corrupted server. The team also found weak bindings that could let responses inside a secure channel be swapped under some conditions. They proposed fixes, and the repaired protocol, SCEP+, shipped in a later software version.
arxiv-2512-09633:
Senem Aktas and colleagues benchmark a new generation of video object trackers on fast moving objects, a known weak spot. Several recent tracking pipelines extend the Segment Anything Model 2, following and segmenting an object from a single example template the user marks on an opening frame. These trackers post strong results on standard datasets, which may hide their behavior when objects move extremely fast.

The FMOX evaluation puts four systems, the original SAM2 plus EfficientTAM, DAM4SAM, and SAMURAI, on datasets built specifically around fast moving objects. The goal is a detailed picture of current limitations rather than a single leaderboard number. The authors analyze how each tracker behaves across the challenging sequences. Overall, DAM4SAM and SAMURAI handled the demanding material best. The study is offered as guidance on where SAM2-based tracking still fails and where its extensions genuinely help.
arxiv-2512-09933:
Molla Basir Ahamed and Sabir Ahammed prove Bohr type theorems in the world of octonions. Bohr's classical theorem bounds how the coefficients of a bounded analytic function can behave. Here the functions are slice regular, the right notion of well behaved for octonions, the largest alternative division algebra. They live on the open unit ball and stay bounded by one in absolute value. The authors first establish Bohr's theorem for the Cesáro operator acting on these functions. They then treat the Bernardi operator.

From the Bernardi result they derive Bohr type inequalities for the Libera and Alexander operators. Finally, they obtain similar inequalities for certain integral transforms of these functions, namely discrete Fourier and discrete Laplace transforms. Every result is proved sharp, meaning the constants cannot be improved. The paper extends a century old circle of ideas from ordinary complex analysis into noncommutative, nonassociative territory.
arxiv-2512-10133:
Gabriel F. A. Bastos and Jugurta Montalvão estimate Shannon entropy when data are scarce. Entropy measures uncertainty or information content, and many applications must estimate it from samples smaller than the number of possible outcomes. In that undersampled regime, naive estimators are biased downward: unseen outcomes and their missing probability mass are simply ignored. The authors' estimator exploits the decomposability of entropy, splitting the problem into pieces. It then compensates for the bias by estimating the missing mass and the number of unseen outcomes explicitly.

Experiments show the method beats classical estimators in undersampled regimes. It also performs comparably with well established state of the art estimators, a strong result for a principled, transparent construction. The manuscript is short, six pages, and was accepted at an international conference on artificial intelligence and data sciences.
arxiv-2512-10333:
A team led by Shaima Farhana studies how artificial intelligence adoption affects industrial firms in two contrasting economies, Yemen and Saudi Arabia. Their scheme extends the classic technology organization environment model with AI as a named force. The question is lasting performance: can AI improve factory results and environmental outcomes together, in a fragile economy and in a fast changing one? Data come from field surveys returned by managers at hundreds of small and medium firms across both countries. The authors analyze the responses statistically, with partial least squares modeling.

The scheme shows strong positive effects on both fronts. Workplace results themselves mediate the link to environmental gains. Context changes the mechanism. Saudi firms benefit through state support and advanced technology. Yemeni firms lean on low cost adoption and nimble organization to work around structural constraints.
arxiv-2512-10433:
Hojun Lee and co-authors address a misuse of image generators: anyone can fine-tune a text-to-image model on someone else's pictures to copy a person or style. Earlier defences mostly blurred or degraded the protected images, which is passive, unstable. And gives the owner little say in what the copied model ends up producing instead.

Their method, TAFAP, actively steers the copy toward a target concept the owner chooses. Rather than matching single snapshots of training, it aligns the whole training trajectory, borrowing ideas from dataset distillation, so the steering effect is not washed out as fine-tuning proceeds. In their tests, protected images pushed fine-tuned models toward the chosen target in both identity and visual pattern, while output quality stayed high, giving owners a checkable safeguard.
arxiv-2512-10533:
Ashutosh Tripathi and co-authors test whether time-series tools can tame messy satellite data, using the blazar 3C 371 as their case. The TESS telescope watched this bright, radio-loud active galaxy for about three hundred days, but gaps and noise threaten any search for rhythm in its flickering light. The team set out to measure variability timescales and hunt for quasi-periodic signals.

They applied power spectrum, structure-function, and wavelet methods, with autoregressive models, Bartlett periodograms. And wavelet decomposition to fight the gaps and noise, plus recurrence analysis for nonlinear behaviour. The whole run varied on a timescale of about four and a half days, with sector-by-sector values in a consistent few-day range. Some segments showed possible oscillations lasting three to six days, which the authors link to kink instabilities or mini-jets inside a precessing jet.
arxiv-2512-10733:
Vladimir Semenov shows that one oscillator with two memory loops can imitate a whole network. Networks of bistable elements with nonlocal coupling support travelling wavefronts, boundaries between the two stable states that sweep through the system. Semenov studies a single bistable oscillator with delayed feedback through two separate loops, and asks which network effects survive the compression.

The answer is: the important ones. Effects of nonlocal interaction on wavefront travel, previously identified in full networks, reappear entirely in the single delayed oscillator. Adding the second loop speeds up wavefronts, whether their motion is deterministic or noise-driven. It also stabilises fronts at lower noise levels and protects them from the noise-induced destruction that wrecks fronts in the single-delay case. Numerical simulations and physical experiments agree closely, making the little oscillator a cheap laboratory for network behaviour.
arxiv-2512-10833:
Karel Pärlin and co-authors boost a trick for hiding wireless signals in plain sight. Known-interference cancellation, paired with cooperative jamming, can give a communication link covertness and security at the physical layer. The receiver subtracts a known interfering signal to reveal the hidden one. The catch is that the desired signal itself acts as estimation noise against the canceller, capping how much interference can be removed and how much data the hidden link can carry.

Their structure adds decision feedback. Both the known interference and the signal of interest are cancelled iteratively and in succession, each pass using decoded decisions from the last to clean the other up. Measurements show the feedback version cancels the known interference more deeply and raises the useful throughput of the concealed system. The price is a higher computational load, a trade the letter quantifies for designers.
arxiv-2512-11033:
Diego Dado and co-authors question a basic assumption behind maps of dark matter in small galaxies. Astronomers usually assume the gas in a galaxy disk sits in balance, so its rotation speed reveals the gravity, and hence the dark matter, inside. Using the COLIBRE cosmological simulations, the team checked that balance directly across many low mass galaxies.

Imbalance turned out to be widespread, and rotation based speed estimates commonly carried sizable errors, worst in the inner regions that matter most for dark matter profiles. Star formation feedback, clumpy self gravitating gas, black hole energy, and lopsided gravity drove most of the disturbance. Most simulated disks would fail standard rotation analysis. The authors suggest much of the observed variety in dwarf rotation curves may reflect unsettled gas, not varied dark matter.
arxiv-2601-06633:
Zhangqi Duan, Nigel Fernandez, and Andrew Lan present KASER in 2026. KASER simulates student errors on open-ended coding tasks for education. Such tasks give detailed insights into student knowledge, they note.

Training language models to simulate student errors is challenging, though. Models often suffer mode collapse when generating plausible wrong answers. They also miss diversity in syntax, style, and solution approach. Student responses vary widely on all three of those axes. KASER is knowledge-aligned, aiming to match errors to student understanding. Better simulators could help teachers anticipate mistakes before grading piles arrive. Computing education readers get a tool for generating realistic wrong answers. That supports practice, feedback, and test design at scale.
arxiv-2601-06733:
Tamara Alshammari and Mehdi Bennis plan sense-based talk for agent teams in a 2026 paper. New 6G nets speed up self-rule, smarts, and links between machines. Big teams of agents thus gain quick, supple ways to act.

That same gain lifts the risk from shocks that can hit such teams. Shifts in the world, faults, and false tales all pose threats to them. Hostile acts by some agents add one more threat to the list. Sense-based talk, led by logic, aims to keep teams in tune through stress. To share sense, not just bits, could screen noise and lies far more. Tough teams need just that screen when the world turns rough round them. The work links talk theory with team strength in one frame for 6G.
arxiv-2601-06933: A 2026 arXiv preprint appeared in 2026. It covers application of analytic functionals to mean field theory and wilson- fisher fixed point. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The authors consider application of the analytic functional approach to the conformal field theories associated with mean field theory and Wilson-Fisher fixed point. The authors study the constraints imposed by the crossing symmetry on the coefficients of the operator product expansion. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07333: Research by Tessa Pulli and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with OSCAR. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. 6D object pose estimation plays a crucial role in scene understanding for applications such as robotics and augmented reality. To support the needs of ever-changing object sets in such context. Modern zero-shot object pose estimators were developed to not require object-specific training but only rely on CAD models. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07433:
A 2026 preprint on arXiv deals with design of optimal controls in acausal LQG problems. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. In control theory, a system which has output depending only on. The present and past values of the input is said to be causal (or nonanticipative).

Respectively, a system is acausal (or non-causal) if its output depends on future inputs as well. Overall majority of literature in stochastic control theory discusses causal systems. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07533:
Julian Schelb and colleagues present Loci Similes, a benchmark for finding echoes between Latin texts. Intertextuality research traces how one writer quotes, copies, or alludes to another. Such links help scholars rebuild the library an author drew on. The connections range from exact quotations to faint paraphrases. Their 2026 preprint supplies test data for that task.

Latin makes the search hard, because word forms change with grammar. A copied phrase may look quite different on the surface. Automated tools need a fair benchmark to show whether they truly find these links. Loci Similes gives the field shared material for comparing methods. Digital humanities scholars working on historical texts are the intended readers.
arxiv-2601-07633:
Guang Yang and a collaborator compare detector designs for tracking fine particle patterns, in a 2026 preprint. Fine-grained scintillator detectors serve precision work in nuclear and particle physics. They reconstruct interaction vertices and the directions of secondary particles. That accuracy separates signal events from background. The design choice under study is the fiber readout geometry.

Traditional two-view systems use crossing X and Y fibers. Three-view designs add a third layer of fibers at another angle. The extra view gives unambiguous three-dimensional voxel identification, the authors note. Benchmarks for both layouts show what the third view buys in practice. Detector builders weighing cost against resolution are the readers. The paper supplies performance numbers for that design decision.
arxiv-2601-07733:
Joseph L. Shomberg runs a reaction-diffusion equation backward using a physics-informed generative network. His 2026 preprint reconstructs the starting state of the Chafee-Infante equation on two-dimensional domains. The final state comes after one hundred explicit forward steps and sits near equilibrium. Boundary values are fixed by Dirichlet conditions. Reconstructing the start from such a smoothed end state is an inverse problem.

His tool is a Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty, guided by the physics of the equation. Generative networks can propose plausible starting states that fit the observed end. Physics information keeps those proposals honest. Inverse problems like this arise in heat flow, chemistry, and pattern formation. The paper speaks to scholars who blend neural networks with known equations rather than treating data alone.
arxiv-2601-07933:
Yeuk Hay Joshua Lam and Daniel Litt link a curvature test to cohomology in algebraic geometry. They study a smooth projective family of shapes over a base. Katz proved the Grothendieck-Katz p-curvature claim for the Gauss-Manin connection on cohomology in their case. The claim links p-curvature that fades at a vast range of primes to monodromy that factors through a smaller group. Their 2026 preprint works on p-curvature and non-abelian cohomology at once.

The Gauss-Manin connection tracks how the field shifts as the shape moves in its family. p-curvature measures its behavior in characteristic p. The non-abelian side extends these tools past the linear case. Progress here feeds the arithmetic of differential equations. The paper serves those in algebraic geometry and number theory. It builds on a landmark proved case to push into richer coefficients.
arxiv-2601-08633:
Victoria Bollo and co-authors present new results from the MUSE-ALMA Haloes survey. Their 2026 arXiv paper, the thirteenth in the series, studies galaxies tied to strong hydrogen absorption. The survey includes 79 galaxies associated with absorption at redshift near 0.5.

An ALMA Cycle 10 large program added observations of 39 systems. Combining MUSE optical data with ALMA radio data links galaxies to the gas around them. Absorbing gas traces the circumgalactic medium, the reservoir that feeds and receives galaxy gas. Readers in galaxy evolution get fresh evidence on how galaxies exchange matter with their surroundings at cosmic midday.
arxiv-2601-08933:
Denis Tramonte tests four forms for how push falls off with range in a galaxy cluster. A cluster is a vast swarm of galaxies held by pull. Hot gas in it pushes out, and that push shape tells us the heat state of the gas. One form is oft called the shared, or universal, form for all clusters.

He fits all four forms to new data from the ACT scope, which reads a faint shift in old space light. Forms span a curved fall, a plain power fall, and a heat based fall. A reader in cluster work gets a head to head fit test. It shows if one shared form can serve, or if each cluster needs its own shape.
arxiv-2601-09433:
David Reid and Ognjen Arandjelović ask whether transformers read ancient Roman coins better than convolutional networks. Their 2026 arXiv paper compares the two model families on coin motif recognition. Automated coin analysis could help researchers mine large collections and help collectors judge what they buy or sell.

Recent work has targeted the semantic elements shown on coins, the portraits, gods, and symbols, using convolutional neural networks. The authors test whether transformer models, now dominant in image tasks, do better on the same job. Reading motifs at scale would turn museum trays into searchable data. The comparison shows which architecture suits this niche of cultural heritage.
arxiv-2601-09633:
Sahil Mishra, Srinitish Srinivasan, Srikanta Bedathur, and Tanmoy Chakraborty grow sorted term lists without hand labor. Their 2026 arXiv paper, TaxoBell, places each term in a soft box in space and learns from the list itself. Such lists, called taxonomies, organize knowledge for catalogs, search, and medical work.

New concepts appear faster than curators can file them. A box inside a bigger box mirrors a child term under its parent term. Trained this way, TaxoBell proposes where new terms belong in the tree. Growing lists this way would keep large catalogs current without armies of editors doing the filing by hand.
arxiv-2601-09733:
Xin Gao and five co-authors treat training data as an engineering problem with a feedback loop. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses OpenDataArena to build better supervised fine-tuning datasets. Dataset construction is a critical but under-theorized stage of model post-training.

In practice, teams pile up data by heuristic rules, with little sense of what each sample adds. A data arena can score and compare samples by their effect on performance. Closing that loop means datasets get designed, not just gathered. Better data recipes would lift every model that is trained on them.
arxiv-2601-09833:
Xiaoxu Ma, Xiangbo Zhang, and Zhenyu Weng measure the personalities of language models from the inside. Their 2026 arXiv paper evaluates traits using internal activations rather than questionnaires. Trait scores from questionnaires swing with small changes in prompt wording or role-play setup.

That instability also gives little insight into why a model scores as it does. Reading activations promises steadier, more explainable measures. Knowing a model's traits helps compare systems and deploy them responsibly. An internal ruler could flag subtle shifts after fine-tuning that ordinary surveys would miss entirely in practice.
arxiv-2601-10033:
Wan Jou She and co authors built a data set of kind talk for care in Japanese. The set is named EmplifAI. It holds talks with patients who live with long term ills. Such patients feel a wide range of moods, from hope to despair.

Those moods shift as care goes on. A reply that fits one stage may miss at the next. The set tags talks with fine mood labels. It spans both bright and dark moods in its tags. Such a set can train tools that reply with care. It can also test how well a tool reads a patient's state.
arxiv-2601-10133:
Ruowei Li and Zhigang Yao fit a low dim sheet to high dim data with wild noise. Real data oft sit near a thin sheet in a large space. But noise can be large with no cap. Past fits may bend the sheet to chase noise.

The team use a curve driven fit. The sheet is smooth, with a set reach. Points are spread near flat on the sheet, then noise is added. The noise is Gauss in form but with no cap on its size. The paper asks when the true sheet can still be found. It gives terms for a sound fit in that hard case.
arxiv-2601-10333:
Florin Hemmann, Vincent Glauser, Ullrich Steiner, and Matthias Saba make random nets to order. Such nets model frames and links at many scales. Waves that cross them can shift phase, trap, spread, or block. Each act rests on the net's shape traits.

To test those acts, labs need nets with set traits on call. Hand made nets are slow to build. The team give fast code that grows nets with the traits asked. It can tune links, gaps, and spread. The tool lets labs sweep traits and watch acts change. That speeds the study of waves in such nets.
arxiv-2601-10633:
Hagen Gress and co-authors report the first tiny resonators made from a two-dimensional polyaramid. Polyaramids form sheets one molecule thick, held by strong hydrogen bonds, much like graphene's carbon sheets. The material here is called 2DPA-1. The team turned its films into vibrating membranes as thin as eight nanometers.

To build them, the team moved thin films onto chips etched with arrays of round microwells. The films span the wells and can ring like drumheads. Such resonators sense mass and force with great care. A strong, light new material for them could sharpen future sensors. The work opens a path for molecular-sheet devices in precision measurement.
arxiv-2601-10833:
Pratima Hebbar and Leonid Koralov study the front of a branching Brownian motion. Particles wander like Brownian motion and split into more particles as they go. In the supercritical case, the cloud expands with a clear front speed. Branching here is compactly supported: births happen only inside a bounded region's influence.

The authors track how particles spread near the front over long times. It is known that normalized counts in a window moving below the front speed settle down. Their work sharpens the picture of that edge zone. Front behavior governs invasions, epidemics, and reaction waves, so exact edge laws matter well beyond this model.
arxiv-2601-10933:
Yizhou Dang and co-authors tackle the long-tail problem in sequential recommendation. Sequential systems learn from each user's history of clicks and buys. Most users touch only a handful of items, while most items are rarely consumed. That imbalance starves the model of signal for both quiet users and niche items. Their fix is tail-aware data augmentation.

Augmentation creates extra training examples where data are thin. Tail-aware design adds them where the tail needs them most, not uniformly. The aim is recommendations that serve niche tastes, not just blockbuster items. The work serves platforms whose catalogs are vast but whose per-user histories are short and sparse.
arxiv-2601-11333:
Manuel Friedrich, Jose Matias, and Elvira Zappale widen a theory of deformations. Their 2026 preprint brings structured deformations to linearized elasticity. Structured deformations split motion into smooth and jump parts. Linearized elasticity is the small-strain theory of solids.

The team gives an integral form for the base energy. That form has both bulk and surface contributions. Bulk terms count strain through the body's volume. Surface terms count what happens at cracks and slips. They reach the form by two routes for safety. One is a direct global relaxation method in BD space. The other starts from nonlinear energies of nonsimple materials. Agreement of both routes strengthens the result.
arxiv-2601-11833: Anthony Joon Hur works on fast brain scan cuts for glioma, a type of brain tumour. Good cuts guide care and surgery. Deep learning gives the best cuts so far. Yet it needs big data sets or heavy machines, which many clinics lack. His method uses a Karhunen-Loève expansion to build a map of odd spots. That map flags parts that do not fit the norm. A light method could bring tumour cuts to small clinics.
arxiv-2601-12033:
Muhammad Alif Al Hakim, Alfan Farizki Wicaksono, and Fajri Koto guard fairness and safety when large models are shrunk. Shrinking, called quantization, cuts the cost of running a model. Its effect on bias and safety was not well mapped, most of all for dynamic forms and many tongues.

They test static and dynamic shrinking on bias and safety test sets. They also guard key weights that hold fair, safe acts. The aim is a small model that keeps its guardrails. Such care matters as shrunk models reach phones and cheap servers.
arxiv-2601-12133:
Dominik Śliwiński studies the spectrum of a new family of operators tied to the Riemann zeta function. The operators come from work by Connes, Consani, and Moscovici. Their eigenvalues are thought to near the zeros of zeta on the critical line as two terms grow large.

That link, if firm, would bear on the Riemann hypothesis, a core open problem. Sliwiński adds spectral analysis of these operators. Each firm step helps test if this route can reach the zeros. The work is pure maths with a famed target.
arxiv-2601-12533:
Md. Ahanaf Arif Khan and six co authors build a dataset for finding faces in overhead images. Faces seen from above look very different from faces seen head on. Their scale can vary wildly, and clutter in the scene adds to the challenge. Standard face detectors, trained mostly on front views, struggle in this top down setting.

Their dataset is called BirdsEye-RU. It holds 2,978 images with over eight thousand annotated faces. Each face is marked so detectors can be trained and graded on the set. Overhead views matter for drones, crowd monitoring, and search tasks. A shared dataset of this kind gives the field a common test bed. It also shows how large the overhead gap really is.
arxiv-2601-12833:
Monika E. Mycroft, Rostyslav O. Serha, Andrii V. Chumak, and Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero prepare quantum states of magnons. Magnons are spin waves in a ferromagnet, and the target mode is ferromagnetic resonance. The team propose to prepare and certify Gaussian quantum states of that mode. Their drive is longitudinal, acting along the magnetization.

Quantum optics strategies for such states rely on light based tools. This approach instead harnesses a purely magnonic feature: spin wave nonlinearity. That nonlinearity generates magnon squeezing, a quantum signature. Squeezed magnons could serve quantum sensing and information tasks in magnetic devices. The work opens a route to quantum magnonics without optical intermediaries.
arxiv-2601-12933:
Sharifa Sultana and six co authors study how Bangladeshi women perceive deepfakes. Deepfake technology grows more accessible each year, and concerns about misuse are escalating. The Global South faces added risk, since digital literacy and regulation are often limited. Prior research focused on detection and media manipulation in general terms.

A gap remains in understanding how individuals in these regions perceive and interact with deepfake media. Women may face distinct risks, from harassment to reputational harm. Hearing their views directly grounds policy in lived experience, not speculation. The study serves debates on platform duties and media education. It centers voices often missing from deepfake research.
arxiv-2601-13033:
Members of the ATLAS team report on hunts for odd signals from dark sectors of nature. ATLAS is a huge detector at the Large Hadron Collider. Many ideas past the Standard Model guess new long lived bits of matter. Such bits would fly some way from the crash point and then decay.

Those late decays are hard to rebuild from the raw hits. They also face odd and tough noise from known paths. The report sums up fresh results from hunts tuned to dark sector ideas. All hunts use proton crash data that ATLAS has stored. For readers, the piece gives a compact tour of how one big team chases faint, strange tracks that standard hunts would miss.
arxiv-2601-13133:
Mingshuang Luo and co-authors build a train path for vision tasks that centre on people. Such tasks span watch cams, health care, and how people use machines. Huge sets of unmarked photos of people now exist. The field needs one broad pre train model that can serve many such tasks.

Their path is self taught, so it needs no hand marks to start. It is led by CLIP, a model that links text and image. It can also adapt to fit each new task. The aim is a single base that lifts scores across many people centred tasks at once. Teams gain a start point that is both broad and cheap to tune.
arxiv-2601-13333:
Yuhan Liu and Yijian Zou bound how close two mixed quantum states are, in set time. That closeness, called Uhlmann fidelity, is a core score for mixed states. To sum it in full needs the roots of huge matrices. The size blows up with each added bit, so full sums fail for many body states.

The pair treat states held as matrix product density operators, a chain form that stores big states in small room. They give a polynomial time rule that yields sworn low and high bounds for the score. Sworn bounds let staff trust a read with no full sum. The work also bears on how mixed state classes are sorted.
arxiv-2601-13433:
Priyanka Mary Mammen, Emil Joswin, and Shankar Venkitachalam test if language models bow to claimed expertise. Past work shows a model's score on sense tasks can be swayed by hints and nods in the prompt. A nod from a famed source may weigh more than one from a lay source. That source effect was thinly probed.

The team varies who is said to back a hint while the hint stays the same. They then read if the model's pick shifts with the claimed rank of the source. They also try to steer that bias once seen. For teams that ship such models, a rank bias is a trust risk in law, care, and news uses.
arxiv-2601-13733:
Chisato Uno and Tetsuo Hyodo study bound states held by two kinds of force at once in 2026. One force is the Coulomb force, the pull between electric charges. The other is a short-range force that acts only up close. Together they can bind particles into states with set energies.

The pair analyze the binding energies and wave functions of these states. They show that Coulomb-driven shifts in energy track the spatial spread of the wave function. That link ties how deep a state binds to how wide it sits. Such links help read data on exotic atoms and nuclei.
arxiv-2601-13933:
Mingming Zhang and co-authors build an agent system to fix security flaws in code in 2026. As software grows in complexity, vulnerabilities grow more prevalent and costly. Fuzzers and other detection tools have advanced much of late. Effective resolution of a found flaw still often depends on human expertise.

Existing automated vulnerability repair leans on manual annotations. Their VulnResolver is a hybrid agent framework for LLM-based resolution. Agents can search, reason, and patch with less hand-holding. Faster, sound fixes would cut the window in which flaws can be exploited. Less hand work in the loop means fixes can start much soon. Small teams with no full-time security staff stand to gain most.
arxiv-2601-14033:
Xiaochen Zhu, Mayuri Sridhar, and Srinivas Devadas protect the answers of AI models served through APIs in 2026. Modern models are increasingly deployed behind such interfaces. Standard weight privatization, like DP-SGD, adds noise to the whole model. That can be unnecessarily noisy at the cost of utility.

Model responses to specific inputs are much lower dimensional and more stable. That fact motivates privacy guarantees directly on model outputs. Their PAC-Private responses handle adversarial composition, where many queries combine. Output-level privacy could keep useful detail while hiding training data. The work keeps the guard on each reply, not on the whole model at once. That focus can save much of the sharpness users value.
arxiv-2601-14133:
Yuzhuo Miao and co-authors protect a robot model's general knowledge while it learns body tasks in 2026. Vision-language-action models harness pre-trained vision-language models for embodied intelligence. Standard robotic fine-tuning inevitably disrupts the pre-trained feature space. That disruption causes catastrophic forgetting of general visual understanding.

Their TwinBrainVLA uses an asymmetric mixture-of-transformers design. Separate branches can guard old knowledge while new skills form. The goal is to unleash generalist models for embodied tasks without the usual loss. Robots that keep broad knowledge adapt better to new homes and jobs. The split design lets one branch guard broad sight while the rest learn touch and grip. That guard is the core bet of the work.
arxiv-2601-14533:
Oscar Bates and five co-authors work on transcranial ultrasound in this 2026 paper. Ultrasound through the skull could serve both imaging and therapy. The human skull is a significant barrier, though, and it distorts the waves. High-fidelity numerical simulations can compensate for skull-induced distortions. They require precise skull templates, typically derived from CT scans. They also need exact spatial alignment to the patient's anatomy.

The team's title names their advance: automatic skull-template alignment without a guidance image. Removing the guidance image simplifies the clinical workflow. The gain is time. A team can set up a run fast and skip a step that used to slow them down. Readers get a method that brings simulation-based correction closer to routine use in brain ultrasound.
arxiv-2601-14833:
E. Legnani, J. Elvin-Poole, and the Dark Energy Survey team report results from the survey's sixth year. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks at how gravity bends light from far galaxies. This bending, called lensing, can magnify galaxies and shift where they seem to sit.

If that shift is not modeled, it can bias maps of how galaxies cluster. The team tests the effect on galaxy clustering and on galaxy-galaxy lensing. They use the survey's main lens sample, called MagLim++. The work checks how much the bias matters for cosmology and for the survey's headline results.
arxiv-2601-14933:
Yogesh Darmwal and Ketan Rajawat tackle hard matrix equations that show up in control theory. Their 2026 arXiv paper seeks matrix answers that are symmetric and positive definite. Such equations also arise in dynamic programming and in stochastic filtering.

For a large matrix, standard methods cost far too much per step. The cheap methods lean on sparsity or on low-rank answers, or need too many steps. The authors propose a rank-one method that moves along curved matrix space. It works within a small subspace at each step to cut the cost.
arxiv-2601-15033:
