Fernando De Terán and Froilán M. Dopico ask what the Jordan form of a typical real matrix looks like. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with real square matrices and their canonical forms. The Jordan form lays bare a matrix's structure, but most matrices share only a few generic shapes.

The authors find those generic real Jordan forms. They prove that all real matrices split into a small count of sets, called generic bundles. The count grows as half the matrix size, rounded down, plus one. Each bundle's closure covers its share of the whole space.
arxiv-2601-15133:
André Eberhard, Gerhard Neumann, and Pascal Friederich teach machines to read a graph out of a picture. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with visual graph recognition. Tasks such as image classification and object detection have leapt ahead, but pulling a relationship graph from an image lags behind.

The authors blame the lack of a canonical way to frame the task. Their approach turns recognition into subgraph prediction. The model predicts the pieces of the graph rather than the whole structure at once. That split gives the learner a cleaner target to aim at.
arxiv-2601-15233:
Jaeyun Moon asks how to describe the basic excitations of a very thin gas. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with dilute gases, the far end of the spectrum of matter. In solids, atomic vibrations are charted in reciprocal space as phonons, labeled by frequency and wavevector.

A gas is usually described quite differently. Its story is told through atoms or molecules that collide and fly in real space and time. Moon seeks elementary excitations for the gas itself. The work builds a bridge between the two pictures of how matter moves.
arxiv-2601-15533:
Zhikang Chen and Tingting Zhu argue that AI world models need firmer ties to physics in a 2026 arXiv paper. A world model simulates how a setting changes under actions. That lets an agent plan by imagining futures, not just reacting. Recent models have grown strong at making video. The authors say looks can mislead.

They name the flaw visual conflation. Sharp, pretty video does not prove a model grasps physical or causal rules. A model can render a falling cup yet miss how gravity works. The paper presses for physical grounding as an imperative, per its title. Grounded models could serve as actionable simulators for planning. Ungrounded ones risk confident plans built on false physics.
arxiv-2601-15833:
T. Haidamak and a large team study a magnetic crystal with sound waves in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their material is EuAl12O19. It is a quasi-two-dimensional anisotropic ferromagnet. Magnetoelastic coupling links its magnetism to its lattice. That coupling plays a crucial role in field-induced transitions in such magnets. Ultrasonic methods suit this physics well. Sound velocity reveals elastic constants with high sensitivity.

The team measures sound velocity in magnetic fields. The fields point perpendicular to the spontaneous magnetization. Changes in velocity mark how the lattice responds as the field drives transitions. Elastic constants are the basic numbers that summarize that response. For condensed matter physics, such data test models of coupled spin and lattice behavior.
arxiv-2601-16133:
Matthias Heinz works on code schemes for a key step in nucleus maths. His 2026 preprint deals with the in medium similarity method. That method solves the core maths for nuclei by a smooth twist of the state maths. The twist is oft cut at a set low order. A key sum, the Magnus sum, builds that twist step by step.

Heinz sets out schemes to work that sum with care. Good schemes cut cost while they keep the result true. Nuclei with more parts need such care to stay in reach. The work aids teams who run large nucleus sums. It sits at the code and maths join of the field.
arxiv-2601-16933:
Jingran Zhang, Ning Li, Yuanhao Ban, Andrew Bai, and Justin Cui add reward checks to video bots. Most video bots build clips by views from both ends. Step-by-step bots can make clips live, frame by frame. Past step bots leaned on big teacher bots. That lean caps their skill when teachers are weak. Their 2026 preprint swaps the teacher lean for reward marks.

Clips gain marks as they grow, and low marks get cut. The bot learns to chase high-mark paths on its own. Live clip tools could gain skill with no big teacher. Such tools serve ads, games, and quick film drafts.
arxiv-2601-17133:
Inderjeet Singh, Eleonore Vissol-Gaudin, Andikan Otung, and Motoyoshi Sekiya join chatbots in a peer web with no hub. Fine-tune work needs rich data from many sites. Those sites can't share raw text, for law and trust. Hub-based crowd learn has one weak point at its core. That hub can fail, and its acts can be probed. Their 2026 preprint builds a peer-to-peer frame in its place.

Peers trade model steps with no boss node. An orchestrated plan keeps the trades in time. No raw text moves in the scheme at all. Banks and wards could train shared bots this way.
arxiv-2601-17333:
Lalit Pant and Shivang Nagar lay out a blueprint for search tools that take plain speech. Their field is Natural Language Query, or NLQ for short. NLQ lets users ask systems in human words, not code-like syntax. The blueprint is tuned for finance knowledge search. Finance data is vast, dense, and time-bound.

The design covers how such a system should be built today. It links user questions to stored knowledge they can trust. Good finance search saves analysts hours of digging. It also cuts errors from poor query syntax. The blueprint gives teams a plan to build from. It stresses fit for finance tasks, not generic chat.
arxiv-2601-17533:
Silong Chen and six co-authors show that training data can be rebuilt from federated language models. These models freeze the main network and train small adapters. Adapters cut compute, storage, and network costs. They seemed to limit gradient leaks too. Past inversion attacks looked blocked by that design. The authors test that belief.

They reconstruct training data from the adapter setup. A working attack proves privacy claims need care. Web-scale apps use federated adapters to guard user text. If text can be rebuilt, that guard is thin. The work warns builders and users alike. It sets a test that future private designs must pass.
arxiv-2601-17633:
Rakesh Nadig and co-authors present Conduit for near-data processing in solid-state drives. Near-data processing moves compute to where data sits. That cuts the data movement bottleneck. SSDs are a natural host. They store datasets too big for main memory. They also hold many kinds of compute units inside.

Conduit makes that power programmer-transparent. Coders need not hand-manage each unit in the drive. Hidden complexity has blocked NDP use for years. A transparent layer could spread it to daily workloads. Big data and AI tasks move vast bytes for small math. Processing in place attacks that waste at its source.
arxiv-2601-17833:
Xiaohui Hu and co-authors build an agent-based tool for auditing Ethereum smart contracts. Their 2026 preprint starts from a hard problem in blockchain safety. Smart contracts hold real money, and flaws in their business logic can be costly. Manual audits do not scale. Static tools raise many false alarms, and fuzzers get lost in deep logic paths.

The team's frame sets software agents on the audit task. Agents can plan steps, call tools, and follow logic across a whole contract. The authors stress cost as well as skill, since audits must run at scale. If the frame works as hoped, it could catch deep flaws that older tools miss, at a price teams can pay.
arxiv-2601-17933:
Laurent Caraffa frames machine learning as a system that must manage its own energy and decay. His 2026 preprint proposes a dissipative learning frame for adaptive systems. Models in the field must adapt for years, stay stable, and work with finite resources. Yet core flaws like forgetting, overfitting, and collapse of features lack a shared, principled account. Fixes like weight decay and dropout are used one by one, without a unifying theory.

A dissipative view treats learning like a physical process with flows and losses. That view may explain why the flaws arise and when fixes help. The goal is systems that stay viable over long runs. The paper aims at a theory base for long-lived learning machines.
arxiv-2601-18033:
Ahana Ghosh, Advait Sarkar, Siân Lindley, and Christian Poelitz test designs that make AI users think before they accept help. Their 2026 preprint studies cognitive forcing functions in AI-assisted writing. Generative tools speed up writing and coding, but they also invite overreliance and lazy thinking. Forcing functions are design moves that make a user engage with the task to proceed. The team runs an experiment on such moves built into execution plans.

They measure effects on trust, overreliance, and how useful people find the tool. The trade-offs are real: friction can guard thought but also annoy. The results guide designers who want AI help without dull users. Keeping human judgment awake is a core design problem of the AI era.
arxiv-2601-18133:
Yu Zhang, Xun Chen, and Miguel Angel Martin Contreras let a neural network draw the field that shapes heavy quark states. Their 2026 preprint builds a holographic model of heavy vector quarkonia. In the bottom-up AdS/QCD approach, a dilaton field sets the rules of the model. Most work picks a simple formula for that field by hand. The authors instead train a multilayer perceptron to learn the field's slope as a smooth function of the holographic coordinate.

A learned field can fit data without the bias of a guessed form. From it, the team computes the spectrum and decay constants of the states. The method joins machine learning with a theory of strong forces. It may sharpen predictions for particles that bind a heavy quark pair.
arxiv-2601-18233:
Daniel W. Boutros, Kolluru Venkata Kiran, John D. Gibbon, and Rahul Pandit study the long-run fate of active turbulence. Their 2026 preprint deals with the Toner-Tu-Swift-Hohenberg equations. These equations model turbulence in active matter, above all the swarming of bacteria in suspension. They blend traits of the Navier-Stokes, Toner-Tu, and Swift-Hohenberg equations. The authors study the global attractor of the system: the set toward which all solutions are drawn as time runs on.

They also work out the attractor's properties. An attractor tells which patterns a swirling bacterial bath can settle into. That knowledge guides both theory and lab work on active fluids. The study anchors a model that is becoming basic to the field.
arxiv-2601-18633:
Tong Shi and four colleagues build talk-ing heads that move in true three dims from a lone still shot and a voice track. Past tools cheat the move with flat warps of the face. Those warps can look fine from the front but break from the side. They also tend to give a poor build of the head's true form, so the whole clip feels off.

Their tool builds the head from soft blobs of light in space, a form that holds up from all sides. The blobs move with the speech, so lips and jaw track the voice. A true build could give clips that work in free-view calls and games. It could also cut the need for a full shoot for each new line. The team aim for heads that look real from each view a user may take.
arxiv-2601-18933:
Kaustubh D. Dhole builds a test set for tiny language models trained like young children learn. Most tests of reasoning in such models assume adult skills: wide world knowledge, hard steps, and grown up speech norms. Baby language models learn from child directed speech and simple tales, so those tests fit them poorly.

His bench, BabyReasoningBench, makes tasks drawn from how children grow and learn. The tasks check which reasoning skills show up when training stays close to what a child would hear. Fair tests of this kind can show what small models truly learn, not just where adult tests mislead.
arxiv-2601-19333:
Rahul Raychaudhury and three co-authors cluster data when exact distances are out of reach. Clustering groups like items together and powers much of unsupervised learning. Classic methods assume they can read exact pairwise distances, which many modern settings cannot supply.

Their setting gives only weak comparison oracles: answers that say which of two distances looks bigger, with noise and limits. Algorithms that cluster from comparisons alone could work where numbers are untrusted or private. The work tests how far ranking style information can carry a classic task that was built for exact numbers from the start.
arxiv-2601-19733:
Nicholas Biglin studies the long-term behaviour of a model for charged matter spreading under its own repulsion. The repulsive pressureless Euler-Poisson system describes a cloud of mass whose parts push each other outward. There is no pressure to resist the spread. The paper works in one dimension with distributional solutions, a weak notion that tolerates sharp concentrations.

Biglin analyses where the mass ends up as time grows large. Asymptotic results describe the final pattern of spreading. Such systems model plasmas and semiconductor flows in simplified form. Knowing the long-run behaviour checks that simulations settle correctly. The work adds rigor to a system whose solutions can form singularities.
arxiv-2601-19933:
Kei Saito studies a habit of language models: they commit to one meaning too early. Given an ambiguous input, a model tends to collapse several valid readings into a single answer. It does so before enough context has arrived to choose safely. That early commitment discards information later turns may need.

His system, NRR-Phi, maps text to a state that preserves ambiguity instead. Multiple interpretations stay alive in the representation until context resolves them. Dialogue systems, legal readers, and translation tools all meet ambiguity daily. A representation that refuses to guess early could cut costly misunderstandings. The work treats ambiguity as information to keep, not noise to remove.
arxiv-2601-20233:
Tài Huy Hà and Nguyen Cong Minh extend two classic formulas of monomial ideal theory. Hochster's and Takayama's formulas describe pieces of local cohomology modules through simplicial complexes, which are shapes built from points and faces. The authors develop a relative version for quotients of monomial ideals.

Their formula expresses the graded pieces for a quotient using relative homology of pairs of degree complexes. As an application, they obtain a relative Reisner criterion that tells when such quotients are Cohen-Macaulay. These results give algebraists sharper tools for a class of ideals that model discrete, combinatorial data.
arxiv-2601-20933:
Precision Jet Substructure of Boosted Boson Decays with Energy Correlators is studied by Anjie Gao, Kyle Lee, and Xiaoyuan Zhang in this 2026 paper. They initiate the precision study of boosted jet substructure using energy correlators. The test case is hadronic Higgs decays. When a Higgs boson moves fast, its decay products merge into one jet. Reading that jet's inner pattern is the challenge.

The authors show the two-body decay leaves a distinct mark. It appears as an angular peak in the correlator. The peak's position is set by the boson's Lorentz boost factor. Such a clean signature could sharpen Higgs studies at colliders. Energy correlators are prized for their calculability in theory. This work brings that precision to a flagship measurement. It may guide how future analyses tag boosted bosons.
arxiv-2601-21033:
Omer Rochman-Sharabi and Gilles Louppe teach diffusion models to obey hard rules. Their 2026 paper presents Predict-Project-Renoise, a sampling framework. Diffusion-based neural emulators show promise for scientific work. Vanilla models, though, cannot guarantee physical accuracy. Nor can they promise that constraints will hold. A generated weather field or flow must respect laws and observations. The framework enforces hard constraints at generation time.

The name sketches the loop. The model predicts a sample, projects it onto the constraint set, then renoises and repeats. Projection forces each draw to satisfy the rules exactly. Physical laws and observational consistency are the target constraints. That guarantee matters when outputs feed real decisions. The work serves scientists who need generative speed without lawless samples.
arxiv-2601-21433:
Katherine Elkins and Jon Chun audit how language models handle instructions that say what not to do. When a user states that someone should not act, a model should treat that as a ban. The audit finds that many models do the reverse and read the ban as approval.

The team tested many models across a set of ethical scenes. Open models endorsed banned acts at high rates, worse under layered wording. Paid models did better but still swung widely with phrasing. The results expose a basic reading failure with real safety stakes, since guardrails often rest on plain negations.
arxiv-2601-21533:
Youngjin Jin, Hanna Kim, Kwanwoo Kim, Chanhee Lee, and Seungwon Shin organize multi-expert AI debates into explicit argument maps. Systems that pool several expert models usually merge their views by simple voting or averaging. That hides which arguments actually drove the final call.

Their framework, ARGORA, builds graphs where arguments support or attack each other. Reasoning for decisions is then grounded in that visible structure. A reader can trace the winning claim back through the debate. Such traceability matters for decisions in law, medicine, and policy, where a bare answer with no visible reasons is hard to trust.
arxiv-2601-21633:
Pu Cao, Yiyang Ma, Feng Zhou, Xuedan Yin, Qing Song, and Lu Yang revisit a trade-off inside latent diffusion models. The autoencoder in these models must do two jobs: rebuild images faithfully and provide a space where generation works well. Recent large-scale studies tilt hard toward generation scores.

The authors note that rebuild quality is reported less and less. Selections based on ablations often crown the best generation score even when rebuild fidelity drops. Their tilted seesaw view argues the balance has swung too far. Restoring weight to fidelity matters for editing tools, where a model must first copy an image well before changing it.
arxiv-2601-21833:
Yuichi Harikane and co-authors report a puzzling galaxy from the early universe. The James Webb Space Telescope has found many bright galaxies at very early times, more than models expected. This 2026 preprint studies one luminous galaxy seen as it was when the universe was young, at redshift eleven.

What surprises the team is how weak its star formation activity looks for such a bright object. A galaxy can shine brightly yet form few new stars if its light comes from an earlier burst or another source. Cases like this test the story astronomers tell about how the first galaxies grew so fast. Each odd example forces the models of early galaxy formation to become more precise.
arxiv-2601-21933:
Rui Zhao and co-authors ask how much a deep visual feature can be distorted before the change becomes noticeable. Deep features, the internal representations of vision networks, now serve as the interface in many systems. Machines, not just eyes, consume images and features.

The just noticeable difference is the largest distortion that stays imperceptible, whether to human or machine vision. Modeling it for deep features, as this 2026 preprint does, lets engineers describe feature quality and control it. That control matters for compression and transmission: bits spent below the noticeable threshold are wasted. While damage above it degrades the systems that read the features downstream.
arxiv-2601-22033:
Ehsan Mirafzali and co-authors borrow an idea from quantum gravity to build generative models. The holographic principle says a volume of space can be described by a theory on its boundary. Its sharpest form is the anti-de Sitter and conformal field theory correspondence, a duality between gravity and field theory.

Their 2026 preprint builds holographic generative flows on that correspondence, combining it with deep learning and transport theory. In plain terms, samples are generated by flowing along a structure inspired by the duality. Crossovers like this are worth testing: the mathematics of holography is deep and highly structured. And generative modeling has repeatedly advanced by importing strong structure from physics.
arxiv-2601-22333:
Mihai Marciu reworks a bold twist on gravity that adds the square of matter's energy and push to the rules. His 2026 preprint takes care of a term past work left out: how the matter rule itself bends when the metric shifts. That term grows out of heat-and-flow grounds.

With it in place, he recasts the theory in a scalar-tensor form, which is easier to test. He then checks the new form for basic stability. The work keeps a fringe gravity idea honest and testable. It shows what the full math, done with care, demands.
arxiv-2601-22433:
Shahria Hoque and a team blend language models with a fuzzy decision method to rank job seekers. Their 2026 preprint notes that picking the right staff is key to a firm's success, and the race for talent is fierce. Their system reads and scores software engineer profiles on its own.

The method, Fuzzy-TOPSIS, ranks options that sit close to an ideal and far from a worst case, while allowing graded, fuzzy scores. Auto ranking can speed a first cut through many files. It must still be watched for bias and error. The work tests how far such a blend can go.
arxiv-2601-22833:
Emilio Santos re-examines the ground rules behind Bell tests, the classic checks of local realism in physics. Bell's conditions say what a local, realistic world must obey in optical experiments. Santos argues that Bell's picture of how detectors respond to signals was far too idealized.

With more physical detector conditions, he builds a local model of an optical setup that breaks the famous inequality. The claim does not end the debate, but it sharpens it. It asks experimenters to state their detector assumptions plainly when they test nature. The critique is aimed at optical experiments in particular, where detector behavior shapes what the data can honestly prove.
arxiv-2601-22933:
Fraser Birks and four co-authors trace how amorphous carbon deforms under stress. In glassy solids, deformation comes from tiny local shear events that group into avalanches. The authors model the carbon with a machine-learned potential, which mimics atomic forces at low cost.

By following the energy landscape with a method called arclength continuation, they resolve how avalanches form and organize. Seeing the steps behind sudden slips helps explain why hard carbon coatings wear or crack. The approach may guide tougher materials for tools and engines. Following the landscape step by step also reveals how separate shear events link into a single avalanche across the sample.
arxiv-2601-23233:
Nguyen Minh Duc and Viet Cuong Ta predict future links in networks that change over time. Temporal link prediction matters for social, financial, and transport systems. Standard temporal graph networks learn from past interactions, but they give single point guesses for future links.

Their sequence diffusion model adds an explicit way to capture uncertainty and the sequential shape of future interactions. Knowing the range of likely futures, not just one guess, supports safer decisions. Diffusion methods bring generative modeling to a classic network task. Uncertainty and sequential structure of future interactions are what discriminative point estimates leave out, and diffusion supplies.
arxiv-2603-01533:
K. K. Venkataratnam looks at brief walls between regions in the very early universe in this 2026 study. Such domain walls can form when a symmetry breaks, and they add energy for a short time. The question is whether that brief phase left any mark on the seeds of galaxies we see today.

Venkataratnam treats the walls as a short-lived shift in the expansion rate during inflation. Solving the changed expansion law gives a smooth rate that soon returns to the standard path. Fluctuations are then matched across the shift from the wall phase to normal inflation. Only waves that left the horizon near the shift change their path, so the seed spectrum shows narrow, scale-linked dips. Far from the shift, inflation keeps its usual success.
arxiv-2603-01833:
Ravshan Ashurov and Damir Shamuratov recover a hidden source term in a fractional diffusion equation. Their 2026 work uses Caputo derivatives, which let diffusion carry memory of its past states. The unknown is the spatial part of a source that splits into separate space and time factors.

Extra data at one interior time pins down that spatial part, a classic overdetermination trick. The spatial operator is a self-adjoint positive differential operator of order at least two. Solutions are written spectrally with a multinomial Mittag-Leffler function, the fractional cousin of the exponential. Sharp asymptotic expansions for that function yield a uniform lower bound on a key denominator. Those bounds give conditions for a classical solution to exist, and uniqueness holds under natural data assumptions, despite the problem being ill-posed.
arxiv-2603-02033:
Melis Yardimci, Samet Ok, and Belinda Kalomeni track brightness rhythms in three symbiotic binary stars over up to fourteen years. Their 2026 study merges ground and space monitoring in several wavelength bands. Symbiotic binaries pair a cool giant with a hot companion that feeds on its wind.

All three systems show coherent modulations apart from their orbital cycles, on scales of tens of days. One system dominant rhythm and its harmonic point to pulsations of the cool giant. The other two show stable mid-length rhythms that mix pulsation with disk or circumstellar effects. Space data add rapid signals down to tens of minutes in two systems. Those fast flickers suggest accretion or rotation activity layered over the slower giant pulsations, which constrains mass transfer models.
arxiv-2603-02333:
Xiaoyu Luo, Wenrui Yu, Qiongxiu Li, and Johannes Bjerva characterize memorization in diffusion language models in this 2026 paper. Standard language models sometimes repeat their training data word for word. That raises privacy and copyright risks for real users. Diffusion models generate text by unmasking, a very different process, and their memorization was unmapped.

Their framework covers both prefix-based and diffusion generation under any masking pattern. One theorem shows that finer sampling steps strictly raise the chance of exact data extraction. Standard generation appears as the extreme case of that scale. Experiments across model sizes and sampling styles confirm the theory. Under matched tests, diffusion models leaked far less personal data than standard models.
arxiv-2603-02633:
Mohammed Nowaz Rabbani Chowdhury, Hsinyu Tsai, Geoffrey Burr, and colleagues address a hardware problem for very large language models in 2026. Mixture-of-Experts models use only a few expert parts per input, yet still hold huge numbers of weights. Analog in-memory chips could run them with far less energy, but chip noise hurts accuracy.

Their fix splits the work instead of retraining the model. Experts shown to be noise-sensitive, plus attention layers, run on normal digital hardware. The rest run on the analog chips. Tests on two large expert models across several benchmarks kept accuracy steady despite analog flaws. The split makes low-energy hardware usable for models too big to retrain.
arxiv-2603-03133:
How a two-dimensional sheet stacks and what coats its surface decide whether aluminum ions can move in and out. This 2026 study uses density functional theory, a quantum simulation method, to test MXene materials as cathodes for aluminum-ion batteries. The candidates, two layered carbides, offer wide interlayer spacing and strong conductivity beyond lithium chemistry.

Four stacking arrangements and two ion sites were compared. Oxygen-coated layers in one stacking stayed remarkably stable, with the vanadium carbide barely swelling as aluminum entered, matching experiments. That stable stacking slowed ion motion compared with the alternative arrangement. Oxygen coatings also promised high storage capacity, while fluorine coatings destabilized badly after ion entry. The findings give battery designers concrete rules for tuning these sheets.
arxiv-2603-03233:
Zihang Zeng, Jiaquan Zhang, Pengze Li, and colleagues pit AI agents against each other to keep scientific code honest. Multi-agent systems can attack hard science problems, but language models hallucinate code and tests alike, and errors compound across agents. Jeongtae Lee and seven colleagues speed up language model generation with a new acceptance rule for speculative decoding. In that technique a small draft model proposes tokens and a large target model keeps only good ones. Their 2026 method, DropMatch, judges draft tokens by sampling: it applies dropout, a classic randomness trick, only to the model's final head and draws several decoding paths.

Wooster Beach founded the eclectic school, and Volume I of The American Practice of Medicine, from 1833, is its founding textbook. Beach broke with the harsh dosing of his day, the bleeding and calomel of heroic medicine. In its place he taught botanic practice, cures drawn from plants.

Readers today find in these pages the opening shot of a medical movement that rivaled regular practice for decades.

Volume II of Wooster Beach's American Practice of Medicine, from 1833, carries his founding textbook forward into daily work.
