As the middle third of the set, it shows eclectic medicine finding its feet as a system of its own.
beach-american-practice-vol3-1833:
With Volume III in 1833, Beach's American Practice of Medicine stands complete in three volumes. Wooster Beach wrote as the head of a young school, the eclectics, who picked the best remedies from every system. Botanic cures stand at the center of his teaching from first page to last.

The closing volume rounds out the course of diseases and treatments the set set out to cover. Together the three gave American country doctors a full practice guide that trusted plants over the lancet. The set marks the start of organized eclectic medicine in the United States.
cia-0000009033:
Major C. J. Ramsay's name anchors photo comparison case number 10,407, reported in April 1969. Specialists compared images that might show the missing major against his known photographs. The case number and name together show the system's two faces: bureaucracy and one officer's fate.

Results in such cases were phrased with care, since families and commanders read them closely. A finding could direct searchers, or tell them a lead was dead. Ramsay's file was one among thousands, yet each got the same measured treatment. The paper preserves that treatment at the level of a single named man.
cia-0000009833:
American prisoners were moved through Cambodia, a January 1967 CIA report tracks. Captives taken in South Vietnam's border regions were often marched west into Cambodian sanctuaries. From there, some were sent north; others stayed in border camps.

Movement through a third country hid prisoners from the war's official geography. Officials in Washington had to follow men across a border their own maps treated as closed. Each transit report added a segment to a captive's route. This file records the Cambodian segment early in the war, when the cross-border sanctuary system was still taking clear form.
cia-0000009933:
Twelve American prisoners of war were sighted in the Rung Dau jungle, in Dinh Quan district, a November 1971 report states. Dinh Quan lies northeast of Saigon, in country where rubber plantations meet jungle. Twelve men together formed one of the larger southern groups on record.

A dozen prisoners in one place implied a camp, a march, or a gathering for transfer. Each possibility pointed officials toward different checks. Group size also shaped the report's credibility: big claims drew big scrutiny. This file preserves the sighting as claimed, a large number in a jungle district, in the southern record.
cia-0000011833:
In November 1966 the CIA forecast what would follow a United Nations resolution to end a mandate. The resolution of that season concerned South West Africa, which the General Assembly voted to take back from South Africa. Pretoria had ruled the territory since the First World War and refused to give it up.

The paper weighs the likely results: legal fights, pressure on South Africa, and unrest inside the territory. It also judges how far the world body could push a defiant member state. The forecast opens the long struggle that ended with Namibia's freedom in 1990.
cia-0000013233:
Procedures for detaining and executing prisoners in Tuyen Duc province fill a CIA paper from January 1971. The procedures come from the Viet Cong system in that southern highlands province. Their order is chilling to read today. Capture, judgment, and death are reduced to plain steps. They were applied in that province to men whose names the file may never fully recover for their families.

The paper sets the system's darkest rules down without flinching. That plainness makes it hard to read, and necessary to keep. For readers, it is the southern system's lethal logic, preserved so the record cannot be softened later.
cia-0000013833:
A captured American pilot is the subject of a CIA item from November 1966. The item preserves the incident's bare facts in the file's plain form. Somewhere over Vietnam an airman's war ended in a parachute and a capture. The item records what was known at the time. It notes the loss and the place as reported. It also marks the man's entry into the prison system this file maps in such detail.

The bare facts were all the files had, and they were entered with care. Every name in the accounting began as a note like this one. For readers, the item is the capture note in its plainest form.
cia-0000015333: A letter to Joseph Karth from Lawrence Houston fills a CIA file dated May 5, 1961. It concerns Karth's inquiry of June 30, the title notes. Karth sat in Congress, where saucer questions carried a member's weight. Houston, the agency's top lawyer, handled such mail at the very top level. Houston's letter to Karth is held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015433: Photo experts examined UFO photography for the CIA in a record dated January 5, 1967. Their craft was reading grain, light, and angle to judge whether a picture showed a real object. Most saucer photos of the era were too blurred to prove much either way. A formal analysis entry shows the agency still testing camera claims with lab methods in the late sixties.
cia-0000022333: The Powers trial depicts the pilot as a criminal, in a Soviet line kept by a CIA record dated in 1969. Nine years after the trial, Moscow's telling still cast Powers as a common offender. The agency filed the echo, not just the event. Long afterlife in enemy print was part of how a Cold War case kept its shape.
cia-0000022533: Captain Kurt C. McDonald is named in photo comparison case number 10,145, with results kept in a CIA record dated in 1969. The title gives his last name in full, which an older summary shortened. Matching a named man's face against wartime pictures was careful, hopeful work. Results, welcome or not, were written down so the case could move forward.
cia-0000027133: Soviet submarine accidents are the subject of a CIA item whose publication date the catalog lists as unknown. The file is dated in 1977. Soviet boats suffered grave accidents in secret through the Cold War, and Western agencies pieced them together from hints. An accident file served both safety lessons and the wider watch on the rival fleet under the seas.
cia-0000028333: Nicaragua's repression of the Miskito Indians is recorded in a CIA item dated in 1982, marked unclassified in the title. The Miskito lived along the Caribbean coast, far from Managua in culture and language. The Sandinista government's forced moves of Miskito villages drew world protest that year. An open file on it served officials answering public questions about an ally turned foe.
cia-0000036633:
Photo comparison results filed as Christmas 1969 number 19 concern the MIA and POW case of Harrison. A CIA record dated November 4, 1969 holds those results. The Christmas label came from prisoner photographs released around the holiday season.

Analysts matched faces in the photographs against known pictures of missing men. A numbered result like this one gave officials a judged answer for a single case. The file shows how one family's question moved through a large and careful system. The work was slow and exact, and it was done under great emotional weight. Harrison's case was one of many checked against the same set of released images.
cia-0000037033:
Photo comparison results for James Patterson fill a CIA record dated January 5, 1971. The work is tied to the Christmas 1969 photographs of prisoners and missing men. Patterson's name and rank, a first lieutenant in the file's terms, anchor the case.

Analysts compared Patterson's known likeness with faces in the Christmas photographs. Their result gave the case a judged answer after more than a year of waiting. The file shows the identification drive at work on one officer's case in detail. Christmas photographs mattered because Hanoi released few images, so each one was studied for months. Patterson's result closed a long wait for the people who had asked about him.
cia-0000037533:
Three civilian captives, identified as American newspapermen, are mentioned in an untitled CIA record dated July 2, 1972. Reporters who covered the war in Southeast Asia sometimes fell into enemy hands. Their cases sat apart from the military prisoner lists, in a file of their own.

Inside, the three civilians are noted as captives, with their trade named in the title. Civilian cases were easy to overlook beside the long rolls of missing soldiers. Keeping them in the record mattered, since their families waited for word just as soldiers' families did, and the accounting owed them the same care.
cia-0000045933: Hanoi reported its findings on controversial missing-men cases in a dispatch kept by a CIA item dated November 1, 1991. The hard cases were the ones families and officials argued over most, where proof ran thin on both sides. Vietnam's answers, whatever their worth, became part of the record the two sides negotiated from.
cia-0000046933: A report placed an American prisoner of war in a Viet Cong camp in Dam Doi District, and a CIA item dated October 3, 1971, preserved it. Dam Doi lay in the far south of Vietnam, in the Mekong Delta country. A sighting or report like this one could be a family's first word of a man in years.
cia-0000049233:
Rightist terrorism in El Salvador is the subject of a CIA paper from 1980, the civil war's first full year. Terror from the right — death squads, bombs, and threats — was aimed at the unions, the church, and the left. The paper survives in the files later gathered for the Truth Commission.

Written this early, the paper catches the terror while its patterns were forming: who organized it, whom it targeted, and how the state answered or looked away. Later investigators built on such early papers to test claims about who knew what, and when. It is among the series' founding documents on the squads.
cia-0000049333: Dated November 3, 1980, declassified CIA document 0000049333 covers civilian-military agreements in El Salvador and carries a Truth Commission note. Its subject is the arrangements between civilian leaders and the military. The file is a short agency paper whose title gives its whole scope, kept as part of the declassified record on El Salvador during that year.
cia-0000102933: Use of Prison Labor in Komi ASSR for Forest Clearing and in Sawmills, with dates of information from 1971 in cut-short form. The record is declassified CIA document 0000102933, dated August 3, 1982. Timber work replaces pipelines here. Readers find a short forestry labor record It shares its date with another item. That item, on MVD involvement, sits nearby in the catalog. Its catalog entry preserves the original heading word for word.
cia-0000112333: Take 8 of Many -- Gorbachev Urals Visit is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112333, dated March 5, 1990. The title marks an installment: take eight of many, on Gorbachev's visit to the Urals. Take is the wire service word the heading uses for a part. The brief record is one numbered dispatch in a longer series from 1990.
cia-0000112833: Untitled Statement by S. Toropovsky is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112833, dated October 5, 1945. The catalog marks the file untitled, then names a statement by S. Toropovsky. No topic for the statement is given in the heading itself. The brief record is a statement item, one of two Toropovsky filings in this wartime group of files.
cia-0000124333: An April 1959 CIA document collects newspaper readers' responses to students' pleas to free Americans held in China. The heading misspells readers in the original file. Students were campaigning for prisoners still held years after Korea, and the paper gathers the public's reaction. Press reaction was clipped and counted because the held-men issue had become a domestic political question, not only a diplomatic one, by the late nineteen fifties.
cia-0000132633: A trade deal between Communist China and Cuba fills a CIA document dated June 1, 1960. Its headline calls the deal a trade post, wording kept from the original and most likely meaning a pact. Trade papers were the currency of communist solidarity that year. Beijing's commerce with Havana was growing fast. The short document covers the deal and its terms.
cia-0000135633: Brigade 2506 records include this Spanish document dated 4 February 1961. The exile force was in the last stretch of training for its April 1961 landing at the Bay of Pigs, one of the Cold War's most famous failures. The catalog offers no subject for this particular item, and the earlier summary added none that could be checked. It is presented as what it is: a dated Spanish text from the brigade's declassified files, held through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000135933: The open CIA files hold a cable dated 1 January 1954 that deals with a review of intact and potential assets. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136033: Cable in the declassified files, dated 2 February 1954, covers news of a successful contact joined to a request, the object of the request cut off. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136233: The CIA cable of 4 May 1954 is about the urgency of settling the situation to avoid a bloody showdown, and it survives in declassified form. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136633: The catalog places this Spanish-language 2506 Brigade document at 3 February 1961 and flags the date as estimated. The exile brigade was in final training that month. Estimated dates in this file come from the declassification process. No subject is named for the item in the record. It is kept in Spanish as released, part of the brigade's February archive, its exact day approximate.
cia-0000137333: Castro's health and state of mind concern the CIA briefing for the 1 August 1960 National Security Council meeting. Argentina's ambassador, who walked in as Castro spoke on 23 July, felt Castro could not speak freely because of a pro-communist acting foreign minister and Guevara's presence. Former President Prio, after three hours with Castro, told an agency source Castro appeared very nervous, his conversation disjointed with lapses in memory. During the 26 July rally speech he looked, on television, in poor physical shape and tired.
cia-0000139033: Railroad leaders move in Harbin, this August 1946 report relates. Major General Yezhoff directs the Changchun Railroad. He left Harbin for Manchouli with President Juravleff. Important consulate staff traveled with them. The train used two passenger cars, two flat cars, and two freight cars. Yezhoff was bound for Moscow. Juravleff was bound for Chita. Vice President Koroleff was left in charge. Other sources doubt the report. A note rates it unlikely. The consulate should stay open whoever controls Harbin, they point out.
cia-0000141133: A prisoner's testimony is excerpted in this January 1961 file from an article titled History of an Aggression, a Cuban account of the coming invasion's prelude. Mercenary Pedro de Armas testified, the excerpt begins; he was the third prisoner at the Australia Sugar Mill. When he arrived, the Cubans asked him, without pressuring him, whether he wanted something, and the fragment ends there. Only a few lines survive in this sample, so the article's broader charges cannot be summarized from this copy.
cia-03155133: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1956/09/20, a CIA publication. The September briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-03176133: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1958/05/31, a CIA publication. The May briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-03448333: August opened with this 1955 intelligence summary. The analysts briefed Washington on the latest global news. Cold War routine in high summer. Time has kept the file intact. This declassified CIA bulletin is preserved here. It is stored.
cia-06157033: REDEPLOYMENT OF PAVN 7TH DIVISION TO ATTACK SOKH SAN CAMP; STRATEGY AND RESULT, a CIA document. The Vietnamese redeployment. This file preserves that declassified paper. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-06199633: REPORT OF EVALUATION, a CIA document. The evaluation report. This file preserves that declassified paper. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-06235333: AR 7-12 CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE AGENCY USE OF ALTERNATIVE DISPUTE RESOLUTION AT T, a CIA regulation. The dispute rules. This file preserves that declassified paper. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
cia-06715733: ISCAP APPEAL 2011-031, a CIA document. The declassification appeal. This file preserves that declassified paper. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cocles-physiognomiae-chiromantiae-1533:
Bartolomeo Cocles teaches two arts of fate in his Compendium of 1533, in Latin. One art reads the face and frame for the soul's bent. One reads the palm: its lines, hills, and marks, for wealth, love, health, and death. Cocles was a sage of Bologna whose own death, tales say, was told by his own art years ere it came on him by a foe's hand.

His brief rules and draws made the pair of arts a set craft. Print runs roamed the West for years. The book is a chief hand book of fate lore.
danby-mishnah-1933:
Herbert Danby, an Oxford scholar of Hebrew, published his English translation of the Mishnah in 1933. The Mishnah is the great code of Jewish oral law, set down in writing around the year 200. Danby's was the first complete English Mishnah, and it stayed the scholarly standard.

The code runs in six orders: seeds and farm law, feast days, marriage, civil law, holy things, and rules of purity. Each tractate gives the rulings of the early rabbis in terse, argued form. Danby's notes clear up hard points as the law proceeds. The Mishnah is the base layer under the Talmud and all later Jewish law.
diary-and-notebook-1833-1839-and-1851-18: Diary and Notebook, 1833-1839 and 1851, 1833. The phrenologist's diary. This book preserves that diary. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
enchiridion-leonis-papae-1633:
The Enchiridion of Pope Leo is a little handbook of prayers ascribed to Pope Leo III. This edition of 1633 carries the famous text that soldiers bore into battle for centuries. An enchiridion fits the hand, and this one was made to be carried on the person as protection.

Its prayers promise safety against weapons, storms, and sudden death. The legend tells that Leo gave the book to Charlemagne himself. Christian protective magic fills its pages, psalms and crosses arranged as armor. Armies of early modern Europe marched with such books in their kits. The Enchiridion shows faith and magic sharing one small volume, blessed by a pope's borrowed name.
europmc-pmc10211233: A medical paper on traumatic shock. The wound shock. This article preserves that trauma medicine. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc10215733:
Abu Shelbayeh and co-authors review PGC-1 alpha, a master regulator of the mitochondrial life cycle and stress response, in a 2023 paper. Mitochondria are the cell's powerhouses, and they both produce and suffer damage from reactive oxygen species. PGC-1 alpha is a switch protein that coordinates energy use and mitochondrial renewal.

The review explains how the protein responds to exercise, cold, and cell stress. It covers its role in building new mitochondria and in defending against damage. The paper links this one regulator to metabolism and aging. It also links it to disease.
europmc-pmc10303833:
Chen and colleagues review the NLRP3 inflammasome and its part in inflammation-linked diseases, in a 2023 paper. The inflammasome is a protein machine inside immune cells. When triggered, it activates enzymes that release strong inflammatory signals, chiefly interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-18, which defend against infection but can also drive disease.

The review explains how the machine is assembled and switched on. It follows its roles in gout, diabetes, Alzheimer's, and other disorders. It also surveys drugs that block it. The paper links one molecular machine to a wide map of illness.
europmc-pmc10700133:
Szymanski and co-authors built an autonomous lab in 2023 that makes new materials with no hands on the bench. The lab, called A-Lab, plans and runs solid-state synthesis with robots. It draws on physics data banks, past papers, and machine learning to pick targets and recipes. Targets were new oxides and phosphates flagged as stable by large data sets.

Over 17 days of nonstop work, the lab made 36 compounds from 57 targets. Recipes came from language models trained on past papers, then tuned by active learning. Szymanski reports that the failed runs gave clear hints to fix screening and design. The high hit rate backs AI-run labs as a way to speed materials work.
europmc-pmc10770133:
Mao and co-authors found in 2023 how low oxygen reins in the cell's main energy path. That path, oxidative phosphorylation, burns oxygen to make ATP, the cell's fuel coin. How cells match its pace to scarce oxygen was unknown. The team traced a lactate tag placed on proteins in mitochondria, the cell's power units.

An enzyme called AARS2 places the tag when oxygen runs low. Mao shows it tags two fuel gate enzymes, PDHA1 and CPT2, and switches both off. That cuts the flow of fuel from sugar and fats. A second enzyme, SIRT3, can strip the tag and restart the path. In mouse muscle, the tag rose with hard exercise and capped run endurance.
europmc-pmc1257433:
Moore and McQuay pooled trials on opioid side effects in non-cancer pain in 2005. Side effects can limit opioid use for long-term pain. Prior summaries covered only strong opioids for severe pain. Their review took all oral opioids in randomized trials.

Thirty-four trials with 5,546 patients met the criteria. Most patients took opioids for moderate, not severe, pain. Any oral opioid raised side effect rates above placebo. Dry mouth alone affected 25 percent of patients. Moore notes wide variation in drugs and doses limited finer breakdowns. Nausea and constipation rates were also tallied across trials.
europmc-pmc1282333:
Haft, Selengut, Mongodin, and Nelson catalogued CRISPR-linked protein families in 2005. CRISPRs are repeating DNA patterns found across bacteria and archaea. Repeats run 21 to 37 base pairs with spacers between them. Some spacers match invader DNA and may confer immunity.

Only four Cas protein families were known at the start. Systematic searches near CRISPR sites found many more families. Models were built for 45 Cas protein families total. The models spot members with high accuracy across species. Two known development regulators in one bacterium were reclassified as Cas proteins. Multiple CRISPR subtypes emerged from the patterns.
europmc-pmc1435933:
Building family trees from proteins needs a model of how amino acids swap over time. Keane and co-authors warned in 2006 that picking such a model by habit can mislead. They showed one data set giving two strong but rival trees, based only on which model was picked.

The team tested model choice on data from bacteria, archaea, and other life groups. No single model fit all sets best. In two large sets, a model first built from virus proteins won. Keane argues that tests, not the source of a model, should guide the choice. Sound stats exist for picking well.
europmc-pmc1534033:
How data are cleaned before analysis can steer the whole result. van den Berg and co-authors proved that in 2006 for metabolomics, the study of small molecules in samples. Amounts of these molecules can differ five-thousand-fold, drowning quiet but vital ones.

The team tried seven fixes, from centering and scaling to log transforms, on a real data set. Each fix changed which molecules ranked as most important. Fixes also changed how much lab error swayed results. van den Berg warns there is no best fix for all cases. The right choice hinges on the question, the data, and the method.
europmc-pmc1564033:
What makes children eat their fruits and vegetables? Rasmussen and co-authors reviewed 98 studies in 2006 on children and teens aged 6 to 18. Many candidate factors had thin proof behind them, often from few studies.

Six factors held the strongest, steadiest support. Girls and younger children ate more than boys and older teens. Higher family income and education tracked with higher intake. Taste preferences, parents' own intake, and having produce at home all raised intake. Rasmussen urges programs to work through the home and parents, where the best-backed levers sit. This first part covers the number-based studies.
europmc-pmc1635533:
A stress pathway doubles as an immune commander in worms. Troemel and co-authors showed in 2006 that the p38 MAPK pathway, through the kinase PMK-1, drives gut immunity in C. elegans. Worms lacking PMK-1 fall prey to germs easily.

PMK-1 switched on candidate antimicrobial genes, including lectins and toxin-like proteins. A quarter of its target genes rose during Pseudomonas infection. A second pathway, insulin signaling through DAF-16, ran in parallel with almost no shared targets. Worms with that pathway muted lived longer, but only if PMK-1 worked. Troemel proposes immunity itself is a key driver of worm longevity.
europmc-pmc1790633:
Fahlgren, Carrington and co-authors sequenced small RNA molecules in the plant Arabidopsis thaliana in 2007. The molecules are microRNAs, short strands that dial down gene activity after a gene is read. Some plant microRNA genes are ancient and shared with mosses, while others seem young.

Using high-throughput sequencing, the team found 48 microRNA families that are not conserved in other plants. Nearly all were carried by a single gene each. For 16 young loci, the folded RNA arms showed they arose by inverted duplication, a copying accident involving nearby protein-coding genes. Some young microRNAs still regulate the gene family that spawned them, while others have drifted away or now target a different family. The authors argue microRNA genes are born and lost often.
europmc-pmc1794533:
Bondeson and co-authors probed in 2006 what drives cartilage breakdown in osteoarthritis, a joint disease of wear and tear. Focus falls on the synovium, the joint lining, whose immune cells called macrophages release proteins named cytokines. The team grew synovial cells taken from patients having a knee or hip joint replaced.

They removed macrophages from the cell dishes using beads tagged for the marker CD14. Without macrophages, output of the cytokines interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha fell sharply. Output from the fibroblast cells left behind also fell hard: interleukin-6, interleukin-8, and the tissue-cutting enzymes MMP-1 and MMP-3. Those enzymes, plus aggrecanases, chew up aggrecan, a key cartilage building block. The results cast synovial macrophages as a central driver of the joint damage.
europmc-pmc1884133:
Spitz reviewed oesophageal atresia in 2007, a birth defect where the food pipe ends blindly instead of reaching the stomach. In 86 percent of cases a fistula, an abnormal channel, joins the lower pipe to the windpipe. The condition affects about one baby in 2,500 live births.

Newborns cannot swallow saliva and drool heavily, needing repeated suction. Half of cases come with other defects, often in the VACTERL pattern spanning spine, anus, heart, windpipe, kidneys, and limbs. The cause is largely unknown, though animal work implicates faulty signaling by the gene Sonic hedgehog. Nearly all cases are sporadic, with a one percent recurrence risk for siblings. A small or missing stomach bubble on the 18-week pregnancy scan, especially with excess womb fluid, can flag the defect before birth.
europmc-pmc1885833:
Fang, Gould and co-authors uncovered in 2007 a sorting rule that sends cell proteins into exosomes, the tiny vesicles cells release. Exosomes bud from internal membranes with the same orientation as the cell itself. How cargo gets chosen for them was unclear.

Working in Jurkat T cells, the team found a pathway that selects proteins by two traits: clustering into higher-order oligomers, meaning groups of groups, and anchoring at the cell membrane. It ignored a protein's function, sequence, and anchoring style, and ran apart from the classic class E sorting machinery. Clustering alone could also route membrane proteins into HIV-like particles. Diverse viral Gag proteins carried exosome-sorting information, and clustering proved a primary driver of HIV Gag budding. The results support the idea that retroviruses hijack a normal exosome pathway.
europmc-pmc2039733:
Haug, Høstmark and Harstad reviewed the health effects of cow's milk in human nutrition in 2007. Milk use has fallen in western countries, partly over claimed harms from milk fat. Yet milk carries many useful nutrients, including oleic acid, omega-3 fats, vitamins and minerals. The review weighs those benefits against concerns about milk protein, fat and sugar for some people.

Full-fat milk slowed stomach emptying compared with half-skimmed milk, which may help control blood sugar and appetite. Fermented milk's low acidity may do the same. Feeding regimes can change nutrient levels in milk itself. The authors find no evidence that moderate milk fat intake raises disease risk. They question rising use of sweetened milk products and call for more study of heated milk products.
europmc-pmc2072833:
Long and co-workers tested in 2007 whether nano-sized titanium dioxide harms brain cells in the lab. The material is used in sunscreens, paints and foods, and its light reactivity could drive oxidative stress, damage from reactive oxygen molecules. They exposed mouse immune brain cells, rat dopamine neurons and young rat brain cultures to a commercial powder called P25.

The particles clumped quickly in test fluids, reaching about 330 nanometres in culture medium. Immune cells released reactive oxygen species at once and for a prolonged period. Gene activity shifted toward inflammation and cell death pathways. Isolated neurons survived even after 72 hours. But in mixed brain cultures, just 5 parts per million damaged neurons within six hours. The authors blame immune-cell-generated reactive oxygen for that harm.
europmc-pmc2124533: A medical paper on the pathological anatomy of hydrazine poisoning. The rocket fuel's damage. This article preserves that toxicology. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2124833: A medical paper on the alleged existence of adrenalin in pathological sera. The phantom adrenaline. This article preserves that endocrinology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2124933: A medical paper with a technique for cultivating a large quantity of tissue. The mass tissue culture. This article preserves that cell biology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2125433: A medical paper with experiments with poliomyelitis in the rabbit. The rabbit polio. This article preserves that virology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2125533: A medical paper with methods for determining pneumococcus types. The typing methods. This article preserves that bacteriology. Future scholars will discover it. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2128433: A medical paper with studies on pneumococcus immunity, active immunization of monkeys. The monkey vaccine. This article preserves that immunology. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2131533: A medical paper on material from lymph nodes, the heterology of lymphoid tissue. The varied nodes. This article preserves that immunology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2140933: A biology paper with micrurgical studies in cell physiology, the action of CO2 and salts. The gassed cells. This article preserves that cell biology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2362033:
Leach and a large expert group set out guidance in 2005 for scanning vessel-targeting cancer drugs in early trials. The drugs either block new blood vessel growth or attack tumor vessels directly. Tumor size changes slowly, so doctors wanted scans that show a drug working within days.

The paper reports a workshop on one scan type, dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI, which tracks dye flow through tumors without any surgery. The group reviewed how such scans were then used to judge drug action in early-stage trials. They agreed the method could show vessel effects before tumors shrink. Their recommendations covered scan design, measurement methods, and study planning, aiming to make results comparable between hospitals. The guidance came from a Cancer Research UK advisory committee on drug measurement tools.
europmc-pmc2430533:
Kilpatrick, Meola, Moudy, and Kramer studied how heat and virus strain shape West Nile virus spread in 2008. The virus, carried by Culex pipiens mosquitoes, arrived in the United States in 1999. A newer strain, WN02, displaced the original NY99 strain after 2001 because mosquitoes passed it on more efficiently.

Feeding mosquitoes the two strains at varied temperatures, they found the WN02 edge grows with both time since feeding and warmth. Transmission of both strains accelerated steeply as temperature rose, following the fourth power of temperature in their best fit. That is far sharper than the straight-line degree-day models forecasters commonly use, which therefore understate heat's effect. The authors concluded that viral evolution and warming together steer where and how hard this virus strikes, and they offered their curve for prediction.
europmc-pmc2432033:
Paré and colleagues searched the genome for what sets a blood inflammation marker in 2008. The marker, soluble ICAM-1, is a sticky molecule shed from cell surfaces, and its level tracks risk of heart attack, stroke, malaria, and diabetes. The study scanned DNA from 6,578 women in the Women's Genome Health Study.

Three variants in the ICAM1 gene itself each independently tracked the marker's level, passing the strict genome-wide significance bar. A surprise second hit sat in the ABO blood group gene region on chromosome 9. That single variant correlated with marker levels at a significance of 5.1 times ten to the minus 29, far beyond chance. Since ABO determines blood type, the authors said blood group chemistry appears to regulate inflammatory adhesion, a role nobody had shown before. The two loci together extend earlier, narrower gene studies.
europmc-pmc2577133:
Kadler, Hill, and Canty-Laird reviewed in 2008 how collagen fibrils, the ropes that give tissues their strength, are built in the body. Collagen can assemble itself into fibrils in a test tube, suggesting a self-running process. But in living tissue the picture differs: collagen I fibrils never form without a scaffold protein called fibronectin, and cartilage's collagen II fibrils need collagen XI to start.

The authors propose a division of labour. Fibronectin and the integrins, cell-surface anchors that grip it, act as organisers that decide where a fibril will be assembled. Minor collagens V and XI act as nucleators, the seeds that start fibril growth at those chosen sites. They frame this as a working hypothesis for how cells control an otherwise automatic process.
europmc-pmc2592633:
Obbard, Gordon, Buck, and Jiggins reviewed in 2009 how RNA interference, a gene-silencing system, evolved to fight viruses and the jumping genes called transposable elements that infest genomes. RNAi destroys viral RNA, and hosts even encode small RNAs aimed at viral sequences. Viruses in turn have evolved many ways to suppress or dodge the system.

Extending earlier analyses of RNAi gene evolution, the authors find that viral suppressors of RNAi, anti-element RNAi genes, and antiviral RNAi genes all evolve unusually fast. That rapid change on both sides is the signature of a long arms race pitting hosts against parasites. Over longer spans, key RNAi genes were repeatedly duplicated or lost across animal lineages. RNAi also silences transposable elements by degrading their messages and by locking their DNA into silent heterochromatin.
europmc-pmc2613033:
Tanaka and colleagues ran a genome-wide association study in 2009. They hunted genes that set blood levels of polyunsaturated fatty acids. These fats are involved in inflammation and heart health. They scanned the genomes of 1,075 participants in the Italian InCHIANTI ageing study and measured six fatty acids of the omega-3 and omega-6 families in their blood plasma.

The strongest signal by far sat on chromosome 11 in a cluster of three desaturase genes, FADS1, FADS2, and FADS3. One variant near FADS1 explained 18.6 percent of the variation in arachidonic acid, and it also tracked two other fatty acids plus higher cholesterol. A second region, holding the elongase gene ELOVL2, influenced the long omega-3 fat EPA. Both findings replicated in an independent study of 1,076 people.
europmc-pmc2615833:
Mathur and Pedersen argued in 2008 that exercise fights chronic disease partly by calming low-grade inflammation throughout the body. Smouldering inflammation is now seen as a driver of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and several cancers, which together cause about 60 percent of deaths worldwide. Regular exercise protects against these conditions. The authors propose an anti-inflammatory mechanism centred on muscle.

They highlight IL-6, the first recognised myokine: a signalling molecule produced and released by contracting muscle fibres that acts on other organs. On this view, skeletal muscle is an endocrine organ, an internal gland, whose secretions during activity counter inflammation elsewhere. The authors suggest myokines carry many of exercise's benefits against these diseases. On this view, inactivity itself is a risk factor.
europmc-pmc2652833:
Takeuchi and co-authors scanned the genomes of 1,053 Swedish patients in 2009 to find genes that set the right dose of warfarin. This blood-thinning drug prevents strokes and clots, yet the dose people need varies twenty-fold. Too little leaves clots free to form; too much risks severe bleeding.

Two gene regions were already known to shape dose: VKORC1, the drug's target, and CYP2C9, which breaks the drug down. The scan confirmed both with strong signals, then adjusted for their effects to look deeper. A third gene emerged, CYP4F2, which also helps process the drug. A check in 588 more patients confirmed the finding. Together the three genes explain a large share of why a dose that suits one patient endangers another, pointing toward gene-guided prescribing.
europmc-pmc2672333:
Seo, Keum, and Li reviewed in 2009 how bacteria break down aromatic compounds, a family of stubborn pollutants built on carbon rings. Oil spills and industry leave soils laced with these chemicals, including tar-like mixtures that linger for decades. Living cleanup, using microbes to eat the pollution, depends on knowing exactly how they digest each compound.

The review walks through the digestion routes for six major ring pollutants, from two-ring naphthalene up to the five-ring benzo[a]pyrene, a known carcinogen. It then covers ring compounds that carry sulfur, nitrogen, or oxygen in the ring itself, and versions dressed with extra carbon groups. New tools read a cell's full protein output at once. They also read its full chemical output. These tools are speeding the mapping of the routes. Each mapped route, the authors note, is a candidate for engineered cleanup.
europmc-pmc2688933:
Zimin and colleagues presented in 2009 a new assembly of the domestic cow genome, piecing its 2.86 billion DNA letters into a far more trustworthy order. A reference genome underpins everything from disease gene hunts to expression studies. Errors in it waste years, as researchers chase variants that never existed.

Built with improved assembly software, the new cow genome closed gaps that riddled earlier drafts. It also corrected flipped and wrongly deleted stretches that earlier assemblies had published as fact. A portion of the Y chromosome, the male-determining chromosome usually left unfinished, was described as well. The authors stress the practical stakes: diversity surveys, gene models, and studies of how genes are spliced all read off this map. A cleaner map of an animal this important to farming and biology pays off across hundreds of later studies.
europmc-pmc2710333:
Marchal-Crespo and Reinkensmeyer reviewed in 2009 control methods for robots that help people retrain movement after stroke or spinal cord injury. A controller is the software that sets how a robot pushes, guides, or resists a limb. Interest in such therapy robots had grown fast, but proof on which control style works best stayed thin.

They sort methods into assistive, challenge-based, haptic, meaning touch-based, and coaching styles, with most work so far on assistive forms. Some assistive forms adapt to how well the user performs on the day. Early proof favors some styles over others, and a few may even cut gains versus plain training, so direct trials are needed.
europmc-pmc2754433:
Babalola and Fatusi examined in 2009 what drives use of maternal health services in Nigeria. Maternal deaths are high there, and global goals press for better coverage. Prior studies focused on the woman and her household, overlooking community and state factors. They analyzed a nationally representative 2005 survey of two thousand one hundred forty-eight women who had a baby in the prior five years.

About three fifths used antenatal care at least once, while skilled delivery and postnatal care reached only about two fifths each. Education was the one personal factor that predicted all three services, and household wealth predicted them at the household level. Urban residence and community media saturation were consistently strong community predictors, which argues for multilevel interventions. Care use thus depends on far more than the woman alone in her home.
europmc-pmc2820433:
Huerta-Cepas, Dopazo, and Gabaldón presented ETE in 2010, a Python toolkit for working with hierarchical trees, the branching diagrams that show how genes or species relate. Such trees are the main output of many genome analyses, yet most existing tools only draw them or run one narrow test, which breaks down on large automated surveys.

ETE lets programs load, cut apart, annotate, and compare trees without manual steps. It reads the extended Newick format, links nodes to outside data like sequence alignments, and includes built-in tools such as predicting gene counterparts across species from tree shape. Its drawing engine renders customized trees automatically. The toolkit is free to download for any lab.
europmc-pmc2851733:
Nazli and colleagues showed in 2010 that HIV itself, without any other germ, can pry open the mucosal barriers it must cross to infect. Gut leakiness in HIV patients lets bacteria slip into the body and stoke chronic immune activation, but the trigger was unclear. The team grew sheets of human genital and intestinal lining cells and exposed them to lab strains and fresh patient isolates of the virus.

Within a day the sheets' electrical tightness fell by a third to over half, with the sealing proteins between cells visibly disrupted, while the cells stayed alive. The virus's envelope protein gp120 drove the damage, partly by provoking the inflammatory signal TNF-alpha; blocking either restored tightness. Virus and bacteria then crossed the loosened sheets in the lab.
europmc-pmc2869233:
Hamza, Barnett, and Li reviewed in 2010 interleukin 12, an immune messenger that steers the body's first response to infection. The messenger, called IL-12, is released mainly by cells that first meet invading germs. It tells natural killer cells and T cells to make another messenger, interferon-gamma, which arms cells to kill germs hiding inside them.

IL-12 also pushes helper T cells toward the type that fights bacteria and viruses inside cells. The review covers its two-part structure, shared with a small family of related messengers, and the signals it triggers inside responding cells. Because it shapes defense so strongly, IL-12 has been tested as a treatment booster against viral and bacterial infections and some cancers, and the authors weigh where it may help.
europmc-pmc2871133:
De Pascual-Teresa, Moreno, and García-Viguera took stock in 2010 of the evidence that berry and cocoa compounds protect the heart. The compounds are flavanols, found in cocoa and tea, and anthocyanins, the red and purple pigments of berries. Fifteen years of lab and human studies suggest effects well beyond their antioxidant power in a test tube.

These compounds grip proteins directly and switch cell signals that govern survival, growth, and blood vessel behavior. Lab and clinical studies link them to better vessel function and lower levels of several heart risk factors. The review also covers each compound's structure and food sources. It weighs how much the body absorbs, since that decides whether lab effects can plausibly occur after a normal meal or drink.
europmc-pmc2907333:
Chao, Shepard, and Wells reported in 2010 that breast cancer cells regain a lost adhesion protein when they settle in new organs, reversing a famous step in cancer spread. To break away, tumor cells usually shed E-cadherin, the glue of epithelial sheets, in a shift toward a wandering state. Comparing primary tumors with their own metastases in liver, lung, and brain, the team expected even less glue at the distant sites.

The opposite appeared in most cases: about three fifths showed more E-cadherin in the metastasis than in the primary tumor. Lab experiments with a wandering breast cancer line showed the cells can switch the glue back on in organ-like conditions. That is a true reversal, not selection of glued stragglers. Settling down may require becoming epithelial again.
europmc-pmc2936333:
Sohaebuddin and colleagues tested how tiny engineered materials harm cells in a 2010 study, varying material type, particle size, and cell kind. Reports on nanomaterial safety often clash, partly because these factors differ between studies.

They exposed fibroblasts, immune macrophage cells, and airway lining cells to titanium dioxide, silica particles, and carbon nanotubes of several widths. Harm was tracked through energy activity in mitochondria, reactive oxygen output, and membrane damage. Outcomes depended jointly on makeup, size, and cell type, with some exposures pushing cells toward programmed death and others toward rupture.
europmc-pmc2944833:
Wu and colleagues solved the crystal structure of human AKT1, a growth and survival kinase often faulty in cancer, together with a selective blocking drug in 2010. How such blockers grip the protein had stayed unknown.

The structure shows the drug wedged at the meeting face of the protein's two main parts, the lipid-binding head and the catalytic body. Key contact residues explain its grip and selectivity. The head appears to lock the body in an off state, while the body in turn disturbs the head's lipid binding site. The picture guides design of new AKT blockers.
europmc-pmc3001433:
Piechnik and colleagues presented ShMOLLI, a faster heart imaging method that maps a tissue property called T1 within a single short breath hold, in a 2010 study. T1 maps reveal fine changes in heart muscle, but older methods demanded breath holds many patients cannot manage.

The shortened sequence fires repeated recovery pulses without waiting for full reset, then interprets the samples conditionally on the scanner itself. Simulations and phantom tests at two magnet strengths agreed well with the standard method. Scans in healthy volunteers, contrast patients, and recent heart attack patients did too, where values were in the usual range. Heart rate no longer skewed results.
europmc-pmc3008733:
Kaptchuk and colleagues tested whether placebo pills help irritable bowel syndrome even when patients know they are fake, in a 2010 randomised trial. Placebos clearly ease symptoms, yet doctors assumed deception was essential.

Eighty patients, mostly women, received either openly labelled inert pills, honestly described as sugar pills that had helped through mind-body self-healing, or no treatment, with equal provider attention. After three weeks the open placebo group scored clearly higher on global improvement and other symptom scales. The result challenges the ethics-tinged assumption that placebo care requires tricking patients.
europmc-pmc3033533:
Nutting led the PARSPORT trial, reported in 2011, which tested a gentler form of radiotherapy for throat cancers in the United Kingdom. Standard radiation often damages the saliva glands beside the jaw, leaving a lasting dry mouth that harms speech, swallowing, and teeth. The newer method, called IMRT in short, shapes the dose to spare those glands.

Ninety four patients were assigned by chance to standard treatment or the gland sparing method at six centers. A year later, severe dry mouth affected far fewer patients in the sparing group, and the gap widened at two years. Saliva flow and dry mouth related quality of life also recovered better. Cancer control and survival did not differ between groups. Fatigue right after treatment was, however, more common with the newer method.
europmc-pmc3056833:
Chi and colleagues described in 2011 how skin melanoma presents and fares in ethnic Chinese patients, using more than five hundred consecutive cases at one center since 2006. Melanoma is uncommon in Asia and poorly documented there, and its pattern differs from Western cases. Most tumors in this series grew on the palms, soles, or nail areas, or on inner moist surfaces, types that are rare in fair skinned populations.

Most patients arrived with locally advanced disease, and about two thirds of skin cases showed ulceration. Overall, roughly two in five patients were alive five years after diagnosis, with survival falling steeply by stage. Stage and ulceration were the strongest predictors of survival. Among patients without spread, wider surgery and added therapy after surgery predicted longer freedom from relapse. Tumor subtype by itself predicted neither outcome. The authors call for earlier detection in China.
europmc-pmc3156233:
Jae-Seong Yang and colleagues built a free online tool for analysing lifespan experiments in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Aging research leans on survival data, timing deaths in worms, flies, or mice under different genes and conditions. Judging such data well takes several statistical methods that many labs find cumbersome to run.

Their web application computes standard survival curves and average lifespans from data that include animals still alive at the end. It adds tests comparing mean survival, whole curves, and survival at chosen time points, and draws the plots researchers need to read results. It can also compare spread between datasets and estimate how risk factors scale survival. The platform aims to make rigorous lifespan analysis routine in aging studies.
europmc-pmc3159133:
Tianjing Li and colleagues argued that a powerful treatment-comparison method needs more groundwork in a 2011 commentary in BMC Medicine. The method compares many treatments at once by mixing head-to-head trial results with indirect evidence through shared comparators. A methods meeting at Johns Hopkins in 2010 took stock of the challenges.

Valid results, the group stresses, demand a rigorously run systematic review at every step: framing the question, choosing studies, judging bias and evidence quality, running the analysis, and reporting plainly. Indirect comparisons rest on assumptions that are easy to break quietly. The commentary maps research needs at each stage rather than teaching the method itself, aiming to make attractive network comparisons trustworthy enough for treatment decisions.
europmc-pmc3174933:
Vincent Ranwez and colleagues built an alignment tool that tolerates broken gene sequences in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Aligning protein-coding DNA normally goes through the protein translation. But a single extra letter or an early stop signal wrecks that route, so faulty sequences and dead genes were usually thrown out. Their algorithm aligns the DNA directly while respecting codon structure.

The method runs at the same cost as the classic alignment algorithm and extends to many sequences at once. It is the first automatic way to align coding datasets containing non-working copies without scrambling the reading frame. It also exposes undocumented frame errors hiding in public databases and can align raw reads against a reference gene. The program is open source with a web version.
europmc-pmc3192833:
Amaury Vaysse and colleagues scanned dog genomes for the marks of breed selection in a 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. Breeds differ spectacularly in size, shape, and behaviour after intense recent selection, making dogs a natural laboratory for trait genetics. The team genotyped more than five hundred dogs from dozens of breeds at a dense set of markers.

Forty-four regions stood out as extremely different between breeds, and variation there tracked breed differences in body and behaviour traits, including new links. Within single breeds, hundreds of swept regions showed erased variation, some stretching enormous lengths best explained by selection rather than chance. Candidate regions were rich in development genes. One region tied to body size and ear shape was sequenced deeply to list the likely causal variants.
europmc-pmc3195333:
Gregg Robideau and colleagues tested a standard DNA barcode for water moulds in a 2011 paper in Molecular Ecology Resources. These organisms include devastating plant pathogens, and naming the species correctly is the first step in any outbreak response. The team sequenced the animal-standard barcode gene from more than twelve hundred isolates spanning over twenty genera, alongside the community's traditional barcode.

The new barcode, read from the cell's energy compartment rather than the nucleus, identified species practically and sometimes split species the traditional marker could not. A third common marker performed poorly on a subset. The authors conclude both barcodes are valid and complementary, and they release the large reference dataset to strengthen identification resources for a group where mistakes are costly.
europmc-pmc3211033:
Shang-Der Chen and colleagues reviewed how mitochondria contribute to brain injury after stroke in this 2011 article. When blood flow to part of the brain is cut off, mitochondria produce excess reactive oxygen species, unstable molecules that damage cells. The same organelles also run defense systems, and the review weighs both roles.

On the harmful side, oxidative stress triggers a mitochondria-led death pathway in neurons, involving cytochrome c release and cell suicide proteins. On the protective side, a regulator called PGC-1 alpha switches on antioxidant enzymes and drives the building of new mitochondria, helping neurons survive. The authors summarize experimental evidence for these mechanisms, framing the balance between injury and self-protection as a target for future stroke treatments.
europmc-pmc3246833:
Christian Hübschle, George Sheldrick, and Birger Dittrich introduced ShelXle in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Applied Crystallography. ShelXle is a graphical front end for SHELXL, a workhorse program in crystallography whose text-based files many users find fiddly to edit and check by hand. The new interface aims to make day-to-day work with those files friendlier.

The program pairs an editor, with syntax highlighting tuned to SHELXL-associated files, with an interactive three-dimensional display of the structure being worked on. Crystallographers can thus move between the numbers in a file and a picture of the molecule, spotting mistakes in either view. Because it is built with the Qt toolkit, it runs as a modern desktop application. The authors present it as a practical aid for the many laboratories that refine structures with SHELXL.
europmc-pmc3266933:
Rebecca Skalsky and colleagues comprehensively mapped where microRNAs bind in Epstein-Barr virus-infected B cells, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Pathogens. The virus, linked to several B cell cancers, makes its own microRNAs and switches on host ones, but few targets were known. The team used a crosslinking method that freezes microRNAs onto their target messages, then sequenced the catch.

They catalogued thousands of interaction sites across thousands of cellular messages, including hundreds matching viral microRNA seeds, and confirmed a sample of interactions with reporter tests. Viral microRNAs mostly target the host's own transcripts, hitting processes central to infection such as innate immunity, cell survival, and cell growth. A host microRNA cluster under the control of the myc gene was shown to regulate latent viral genes. The survey is a step toward defining what the viral microRNAs do and where drugs might intervene.
europmc-pmc3279133:
Moïra François and colleagues discovered why frozen stem cells underperform in immune therapy, in this 2012 paper in Cytotherapy. Mesenchymal stromal cells can calm T cells, yet clinical results were inconsistent, and a major trial in graft-versus-host disease had failed. The team suspected the problem lay in the cells themselves: trials infuse banked cells straight from the freezer, while laboratory studies use cells in active growth.

Freshly thawed cells from healthy donors switched on heat-shock proteins. They failed to respond to the licensing signal interferon-gamma by making the suppressive enzyme IDO. They were also poor at restraining T cell proliferation. A single day of culture after thawing fully restored their responsiveness and suppressive power. The authors argue this thaw-and-infuse practice may explain the disappointing trial results, and that a short recovery culture could fix it.
europmc-pmc3305333:
Lill and a very large team of collaborators built a database that gathers all genetic studies of Parkinson disease, describing it in 2012. More than eight hundred published studies had linked dozens of gene regions to the disease, but the findings were scattered and often conflicting. Their resource, called PDGene, collects the data and reanalyzes it in a uniform way.

Screening tens of thousands of articles yielded over eight hundred usable studies, plus raw data from large genome scans. Combined analyses covered millions of genetic variants. Eleven gene regions passed the strictest bar for a real link to disease risk, and the team reports one further region with fresh strong evidence. All results sit in a free online database designed to grow as new studies appear.
europmc-pmc3362933:
Gandhi and Abramov reviewed the case that oxidative stress drives common neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. The brain looks like a prime target for such damage: it consumes large amounts of oxygen and is rich in fats that oxidise readily, generating free radicals as a by-product.

Signs of oxidative stress appear in diseased brain tissue, and laboratory models suggest it contributes to neuronal death. Yet, the authors note, antioxidant treatments that should help on this logic have repeatedly failed in clinical trials. They examine where free radicals originate in these diseases and why translating an attractive hypothesis into a working therapy has proved so difficult.
europmc-pmc3444133:
Razak, Zayegh, Begg, and Wahab reviewed systems in 2012 that measure pressure under the foot during walking and standing. That pressure field reveals how load spreads between sole and ground. Its readings feed gait and posture research, diagnosis of leg and foot problems, shoe design, sports science, and injury prevention.

The review compares the sensors themselves, as reported across the literature, and the full measurement systems built on them, with honest strengths and weaknesses. It closes by proposing a wireless system meant to map the strongest pressures beneath the foot accurately and reliably. That design rests on sensors chosen for straight-line response and no lag on release. The survey maps what a builder must trade off.
europmc-pmc3466233:
Mooney and co-authors asked whether short protein chains called peptides share traits that make them active in the body, whatever their job, in a 2012 PLoS ONE paper. Past prediction tools were built for single classes, such as germ-killing peptides. The team tested whether those tools could spot other classes, like toxins and venoms, and built a general predictor named PeptideRanker.

The older tools did carry over to some other classes better than expected. PeptideRanker, trained separately on short and long peptides, matched or beat the class-specific tools in most tests. Short and long peptides leaned on different traits. Mooney's group concludes that shared features exist across classes, so general prediction can speed the search for new useful peptides.
europmc-pmc3480633:
Vago and Silbersweig proposed a framework for how mindfulness works in the brain, in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2012. Mindfulness training helps many mental disorders and eases stress, but the term covers states, traits, and practices, which muddies research. Their model, called S-ART, breaks the skill into self-awareness, self-regulation, and self-transcendence, meaning a loosening of self-focus that favors kindness to others.

The authors map each part onto brain networks and mental processes, from attention control to letting go of old emotional habits. Meditation, they argue, trains people to notice the biases that distort self-related thought. Vago's framework aims to guide sharper studies and better-targeted treatments. It also gives teachers a plain map of what practice is meant to change.

europmc-pmc4396833: Inflammation got a sympathetic-response review. This 2014 paper reviews the sympathetic response in inflammation. The authors map the mapping. Their review guides immunology. europmc-pmc4424433: Resistance got a humans-livestock-environment review. This 2015 paper reviews resistance across humans and livestock. The authors map the mapping. europmc-pmc4456433: Touch got a Piezo1-chemical-activation study. This 2015 paper chemically activates the Piezo1 channel. The authors reveal the activating. Their work guides neuroscience. europmc-pmc4489233: Proteins got a TOPCONS topology server. This 2015 paper presents TOPCONS for membrane topology. The authors reveal the presenting. Their work guides bioinformatics. europmc-pmc4536333: Whales got a bowhead-longevity-genome study. This 2015 paper sequences the bowhead whale genome. The authors reveal the sequencing. Their work guides genetics. Keane's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped aging science. It is a landmark.

frus-1861-d133:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 June 1861, the day Seward also wrote to him. The dispatch is document 133 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The same day crossing in the Paris file mirrors the London one. Neither man could shape his words to the other's last page. Their trust in each other had to bridge that gap, and in the Dayton file it plainly did. Their bond, built by mail, held firm through the storms of the autumn. The storm of the Trent would strain that bond and, in the end, prove it.
frus-1861-d233:
The mail from abroad brought Seward a letter from Mr. Murphy, dated 10 April 1861. Congress received it as Document 233 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the month the Civil War began, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d33:
To Brussels on 5 August 1861, William H. Seward sent a letter for Henry Sanford. It is document 33 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

August brought hard lessons about the length of the war ahead. Seward shifted to a longer game abroad, built on patience and firm law. His letter to Sanford in Brussels forms part of that shift, guiding a keen envoy through a changed season. A firm letter to Brussels also spoke, by echo, to Paris and London beyond it. An echo in Paris and London gave a Brussels letter a reach beyond its size.
frus-1862-d133:
Writing home was Charles Francis Adams's duty, and his letter of 22 August 1862 went to Seward. Congress received it as Document 133 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d233:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, addressed William Stuart on 5 September 1862 in a letter printed as Document 233 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart handled Britain's Washington business while Lord Lyons was away.

Five days into September, the Maryland campaign was under way and no one knew its outcome. Stuart had to report that uncertainty home while keeping his dealings with Seward smooth. Letters from these days are valuable because they were written without knowledge of Antietam, the battle that would soon change the terms of every discussion. Stuart had served at the legation for years before he took charge of it.
frus-1862-d33:
A State Department letter of 15 March 1862 told Charles Francis Adams what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 33 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d333:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 10 October 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 333 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mid-October brought Gladstone's Newcastle speech praising Southern nationhood, which echoed in Paris as a sign Britain might move. Seward's mail that week countered the impression with the administration's steady line. This dispatch is part of the paper battle that ran beside cabinet meetings in two capitals, each side reading the other's press for clues. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d433:
On 7 August 1862 Gabriel García Tassara addressed a note to Secretary of State William H. Seward from the Spanish legation in Washington. It is Document 433 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Spain's minister wrote in a month when Union fortunes looked thin and European capitals debated whether to step into the war. Tassara's business ranged over the standing questions of the two governments, with Cuba and the Mexican affair never far away. For the reader, his notes pair with the Madrid reports of Perry and Koerner: the same relationship seen from both capitals. Together they explain how Spain stayed out of the war while keeping its empire intact.
frus-1862-d533:
Roest van Limburg wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 June 1862, carrying the Dutch exchange into its second week. His note is Document 533 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

By the second week the June matter had a shape: statements made, answers given, points still open. Van Limburg's persistence was his government's instruction, since Dutch commerce felt every extension of blockade law. Seward met the pressure with courtesy and firmness in roughly equal parts. The note is worth reading as part of the whole run from 5 June. There the reader can watch a diplomatic question being narrowed, letter by letter. It narrows toward the ground both governments could accept.
frus-1862-d633:
On 16 October 1862 Edward Joy Morris wrote from Constantinople to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is Document 633 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the Turkish file's last paper of the year.

By October the news of Antietam was reaching the eastern Mediterranean. Morris could report its reception at the Porte. He could also report the post's autumn business. The Ottoman government, itself an empire of many peoples, watched national rebellions with professional interest. His closing report for the year rounds off a file that shows the Civil War's diplomacy at its widest stretch. The same conflict was discussed in the same season at both ends. The line ran from Madrid to the Bosphorus.
frus-1863p1-d133:
On 27 March 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 133 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, the middle piece of three sent that day.

Adams's middle sheets often bore the weight of a day's set: the fullest talk, or the claim worked out in depth. This letter holds that place in the 27 March three. Seward read such mail to judge Britain's next step on the war. Filed in the volume, the set shows a post doing in one day what lesser posts did in a month.
frus-1863p1-d233: Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 13 July 1863. It is document 233 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, within the orders that steered American policy toward Britain during the Civil War. Through such letters Washington told its man in London what to press, protest, or let pass.
frus-1863p1-d33:
On 16 January 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams held the London legation. The letter is document 33 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, one of three he sent on that date.

An envoy split his mail so that each sheet could be filed, read, and acted on by itself. Adams's triple mail of 16 January shows that craft at full stretch. This letter is the middle piece of the set. With its mates, it gives a full day's view from the post that stood between the Union and the world's strongest sea power.
frus-1863p1-d333:
From the British legation in Washington on 9 December 1862, Lord Lyons sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 333 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

London watched for any sign that Washington meant to widen the war. Lyons's job was to read American intentions and report them home faithfully. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d433:
Document 433 in the volume is a letter of 30 March 1863 from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d533:
25 May 1863 is the date on a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d633:
Writing on 28 October 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons in an official letter. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d133: A third Early letter in three days, dated November 16, 1943 and addressed to the same four officials, stands as Document 133 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Two Early letters sharing one date and one set of names suggest split business, perhaps security and schedule, though the record does not divide their topics. Both are printed in the Foreign Relations series. The cluster shows how much summit work ran through staff paper.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d233:
President Roosevelt received a short secret telegram from Secretary of State Cordell Hull, sent from Washington on 18 November 1943 about the crisis in Lebanon. French authorities there had seized the country's leaders, and Britain was asking for American backing of the policy it had ordered its minister, Richard Casey, to follow.

Under that policy, if General Catroux had not freed the Lebanese political prisoners by that night, Casey would fly to Beirut the next day with an ultimatum. Unless the prisoners were released and the French delegate Helleu recalled by ten on Sunday morning, Britain would declare martial law. It would free the prisoners itself and let the Lebanese parliament meet again. It would insist the step was a military need with no political meaning.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d33: Stalin wrote to Roosevelt and Churchill jointly on September 12, 1943, and the message stands as Document 33 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Three-way letters were the exception in a correspondence that usually ran in pairs, and they marked points where the whole alliance had to move at once. The record gives the date and the three names. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series among the September summit papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d333:
President Roosevelt wrote a warm personal letter to Dr. H. H. Kung, China's minister of finance, from Cairo on 26 November 1943. Kung had sent him a gift of Chinese tea with a letter of 17 November, forwarded from Washington, after Roosevelt had earlier sent cigars to Chungking by Madame Chiang.

Roosevelt thanks him for the tea, saying he is glad of it since he is substituting tea for coffee more and more. The Cairo visit with the Generalissimo and Madame Chiang, he reports, has been delightful and a true success, and the beginning, he hopes, of many such conferences. The Chiangs have raised China's inflation problem with him, and will pass Kung a suggestion of Roosevelt's on their return; he will take it up with Treasury Secretary Morgenthau once home.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d433:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent Harry Hopkins a secret, urgent telegram from Tehran on 3 December 1943 about securing a Soviet representative for the Cairo meeting with Turkey's president. Molotov, his first channel, had left Tehran the morning before.

Harriman is therefore sending Molotov the substance of Hopkins' cable through the Soviet Embassy at Tehran. But time is so short, he warns, that Cairo should also have someone in Algiers inform Vyshinsky directly and offer him air transportation to Cairo. Molotov had stated at Tehran that he would name Vyshinsky to represent the Soviet government at the conference. Harriman has told Molotov of the probability that a plane will be placed at Vyshinsky's disposal in Algiers, if he still wishes him to attend.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d533:
Ambassador Averell Harriman reported to President Roosevelt from Moscow on December 27, 1943, his third direct report in a week. The frequency itself tells a story about the temperature of Soviet-American business that month. The State Department printed the cable in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Harriman had pressed at Tehran for candor between the allies, and his late-December reports tracked how Moscow responded once the talking stopped. Roosevelt relied on these cables to judge whether Tehran's warmth was real. For readers, the report is part of the earliest evidence historians use to date the alliance's high point, and the first strains that followed it.
frus-1944-quebec-d133:
Roosevelt answered Taylor's appeal three days later, on September 3, 1944, in a top-secret telegram routed through Allied headquarters in Italy. The whole message is one sentence.
