It shows the president acting on the Vatican envoy's advice about Italy's relief crisis just before leaving for the Quebec Conference with Churchill.

Roosevelt asked Taylor to have General O'Dwyer report to him as soon as possible. The general should reach Washington by Friday morning, September 8. If that proved impossible, he was to come to Quebec on Monday the eleventh instead. In the event, O'Dwyer made Washington in time and met the president on September 8.
frus-1944-quebec-d233:
Harriman cabled Roosevelt and Hull from Moscow on September 13, 1944, about the Warsaw operation's tangled start. Hull's instructions reached him only late that night. Acting on an earlier air force message, he had already spoken to Molotov, who approved the American operation after telephoning the Red Army General Staff. The Western side of the plan was moving.

The Soviet side was not. Deane asked a Red Army staff officer what the Soviets intended to do on their own account and was told the Red Army had nothing planned. Deane and the British mission head would jointly press the General Staff the next day to carry out Moscow's own promise of assistance. If no satisfactory answer came, Harriman would see Molotov himself.
frus-1944-quebec-d33:
The third Hopkins message to Prime Minister Churchill dated August 28, 1944 completes that day's set in the Quebec 1944 volume. Three papers in a day mark August 28 as a working summit in miniature.

By then the conference's outline was set: Roosevelt and Churchill would meet at Quebec City in mid-September, with Germany's future and the war against Japan at the top of the list. Hopkins's messages carried the American preparation across the Atlantic. For readers, the trio shows the staff process at its most intense, in the last days before the principals took the stage.
frus-1945-50-intel-d133:
Byrnes answered Vandenberg on 8 January 1947. The secretary of state replied to his director of central intelligence within five days, at the very end of Byrnes's own tenure. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Byrnes left the State Department that month, so his answer is among his last acts in this long story. He had been present at the creation. The OSS order landed on his department in 1945. He had signed the secretaries' letters that built the authority. Readers get a fitting symmetry here. The secretary had received the analysts in the wreck of one agency. Now he writes to the director of its heir, days before both men leave the stage.
frus-1945-50-intel-d233:
On 24 April 1948, the President’s Assistant (Steelman) sent a memorandum to President Truman. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 233, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. With the Soviet threat in mind, the Council was deciding what secret work the United States should do abroad.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The points are stated once and left to stand; the file around it holds the answer they drew. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d33:
Russell wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 24 October 1945, carrying the State Department's administration view to the top. He had written to McCormack on the intelligence office's needs two days before. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

An assistant secretary writing to his chief usually asks for a decision or reports a problem too big for his own level. Russell's pair of papers that week shows a manager working both ends of a build-out. One went down to the intelligence office. One went up to the secretary. Readers get the State Department's internal strain in plain form. A new duty, landed by a president's order, that the house had to find room and money for.
frus-1945-50-intel-d333:
The Chairman of the Research and Development Board (Bush) addressed a memorandum to Secretary of Defense Forrestal on 5 December 1947. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 333 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act had just taken effect. The CIA had replaced the old group, and the Council had just begun to meet.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d433:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 13 was issued on 19 January 1950, the same day as a new No. 1. It is document 433 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A high number beside a fresh base rule shows a system both growing and being re-founded at once. The Council was widening the rule book while it restated first principles. This directive belongs to that busy January, when the lines of the intelligence world were drawn once more. The pairing of a new base rule with a new high number sums up the whole series in one day.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d133:
Ambassador Harriman sat down with Soviet official I. M. Maisky in Moscow on 20 January 1945 to sound out Moscow on Germany. His memorandum of the conversation is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Maisky, an assistant people's commissar for foreign affairs, was readier than most to trade early views.

No precise Soviet decisions exist yet, Maisky said, but the leanings were clear. Germany should be broken up; the Rhineland with the Ruhr might stand alone, and a Catholic republic might join Bavaria and Württemberg. German heavy industry would be cut down, steel perhaps to a quarter of its former output. Farm output and light industry should be encouraged, and Germany would need some export trade to live.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d233:
Soviet pressure on Iran, and Britain's plea for a joint stand, are laid before the President on 6 December 1944. Stettinius's memorandum, headed “Soviet-Iranian Relations,” is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It asks for authority in advance, to be used only if events demand it.

London has taken the question up with Moscow again. Soviet pressure forced the Iranian prime minister out; it eased for a time, and now seems to be renewing. Britain rests its plea on the Declaration of Iran of 1943 and on the three-power treaty with Iran. Eden hopes Washington will press the Russians too, on respect for Iranian sovereignty. Stettinius holds back from acting at once, but he wants the President's approval ready so the Department can move fast if the need arises.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d33: Churchill closed the year in this correspondence with a message to Roosevelt on 29 December 1944. It stands as document 33 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta, issued by the Department of State. Greek fighting and the Ardennes battle filled that week, yet the letter also belongs to the longer build-up toward the Malta stop and the Yalta Conference.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d333:
Matching the timing of attacks in east and west filled this tripartite military session at Yalta on February 5, 1945. At General Antonov's suggestion, Field Marshal Brooke took the chair. The day before, Antonov had laid out Soviet needs: Allied armies in the west should attack during February.

Brooke, citing Marshall, answered with dates. The northern offensive would start on February 8, with the Ninth United States Army attacking some eight days later. More operations would run through most of the month. For once, the alliance's two great fronts were being geared to the same calendar, in the same room.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d433:
Matthews's shorthand boils over in these notes of the late session of February 9, 1945. Eden said he had done the work and put together a piece of work. Molotov objected to a new text and wanted the old one. Eden answered with his War Cabinet cable, objecting to his own text of three days before and to how far the talks had drifted from it.

Frankly, Eden said, without something like this text there was no chance of British approval. Molotov said he could not talk from a new text. Eden replied that Molotov had held it for two and a half days. The scraps preserve a quarrel the smooth minutes soften.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d133:
Ambassador Winant cabled the full British delegation list from London on July 9, 1945. The urgent telegram is document 133 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Downing Street had supplied the names of everyone traveling with Churchill to the Big Three meeting.

Churchill brings his daughter Mary and a personal staff of twelve, and Attlee is going. Around the Foreign Office team stand the chiefs of staff, Brooke, Cunningham, and Portal, plus figures such as Lord Leathers, Sir Hastings Ismay, Lord Cherwell, and Sir Walter Monckton for reparations questions. An interpreter staff serves the Prime Minister. Winant puts the whole British delegation at roughly 250 people, a traveling government larger than the American party.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d233:
Ambassador Winant sent Byrnes a history of the European Advisory Commission in a letter dated July 12, 1945. The letter, with its summary report enclosure, is document 233 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Winant had represented the United States on the commission in London for eighteen months.

He tells the Secretary he has long felt the time would come to ask whether the commission had any further function. Its work had narrowed to German and Austrian questions. And it cannot sensibly sit beside the Control Council. The Control Council will hold the widest knowledge of Germany. It will also hold full responsibility for what is done there. Winant assumes the heads of government will close out the commission once the Control Council is running. But its members' experience might serve the planned Council of Foreign Ministers.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d33:
Eight hours alone with Churchill fill Joseph Davies's supplemental report to the President, dated June 12, 1945. Davies writes in detail, he says, so the report may prepare Truman for the atmosphere and attitude that may still confront him at the coming meeting. At Chequers, the two talked from 11 o'clock Saturday night until 4:30 Sunday morning.

They resumed in Churchill's bedroom at 11 on Sunday, the Prime Minister sitting up in bed, until lunch at 1:30. Talks continued that afternoon, and again on Tuesday at 10 Downing Street. The report's scene-setting alone tells Truman much about the man he would meet at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d333:
When and how civil government should return to Germany is the subject of a memorandum by the Joint Civil Affairs Committee. American policy, it states, was to rebuild state, town, and local offices as fast as possible. Those offices were to be purged of Nazi staff and habits, then run under close military supervision.

At the center, though, no German government existed. On June 5, 1945, the four allied powers had taken supreme authority over Germany. Their commanders, sitting as the Control Council, held that authority jointly for matters touching Germany as a whole. The memo maps a country run from the top by occupiers and from below by Germans.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d433:
Food for Berlin is pledged in Murphy's cable from Hoechst of July 12, 1945, relaying the Berlin meeting of July 10. Murphy and General Clay had attended. Clay and General Weeks each accepted commitments, starting July 15, to supply 20,000 tons of food monthly to Berlin's civilian population. The British commander gave a like pledge for his sector.

The meeting stressed that every effort would be made to draw food from indigenous resources. Immediate needs, though, would partly be met from imported stocks. Each supply was proportioned to the size of the sector, and each commitment stayed subject to review by the governments concerned. The question, Murphy notes, would probably reach the coming conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d533:
Harriman presses the Berlin air link in a letter to Vyshinsky dated July 7, 1945. He has told General Eisenhower of their last talk. The talk concerned opening a civil air lines link at Berlin, between Soviet and American planes. He has suggested that Eisenhower, or his representative, discuss the matter with Marshal Zhukov, or with Zhukov's representative.

He hopes Zhukov will be told of the link's value. He hopes Zhukov will be authorized to work out the technical details. The link, he writes, should be set up promptly. Every day adds to the inconvenience, and to the difficulties of contact with the United States and other American missions in western Europe. He closes by asking Vyshinsky's cooperation in a speedy conclusion.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d633:
Joseph Grew, signing as Secretary of State ad interim, wrote a short secret letter to Stimson on June 28, 1945. It is document 633 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The letter closes the exchange on U.S. forces in Iran begun earlier that month.

Grew acknowledges Stimson's letter of June 19, which set out the War Department's views. He thanks the War Department for the military points it raised. Those points, he assures Stimson, will be borne closely in mind. They will guide any talks with the Iranian government on pulling U.S. forces out. The brief letter matters less for new facts than for the record it seals. State and War were now aligned on a slow, staged withdrawal from Iran.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1033:
Assistant Secretary James Dunn reported to the Secretary of State on July 27, 1945. The day before, the European Advisory Commission had signed its agreement amending the 1944 protocol on occupation zones. The agreement creates a French zone in Germany, as promised at Yalta.

Dunn notes the terms were worked out in full line with guidance agreed between the Department and the Joint Chiefs. He suggests the President now approve the agreement and tell Ambassador Winant. The agreement takes force once all four governments approve it. Its terms, Dunn adds, are already being carried out by the military authorities on the ground. Truman's approval is dated July 28.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1133:
George Kennan, the senior American diplomat in Moscow, wrote to the United States team at Potsdam on 22 July 1945. Kennan ran the embassy there while the ambassador was away. His post gave him a rare close view of Soviet conduct and mood.

The team in Germany prized his reading of Moscow's aims while they bargained with Stalin in person. A year later Kennan would write the famous Long Telegram that shaped America's Cold War course. This dispatch shows him earlier, as an insider feeding word to his own side. It is prized evidence of how the Moscow post saw the summit from afar.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1233:
Togo instructed Sato on 25 July 1945, on the eve of the Potsdam Declaration. Tokyo's foreign minister still pushed the Moscow errand. His government wanted a special envoy heard in Moscow before the Allies spoke, and it wanted terms that kept the imperial house safe.

The timing gives this cable its sting. Within a day, the summit would publish terms demanding Japan's surrender, with the throne's fate left vague. Togo wrote in ignorance of that text but in fear of something like it. His message is the last Tokyo instruction of the exchange before the declaration changed the board.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1333:
President Harry Truman sent a message to General George Marshall, chief of staff of the United States Army, on 27 July 1945. Truman was then at Potsdam, in the closing days of the Potsdam Conference, where Truman, Churchill. Stalin met outside Berlin in July and August 1945. Marshall stayed in Washington and ran the Army from there.

The message links the president at the summit with the senior soldier directing American forces around the world. Late July 1945 was a crowded moment: Germany had fallen, the war against Japan still ran on, and plans for the peace were being set. Short papers between the two men show how tightly the political and military sides of the war were joined at the top.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1433:
The last Soviet text in the closing run is dated 29 July 1945, the fifth of that date printed in the volume. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Five texts in one day close the Soviet drafting campaign at Potsdam with a flourish. Two days later the leaders signed the protocol that fixed the settlement these papers had fought over. Readers who work through the run gain something the summary histories cannot give. The feel of a negotiation's final hours, when paper flew and every clause had a price. This text ends the volume's drafting trail, a fitting last word before the results.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-133: This editorial note stands in the unnumbered run after document 710 in the second Potsdam volume. The historians of the Foreign Relations series inserted such notes to guide readers through tangled files. A note of this kind states a source or links the nearby papers to each other. It keeps the published record open and checkable.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-33:
Robert Murphy, political adviser in Germany, set down Soviet economic ideas for Germany in a memo of July 20, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The ideas came from the Soviet delegates Maisky and Sobolev in the experts' talks.

Murphy lists their main points in order. The Control Council's chief task is the elimination of the German war potential. Heavy industry, the basis of that potential, should be kept from recovering in all zones alike. Agriculture and light industry, by contrast, would get a free hand. Two guiding ideas would rule the council and the German administration. One was the reparation obligation, under a plan to be set. The other was the needs of the occupying armies. Murphy notes the aim beneath the wording. Reparations, not imports, should stand as the first principle.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d733:
The Soviet delegation tabled this proposal at Potsdam on July 20, 1945, as document 733. Soviet texts entered the talks in their own style: firm opening lines, held with patience. Each delegation's drafts revealed its aims. This one was printed among the numbered papers of the second Potsdam volume.

Reading the other side's draft is half the work of a conference. The Soviet text lets readers do the same. Its lines show what Moscow put on paper early. Later bargaining can be tracked against it. The document balances the volume's many American drafts. It keeps the record honest: three sides wrote Potsdam, not one.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d833:
Yost wrote this memorandum on August 8, 1945, in document 833. The Central Secretariat's executive secretary was still closing the conference's accounts a week after it ended. His memo belongs to the wrap-up papers of the second Potsdam volume. The secretariat had served three delegations' paper needs throughout.

Post-conference memos by the secretariat are the archive's own diary. They record how texts were gathered, checked, and stored. Readers interested in how history gets kept will value this one. The document also shows the long tail of a summit. The leaders left in a day; their paper took far longer to settle.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d933:
American staff worked out this undated memorandum on the reparations shares during the Potsdam talks. It starts from the Soviet claim to 50 percent of total reparations. The Russian zone, the paper notes, holds about 45 percent of Germany's wealth. A gap of 5 percent would remain to come from the other three zones.

The Ruhr holds about half of all removables in the western zones. The paper proposes offering the Russians a tenth of western removables. Half of that offer would be free, to close the 5 percent gap. The other half would be traded for food, coal, and supplies from the Soviet zone.
frus-1964-68v06-d33: Another 1964-1968 FRUS editorial note from the 1968 Vietnam volume. The turning year. This note provides that context. Coming generations can find it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Readers can find it here.
gao-gaoreports-b-296533: Jess Bruner Fire Suppression took its August 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298533: Celadon Laboratories took its November 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Lab deals get the same full hearing as the rest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299433: Weidlinger Associates doubled its May 2007 protest — two case numbers, one engineering fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both claims for good. The firm challenged the awards as unfair; the call weighs each claim. Engineering bid wars get the full technical hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299533: Battelle Memorial Institute took its May 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The research giant said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the claims against bid law. Even nonprofit research powerhouses must play by the bidding rules.
gao-gaoreports-b-316533: This 2008 GAO ruling is about transfer of Support Function for Principal Federal Officials at Department of Homeland Security. The decision answers a legal question about spending public funds. The library keeps it in the public record of federal fiscal decisions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-233: Services buying reform got a progress report in 2005, and GAO's review tracks the 2003 reform act's implementation. The review checks the follow-through. The government's service contracts deserved the discipline. The progress was tracked. The government's service contracts deserved the discipline.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-433: Base power deals needed minding in 2005, and GAO's report says the handover questions had to be watched. The findings demand the attention firmly. The report warns that the bases' utilities deserved sound management. The bases' utilities deserved sound management. The handover had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-633: Pacific compacts' new requirements were underway in 2005, and GAO's report says implementation of funding and accountability rules progressed. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the island nations deserved honest aid. The implementation had to continue. The island nations deserved honest aid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-833: Defense space personnel needed performance measures in 2005, and GAO's report says management guidance was required to develop the workforce. The findings demand the metrics. The report warns that the star warriors deserved good bosses. The measures had to be developed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-133: Intercountry adoption needed further enhancements in 2005, and GAO's report says agencies improved the process, though more work was required. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the adopted children deserved smooth journeys. The enhancements had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-733: The mail's delivery grades needed work in 2006, and GAO's report says performance standards, measurement, and reporting wanted improvement. The findings target the metrics. The report warns that the nation's letters deserved honest grades. The standards had to be real. The grades had to be honest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-733: The Pentagon's business computers were slowly getting governors in 2007 — GAO's report says corporate-style controls were finally taking hold. The findings credit the progress while noting the distance left. The report's hope: run the back office like a business, and the waste will shrink.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-33: This 2007 GAO report looks at the SEC's watch over self-run trade groups — the stock exchanges and broker clubs that police their own members. GAO found holes in how the SEC kept tabs on these groups and urged fixes. The report pulls back the curtain on an odd setup: an industry that grades itself while a federal agency grades the graders.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-333: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at governmentwide Purchase Cards: Actions Needed to Strengthen Internal Controls to Reduce Fraudulent, Improper, and Abusive Purchases. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-633: GAO published its findings on telecommunications: FCC Needs to Improve Performance Management and Strengthen Oversight of the High-Cost Program in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
goethe-faust-hayward-1833:
Abraham Hayward published his English Faust in 1833, the first complete English version of Goethe's dramatic poem in prose. Goethe's Faust, Part 1, had appeared in German in 1808 and Part 2 only in 1832. Hayward, a lawyer and man of letters, gave English readers the whole work at once.

Faust, a scholar weary of knowledge, bargains with Mephistopheles and is led through love, ruin, and striving. The Gretchen tragedy at the heart of Part 1 became the best known part in English. Hayward's prose was plain where verse translations had failed or cut. His version introduced Faust to the English-speaking world and shaped its picture of Goethe for decades.
govdocs-archive_org-TheOrderOfMelchisede:
Michael Davies, the best-known English writer of Catholic traditionalism, published The Order of Melchisedech in 1979, with a later edition in 1993. Its subject is the Catholic priesthood, defended against both Anglican claims and the changes that followed Vatican II.

Davies argues what a priest is by nature, examines the question of Anglican orders, and attacks the new rite of ordination introduced after the council. He writes as an advocate with deep learning in liturgy and doctrine. The book sets out the traditionalist case on the priesthood in full, and it shaped debate among traditional Catholics for decades.
henrici-cornelii-agrippae-ab-nettesheym-: Henrici Cornelii Agrippae De occulta philosophia, 1533. The three occult books. This book preserves that classic. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
hildegard-physica-1533:
Hildegard of Bingen, the twelfth-century abbess, visionary, and composer, wrote the Physica on the natures of created things. This text is the first printed edition, from Strasbourg in 1533. Nine books treat elements, plants, trees, stones, fish, birds, and beasts, with the healing use of each spelled out.

Hildegard writes from monastery practice and sharp observation. A plant's warmth or cold, its juice and season, decides how it heals. Her medicine joins prayer and herb craft in one system. The 1533 printing carried her natural lore beyond the convent walls. It remains a remarkable woman's guide to the healing world around her.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-low-asher-ben-a:
Asher ben Aryeh Löb, chief rabbi of Carlsruhe, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. Born at Minsk in 1754, he studied under his father, Aryeh Löb, rabbi of Metz. He helped run his father's rabbinical college when the older man's sight failed. He later served as rabbi at Niederwerrn and then at Wallerstein.

The article traces his rise under the Grand Duke of Baden, who reorganized Jewish congregations on the Napoleonic model. In 1810 Asher joined the consistory and became chief rabbi of the grand duchy, a post he held until his death in 1837. The entry describes him as a strict Talmudist of the old school, yet tolerant toward other views. It also records his responsa, published after his death, and notes his son's rabbinate at Bühl.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malka-ben-aha-1: Malka ben Aha, gaon of Pumbedita from 771 to 773, is given a brief entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The article admits that only one fact is known about him. He joined Haninai Kahana ben Huna in opposing Natronai ben Habibai. Natronai had tried, for unknown reasons, to push out the exilarch Zakkai ben Ahunai. The two geonim prevailed, and Natronai was forced to leave Babylonia. He probably settled at Kairwan. The notice rests chiefly on the letter of Sherira Gaon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-me-ati-ha-10533:
Ha-Me'ati is the name of a Roman family of translators, traced in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Ismar Elbogen. They worked in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, turning Arabic science into Hebrew. The name itself is a pun: Me'ati is the Hebrew form of Cento, "one hundred," the town the family's founder came from.

Nathan ben Eliezer, at Rome from 1279 to 1283, leads the entry and was called the Prince of Translators and the Italian Tibbonide. His stated purpose was to replace the medical literature Jews had lost and to answer Christian mockery that Jews had none. His translations include Avicenna's "Canon," writings on the eye, and the aphorisms of Hippocrates and of Maimonides. His son Solomon and grandson Samuel finished and extended his Galen translations, so the entry becomes a three-generation record of one family's workshop.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-messina-10733:
Messina, the Sicilian city on the strait facing Calabria, had a Jewish community that may reach back before the destruction of the Second Temple. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote its history for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The community is first named in the letters of Gregory I, and Benjamin of Tudela counted 200 Jews there about 1170.

The article records hard centuries: Jews executed in 1347 on a false ritual murder charge, a riot bought off in 1475, and full expulsion from Sicily in 1492. Messina was also the seat of the highest Jewish court of appeal on the island, and Moses Ḥefeẓ became its chief justice in 1439. Lists of scholars, physicians, and tax figures fill out the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-milhau-moses-be:
Moses ben Michael Milhau was a French scholar and poet of Carpentras in the later eighteenth century, and apparently the father of Joseph Milhau. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. The family link rests on the genealogy Joseph printed in his own book, and the entry treats it as probable, not certain.

Three of Moses' works appeared together at Leghorn in 1787: a philosophical essay on Job, a rhymed paraphrase of Ruth with reflections, and a rhymed letter of consolation for the sad. A poem honoring Napoleon, printed at Paris in 1806 under the name Moses Milhau, is doubted here, since Joseph's father would hardly still have been living then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-molko-solomon-1:
Solomon Molko, born a Christian in Portugal about 1500 under the name Diogo Pires, is the Marrano cabalist whose career Isidore Singer and Philipp Bloch recount in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A secretary in a high Portuguese court, he tried to join the adventurer David Reubeni and was rejected. He circumcised himself anyway and left for Turkey.

There he studied Cabala with Joseph Taytazak, preached through Palestine to great acclaim, and announced the Messianic kingdom for 1540; a book of his sermons appeared in 1529. In Italy prominent Jews opposed him as a danger, yet Pope Clement VII favored him, and he was credited with predicting the flood that inundated Rome. He died at Mantua in 1532, his mission unfinished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morton-edward-1:
Edward Morton was an English journalist and playwright born in 1858. Joseph Jacobs and Edgar Mels give him a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. For many years he worked as dramatic critic on the Referee and other London papers.

The entry lists his books and stage work in brief. His titles include Travellers' Tales of 1892 and Man and Beast of 1893, which carried a preface by Israel Zangwill. His one-act comedy Miss Impudence was produced at Terry's Theatre in London in 1892. He also wrote the book for San Toy, played at Daly's theatres in London and New York in 1899. Such short notices fix the outline of a working theatre career of the day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-musa-hayyim-ibn:
Hayyim ibn Musa was a Spanish controversialist, physician, and Bible commentator born at Bejar about 1390. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. His medical skill opened the princely courts of Spain to him. There, before the Inquisition, he disputed freely and often on religion with clergy and lay scholars.

His Magen wa-Romah, Shield and Spear, was written in 1456 as a letter to his son. It defends the coming of the Messiah and answers Christian attacks drawn from Nicolaus de Lyra. It also lays down twelve rules for Jewish disputants, beginning with: hold to the literal sense of Scripture. He died in 1460, having also translated medicine from Arabic and commented on Isaiah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neilson-julia-m:
Julia Neilson was an English actress of wide range. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was born in London in 1868. She was educated at Wiesbaden, in Germany. Back in London, she trained at the Royal Academy of Music.

Her fine mezzo-soprano voice first won her gold medals. She sang at the Royal Albert Hall in 1885. In 1888 she debuted on stage at the Lyceum. Gilbert wrote a play, Brantinghame Hall, just for her. Under Beerbohm Tree she played Stella and Hypatia. Her Rosalind in As You Like It won great success. In 1900 she took her own company to the Haymarket. Tours of America and Canada followed from there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nierop-ahasveru:
Ahasverus Samuel van Nierop was a Dutch jurist. Isidore Singer and E. Slijper wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Hoorn on Jan. 24, 1813. He died at Amsterdam on May 15, 1878. He read law at the Amsterdam Athenæum.

He took his doctorate at Leyden in 1839. Amsterdam practice made him a famed attorney fast. Parliament took him in 1851, then dropped him in 1853. Two districts elected him together in 1864. He sat for Haarlem until the dissolution of 1866. He led the Centrale and Permanente commissions for Jews. His pen served Dutch Jews through many legal articles. Commercial law filled the Weekblad and Themis from his hand.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nusbaum-hilariu:
Hilarius Nusbaum was a Polish historian and a worker for his town. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Warsaw in 1820 and died there in 1895. He trained at the Warsaw school for rabbis. He soon turned to work for the poor.

Nusbaum ran a school for Jewish boys that he had founded. He helped build a synagogue in Warsaw about 1850. He also ran a home for children built by Mathias Rosen. There he taught both school work and hand crafts. In time he joined the state board for aid to the poor. His books told the past of the Jews of Warsaw and of Poland.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-leo-p:
Leo Paul Oppenheim was a German man of natural science. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Berlin on May 28, 1863. He left high school there in the year 1882. He read at Heidelberg and at Berlin in turn.

Leo took his degree with a treatise on fossil moths. That is, on winged bugs turned to stone in rock. He wrote next on bugs in the slate of Bavaria. He then turned to the Tertiary age of the earth. His work took him to Capri and Sorrento in Italy. It took him to Venice and the Balkan lands too. He read shell fish, corals, and sea urchins of old seas. In 1902 he took charge of rich finds from Egypt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ozar-nehmad-118:
Ozar Nehmad was a Hebrew yearly book from Vienna. Herman Rosenthal and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Ignatz Blumenthal of Brody founded it in 1836. Just four volumes of the book ever came out in print. They came out in 1836, 1857, 1860, and 1863.

The book held essays in the form of letters on books. The chief Jewish scholars of the age wrote those letters. The first book held fifty such letters in all. Reggio, Luzzatto, and Rapoport were among its writers. Geiger and Dukes wrote for the first book as well. It held verse by Wessely, Rapoport, and Almanzi too. The second book held twenty-four letters by new hands. Steinschneider and Carmoly joined the list of writers then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-passover-aramai:
Passover is the spring festival that marks Israel's escape from Egypt. Emil G. Hirsch and the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board wrote the article. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name comes from a Hebrew root meaning to pass by or to spare.

The festival lasts seven days in the month of Nisan. No leaven may be kept or eaten during that week. The article gives the full rules for the paschal lamb. It tells how the lamb was chosen, killed, roasted, and eaten in haste. It also traces later celebrations, from Sinai to the days of Josiah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peringer-gustav:
Gustav Peringer was a Swedish scholar of the Orient. He was born in 1651 and died at Stockholm in 1710. Crawford Howell Toy and S. Mannheimer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a Christian, not a Jew.

Peringer taught Oriental languages at Uppsala for fourteen years. Then he became the royal librarian at Stockholm. About 1690 the king sent him to Poland. His task was to study the Karaites closely and buy their books. He reached Lithuania, where Karaite towns stood. The mission seems to have failed in silence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pick-aaron-1213:
Aaron Pick was a Bible scholar born at Prague. Isidore Singer and Israel Cohen wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He converted to Christianity and lectured on Hebrew. He lived in England in the early 1800s. His books aimed at close, plain, literal study of Scripture.

Pick translated the twelve Minor Prophets word for word. His version came out in 1833, with Obadiah next. He wrote a treatise on the Hebrew accents in 1837. In 1845 he published a Bible student's concordance. Another book read Genesis as a map of Israel's restoration.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-polak-henri-122:
Henri Polak was a Dutch labor leader and politician born at Amsterdam in 1868. Isidore Singer and E. Slijper wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He learned diamond cutting from his uncle as a boy. Time spent in London drew him to socialism.

Back in Holland, Polak helped found a new social democratic party in 1894. He led the diamond workers union from 1895 on. Under him the union won strong gains for its members. It ended the truck system of payment. It raised wages and cut the work day from twelve hours to nine. The union also ran lectures and a library for its men.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-puckler-muskau-:
Count Walter Pückler-Muskau was a German foe of the Jews. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born near Breslau in 1860. He took a law degree at the University of Breslau. For a short time he served the state as a clerk. He soon left that service for good.

After 1899 Pückler won a bad name across Germany. His speeches were marked by coarse and vile language. He spoke most often in Berlin to large crowds. In all his talks he urged harsh acts on Jews. He called for their shops to be broken and looted. The entry records his campaign as a warning of its time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosen-mathias-1:
Mathias Rosen was a Polish banker born in Warsaw in 1804, where he died in 1865. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. In 1846 he took over his father's banking business in the city.

Rosen's service to the community won him a seat on Warsaw's council of state in 1862. A year later Grand Duke Constantine gave him a special task. He was sent to study the moral, farming, and work conditions of the Jews of Alsace. The entry is brief, but it shows a banker trusted with public duties.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ruhs-christian-:
Christian Friedrich Rühs was a German historian born at Greifswald on March 1, 1781. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He taught history at Greifswald, Göttingen, and Berlin, and served Prussia as historiographer.

Rühs wrote much on the history and literature of northern Europe. After Napoleon's fall he joined the fight over Jewish emancipation in Germany. His 1815 article denied that Jews were fit for German citizenship at all. He argued that Jews formed a separate nation, ruled by their rabbis. The entry stresses that he repeated medieval charges against the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-nahm:
Samuel ben Nahman, or Nahmani, was a Palestinian amora famed as a haggadist. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born early in the third century, he was a pupil of Jonathan ben Eleazar.

Samuel traveled to Babylon in youth, then soon returned to Palestine. Later he went again, on official business, to fix the calendar's intercalation. As an old man he pled at Empress Zenobia's court for an orphaned youth. The youth had committed a grave political crime against Rome's order. Samuel stood close to the patriarch Judah II in his later years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schutzjude-1333:
Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the Schutzjude. The German word means a protected Jew. Such a Jew lived under the special protection of the state's head. In early days of travel and trade, Jews sought letters of protection from kings. Carolingian rulers granted such letters. Later, emperors treated all Jews as their serfs.

The emperor sold protection for yearly payments. He often passed those rights to local lords. The lords issued Schutzbriefe and took Schutzgeld, protection money. After the expulsions of the sixteenth century, returning Jews needed such letters to reenter. Frankfort's Jews of 1617 lived as protégés, not citizens. Their numbers and marriages were capped. Frederick the Great's rules of 1750 split Schutzjuden into two classes. One class could pass its rights to a single child.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sepulveda-13433:
Sepulveda, a Spanish city in the bishopric of Segovia, had Jews by the eleventh century. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Its Jewish quarter was small, though its taxes in 1290 were not. Old town law set cruel penalties for contact between Jews and Christians.

The town is best known for a killing in Holy Week of 1468. Enemies spread word that local Jews had crucified a Christian child. The bishop had eighteen men seized and sent to Segovia. Some were burned and others hanged on that charge. The entry records how a false tale brought death to a small community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sicily-13633:
Sicily is the large Mediterranean island southwest of Italy, split by the Strait of Messina. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on its Jews. The earliest trace of Jews there dates to the late sixth century. Rome's Jews then appealed to the pope for them.

Sicilian Jews had suffered cruelty from local Christians, they said. Pope Gregory ordered stolen property returned or paid for. He strictly banned baptism by force on the island. Little more is heard until the eleventh century. King Roger named Jews of Naro in a patent of 1094. Frederick the Second shielded Sicilian Jews during the Crusades. His decrees of 1210 and 1224 ordered equal treatment. The entry opens a long island history of peril and protection.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simhah-b-samuel:
Simhah ben Samuel of Speyer was a German tosafist of the thirteenth century. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His birth and death years are not known. He signed the decrees of the rabbinical synod at Mayence in July 1223. He studied under Eliezer of Metz.

He wrote notes on the treatise Horayot and tosafot on the Talmud. His Seder Olam held rulings, comments, and rules for religious practice. Later writers quoted most of his rulings from that work. He also wrote on legal documents and on the blessings. The entry shows his reach through later responsa.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sofer-hayyim-be:
Hayyim ben Mordecai Ephraim Fischl Sofer was a Hungarian rabbi born in 1821. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Presburg on September 29 of that year. He studied under Hatam Sofer and Meir Ash. In 1844 he went to Mattersdorf to teach young students.

Sofer became rabbi at Gyömöre in 1852. He later served at Sajó Szent Péter and at Munkacs. In 1879 he was chosen rabbi of the Orthodox congregation in Pesth. He served there until his death in 1886. His works include a four-volume set of responsa. He also wrote a commentary on the Mishnah, Kol Sofer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-louis-140:
Louis Stern was an American merchant and politician born in Germany in 1847. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Ziegenhain on February 22 of that year. His family emigrated to America in 1853 and settled in Albany. In 1867 he moved to New York City.

With his elder brother Isaac, Stern founded the dry-goods house of Stern Brothers. He took an active part in New York Republican politics. In 1897 he ran for Manhattan borough president but lost. He served as a United States commissioner to the Paris Exposition in 1890. In 1904 he chaired the New York commission to the St. Louis fair. He joined the Equitable Life board in 1905. The entry links a retail career with civic service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sussmann-abraha:
Abraham ben Joseph Sussmann was a ritual slaughterer in London. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He worked in the first half of the nineteenth century. His trade placed him inside Jewish dietary law daily. He turned that practice into scholarship in print.

Sussmann wrote a commentary on the Yoreh De'ah code. It appeared in four parts with golden titles. The parts cover the code section by section. He also compiled an index to the final part. Two supplements followed, the later one printed in 1853. It came out at Königsberg under a memorial title. The short entry records a working slaughterer who became an author. His books served others who kept the same laws.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tanhum-ben-jose:
Tanhum ben Joseph Yerushalmi was a Bible commentator of the 1200s. Wilhelm Bacher and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He worked as a philologist and exegete in the Orient. Modern writers call him the Ibn Ezra of the East. He was among the last rationalist exegetes there.

Tanhum lived in Palestine and perhaps in Egypt too. He wrote his works in skilled Arabic. He knew some Greek, philosophy, and natural science. His commentaries cover the biblical books in Arabic. An introduction sketches Hebrew grammar and medieval philologists. Europe knew nothing of him until the 1700s. Pocock then brought fragments west and printed some. Manuscripts rest in St. Petersburg, Oxford, and London libraries. The entry recovers a scholar lost to the West for centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-terefah-14333:
Terefah is the rabbinic term for meat that may not be eaten. Wilhelm Bacher and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The word first meant flesh torn by wild beasts. Rabbis widened it to any fatal flaw in a clean animal.

An animal hurt so badly it cannot live counts as terefah. The Talmud lists eight main signs of that state. They include torn organs, lost organs, and broken bones. The Mishnah names eighteen chief cases in detail. A pierced heart or split windpipe makes meat forbidden. So does a missing liver or holed lungs. The entry gives food-law students a full working list.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tola-14433:
Two men named Tola appear in the Bible, and both are covered here. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The first Tola was a son of Issachar. He traveled to Egypt with Jacob's household. His clan, the Tolaites, appears in Moses' later census.

By David's reign that clan could field 22,600 warriors. The second Tola was the son of Puah. He became a judge in Israel after Abimelech died. He lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim. His home stood near the border of Issachar. He judged Israel for twenty-three years. Shamir was also his burial place, Judges reports.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tryphon-14533: Tryphon, son of Theudion, was one of four Jewish envoys sent in 45 C.E. Isidore Singer and Samuel Krauss wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. The envoys petitioned Emperor Claudius at Rome. They asked that the high-priestly vestments stay in Jewish possession. Josephus records the mission in his Antiquities. The entry also cross-refers a second Tryphon to the article on Tarfon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-valladolid-1463:
Valladolid was a Spanish city where kings of Castile once lived. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. The city had a large Jewish community for centuries. In 1290 its Jews paid heavy taxes along with nearby towns. Kings sometimes granted the Jews special rights and protection.

The entry tells a hard story of attacks and limits. During a civil war, townspeople looted Jewish homes and wrecked eight synagogues. In 1411 the preacher Vicente Ferrer pushed the city to confine Jews to a ghetto. Yet in 1432 a great Jewish synod met there under court rabbi Abraham Benveniste. Later, converts were burned at the stake in the city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-voorsanger-jaco:
Jacob Voorsanger was an American rabbi born in Holland. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Amsterdam on November 13, 1852. He studied at Amsterdam's Jewish seminary. Cincinnati's Hebrew Union College gave him a doctorate. He served pulpits across the United States.

His posts ran from Philadelphia to Houston. Since 1886 he has led Temple Emanu El in San Francisco. In 1894 he became professor of Semitic languages at California's university. He also lectures at Stanford as a chaplain. Voorsanger edited several Jewish papers. In 1895 he founded the paper Emanu El. He wrote a life of Moses Mendelssohn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wahl-saul-13233:
Saul Wahl is said to have sat briefly on Poland's throne. Isidore Singer and Julius Gottlieb wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The tale begins with Prince Nicholas Radziwill. Guilt over his youthful crimes drove him on a pilgrimage. The pope told him to live years as a wandering beggar.

Penniless at Padua, the prince begged for help. Only Rabbi Samuel Judah Katzenellenbogen aided him. The rabbi funded his journey home in princely style. In return, the prince promised to find the rabbi's lost son. He searched the yeshibot of Poland for Saul. The story says he found him at Brest Litovsk. Tradition then makes Saul king for a day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weill-anselme-1:
Anselme Weill was a French doctor. He was born at Bischheim, Alsace, on August 24, 1842. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied at Strasburg and at Paris. During the siege of Paris he served as assistant surgeon. He worked at the Lariboisière Hospital then.

From 1871 Weill served at the Rothschild Hospital. He took his medical degree in 1874. In 1889 he became that hospital's chief physician. The same year brought him an academic honor. In 1894 he received the Legion of Honor cross. His many essays focus on treating tuberculosis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wig-judo-german:
A wig is false hair worn over the head. Cyrus Adler and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In Judaeo German it is called a sheitel. Women wore wigs already in Talmudic times. They supplemented thin hair or served as adornment. The Mishnah calls false hair a strange lock.

On the Sabbath a woman could wear a wig indoors. She could not wear it in the street. Rabbis feared she might remove and carry it. That act would break Sabbath law. Loose, uncovered hair in public was deemed improper. A married woman's covered head marked her status. The entry gathers the rulings behind the custom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wunsche-august-:
August Wunsche (born 1839) was a German Christian scholar of rabbinic books. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Hainewalde, he gave his life to the books of the rabbis. His first works were notes on Hosea and on Joel.

In 1878 he brought out a key book of his life. It pairs the words of the Gospels with Talmud texts. None since Lightfoot had made so full a pair set. In his Bibliotheca Rabbinica he turned the Midrash into German. He turned parts of both Talmuds as well. He also wrote small books on joy and on Bible beauty. With Winter he made a past of Jewish letters in three books. The entry calls that set the best of its kind then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yulee-david-lev:
David Levy Yulee (1811-1886) was an American statesman from the state of Florida. Cyrus Adler and Abram S. Isaacs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Saint Thomas, he went to Richmond to read law. He then moved south to Florida as a planter.

He was sent to Congress as a voice for that land. He sat in the 27th and 28th Congress in that role. At first men knew him by the name Levy alone. He then took the full name David Levy Yulee in life. He helped frame the first state charter of Florida. Twice the state sent him to the Senate at Washington. He served there till he quit in the year 1861. He sat in the rebel Congress in the war years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zelman-samuele-:
Samuele Vita Zelman (1808-1885) was an Austro-Italian poet of Trieste. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Triest, he died in that same port town. He was schooled at the rabbinical college of Padua.

There he was the pet pupil of Samuel David Luzzatto. His works hold both prose and verse in two tongues. One work is a dirge on the death of his great teacher. One set of talks bears a droll name in its title. One work rails at the mob pens of his day in print. His Hebrew poems were bound as one book in 1866. That book holds his hymns, notes, and verse in full. Some of his verse ran in the journals of his age as well.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
June 1876 opens Lippincott's display of the Centennial exhibition. The century series reaches its sixth paper, an introductory survey. Emma Lazarus contributes a poem called Dolores. Sheila Hale concludes her glimpses of Constantinople here.

Constance Fenimore Woolson offers Felipa, a story. Robert Lewis Kimberly writes at Chickamauga. Mrs. Linton finishes Leam Dundas, lost and now found. Lady Barker's South African letters and monthly gossip close it. Modern Huguenots and a story of old Philadelphia appear in parts. Italian medieval wood-sculptors receive Trollope's attention near the close. Trollope writes on the Italian medieval wood sculptors in this number.
marlowe-jew-of-malta-1633:
Christopher Marlowe wrote The Jew of Malta around 1589, in the first rush of his success after Tamburlaine. The play was popular for decades but was not printed until 1633. Marlowe set it on Malta, where Christian knights, Turks, and Jews collide.

Barabas, a rich Jewish merchant, loses his fortune to the Christian governor's seizure. He plots revenge through his daughter, forged letters, and a string of murders, each plot blacker and funnier than the last. The play is a black farce about greed shared by every faith on stage. Barabas himself, ranting and scheming, is one of Marlowe's unforgettable creations.
openalex-w1530211033:
Edward Chan, Jan Damoiseaux, Luis Andrade, and co-authors wrote this report. It appeared in Frontiers in Immunology in August 2015. The subject is naming patterns in antinuclear antibody tests. Labs view these patterns on HEp-2 cells under microscopes. Different labs had used different names for them.

Experts met in São Paulo in August 2014. The workshop was the twelfth on autoantibodies and autoimmunity. A full day session built a shared naming system. Standard names help labs report results the same way. Clear reports help doctors compare tests across hospitals. The report records the first international consensus on the topic.
openalex-w2011400433:
Freya Fowkes, Pascal Michon, Lynn Pilling and colleagues studied red blood cell traits and malaria in Papua New Guinea. Their paper appeared in Malaria Journal in 2008. Some inherited red cell traits are thought to protect against falciparum malaria. The question was how that protection works.

One idea is that parasites grow less well inside altered red cells. If so, parasite levels and immune responses should differ by trait. The team followed over five hundred children without symptoms. The area had intense malaria spread. They measured parasite levels and antibodies to parasite surface proteins. They compared children with several red cell traits and blood groups. The design tested the invasion idea directly in real life.
openalex-w2069494733:
Jose Manjon, Pierrick Coupe, Luis Concha and colleagues proposed a method to clean noise from diffusion brain scans. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. Such scans track water movement in the brain. Measurement noise makes the images grainy. Noise also skews the values doctors compute.

Their filter works on multi-direction scan data. It studies small image patches one at a time. Within each patch, it shrinks the weakest components. That removes noise while keeping real structure. The team tested it on artificial and real scans. It matched or beat leading rival methods. Cleaner scans improve maps of brain wiring. The method needs no extra scan time from patients.
openalex-w2086727433:
William Laurance, Henrique Nascimento, Susan Laurance and colleagues studied edge effects in broken Amazon forests. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2007. Forest edges drive change in fragmented landscapes. The study site is the world's largest fragmentation experiment. It has run for decades near Manaus in Brazil.

Edge effects varied greatly across space and time. Distance to the edge explained some variation. Surrounding regrowth also shaped local effects. Droughts and windstorms added much random change. Tree deaths and species mixes shifted near edges. Carbon storage changed along with forest dynamics. The authors propose that fragments diverge between landscapes. Fragments within one landscape should grow more alike. Conservation plans must heed that pattern.
openalex-w2103469933:
Peter Hotez, Maria Elena Bottazzi, Carlos Franco-Paredes and colleagues reviewed neglected tropical diseases in Latin America and the Caribbean. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2008. These diseases strike the region's poorest people hardest. Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities face high rates. Poverty and exclusion drive their spread.

The review maps disease burden across the region. It covers worms, Chagas disease and other infections. Hundreds of millions live in poverty there. Many lack safe water and basic health care. Urban slums breed vectors and reservoirs of disease. The authors lay out a roadmap for control. Elimination is possible for several diseases, they argue. Investment and political will are the missing pieces.
openalex-w2103647733:
Sandro Sperandei wrote a teaching piece on logistic regression for medical researchers. His paper appeared in Biochemia Medica in 2014. The method weighs odds when several factors act at once. It is much like multiple linear regression in structure. Its outcome, though, is a yes-or-no event.

The piece explains the steps one by one. Worked examples keep the maths easy to follow. It shows how to read each factor's effect. Studying all factors together avoids mixed-up effects. That is the method's main strength, he stresses. Special issues in model building are also covered. Choice of factors gets close attention. The piece aims at clinicians with basic statistics.
openalex-w2156132533:
Carlos Celis-Morales, Francisco Pérez-Bravo, Luis Ibañez, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2012. They asked whether how activity is measured changes its apparent links with health risk. Sloppy measurement can shrink the true benefits of exercise on paper, so they compared body sensors against questionnaires head to head.

Three hundred seventeen adults wore accelerometers for seven days and answered a standard activity questionnaire. Blood fats, insulin, blood pressure, and body measures were also taken. Sitting time from both methods tracked with worse risk profiles across the board. But for insulin and insulin resistance, the questionnaire links were far weaker, with effect sizes less than half the sensor-based ones.
openalex-w2156496933:
The ATLAS Collaboration published this combined analysis in the European Physical Journal C in 2016, with G. Aad among the listed authors. The team merged many Higgs boson studies into one picture of production and decay rates. They also measured how strongly the Higgs couples to other particles, a core test of the standard model.

Data came from proton collisions in 2011 and 2012 at the Large Hadron Collider. Seven decay modes were combined, plus limits on rarer production routes. The overall signal yield came out modestly above the standard model prediction, within its error range. For every coupling model tried, the results fit standard model expectations for a Higgs near the measured mass.
openalex-w2158700333:
Jianguo Liu, Vanessa Hull, Mateus Batistella, and colleagues published this synthesis in Ecology and Society in 2013. They propose a framework for sustainability in a telecoupled world, where distant places affect each other ever more strongly. Studies done in one place often ignore those far-off links, or treat them as fixed outside forces.

Their telecoupling framework joins five parts: human-natural systems, flows, agents, causes, and effects. It grows out of research on linked human and natural systems within single places. Two examples show the framework at work: trade in farm goods and the spread of invasive species. The authors argue feedbacks between distant places must be counted, not assumed away.
openalex-w2341916833:
Alejandro Casas Herrera, María Montes de Oca, María López Varela, and colleagues published the PUMA study in PLoS ONE in 2016. They measured how often chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is missed or wrongly diagnosed in primary care. Four Latin American countries took part: Argentina, Colombia, Venezuela, and Uruguay.

Over seventeen hundred high-risk patients were interviewed, and about fifteen hundred completed lung-function testing. Roughly three hundred met the spirometry definition of the disease. Yet about seventy-seven percent of them had never been diagnosed. The study also checked the reverse error: patients carrying a diagnosis their lung tests did not support. The authors identify factors tied to missed diagnoses, aiming to sharpen front-line detection of this under-recognized disease.
openalex-w2800767933:
Helena Solleiro-Villavicencio and Selva Rivas-Arancibia reviewed oxidative stress and T cells in brain degeneration, in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2018. Degenerative brain diseases share chronic oxidative stress and a disordered immune response. Both are seen as key drivers of the slow neuron loss behind these illnesses. The review focuses on CD4+ T cells, helper immune cells that enter this picture.

Reactive molecules build up when production rises and antioxidant defenses fail. Damage signals then shape inflammation, including which T cells switch on and what they release. The authors trace how this redox imbalance steers brain inflammation over years. Exposures from outside, from pollution to tobacco smoke, feed the same imbalance. Grasping the T cell side may open treatments that calm brain inflammation without disabling immunity. The review gathers a scattered literature into one storyline.
openalex-w3161957533: Prashant Kocherlakota, Luciano Rezzolla, Heino Falcke, and a large Event Horizon Telescope team published this study in Physical Review D in 2021. Its title states that it uses the telescope's 2017 observations of the black hole M87*. The aim was to place limits on any electric charge that black hole may carry. The preserved sample holds only the title page and author affiliations. It has no readable abstract or results, so no findings can be described from it here.
openalex-w3193313333: Lynn Dicks, Tom Breeze, Hien Ngo, and colleagues led a large international expert team. The team assessed the drivers of pollinator decline and the risks it poses worldwide. Their assessment appeared in Nature Ecology and Evolution in 2021. The preserved sample holds only the title page and author list. It has no readable abstract or findings, so the team's conclusions cannot be described here.
openalex-w4220832833:
Sjaak Pouwels, Nasser Sakran, Yitka Graham, and colleagues review non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, in BMC Endocrine Disorders in 2022. The disease, shortened to NAFLD, is now the most common chronic liver condition in the Western world. It tracks closely with obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, and abnormal blood fats. Damage ranges from simple fat build-up to inflamed, scarred liver failure.

Scarring, called fibrosis, is the strongest sign of future illness and liver-related death. A liver biopsy remains the standard way to confirm the disease and its stage. Once diagnosed, weight loss, diet change, and treating the wider metabolic syndrome stay the mainstays of therapy. The review covers causes, day-to-day management, and what weight loss can achieve.
openalex-w4318457133:
Gordon Cheung, Helena Cooper-Thomas, Rebecca Lau, and Linda Wang review how management researchers should report the quality of their measurement scales. Their best-practice paper appeared online in 2023 in the Asia Pacific Journal of Management. Management studies measure things nobody can see directly, such as attitudes and intentions, using multi-item scales. When scales move to new populations or languages, their quality must be proven again.

The authors find that common practice leans too heavily on one statistic, Cronbach's alpha, and on factor analysis results. Both can mislead, and sampling error is rarely considered. They recommend judging reliability and two kinds of validity against several criteria at once. A free R package, measureQ, applies the recommendations and formats the report for authors.
openalex-w7169810833: Neutrons make amazingly fine magnetic sensors. This lab paper builds a way to read tricky wobbling magnetic fields by watching neutron waves overlap and cancel. The authors work out the math that turns wave patterns into field maps. Ultra-precise measuring at the quantum scale.
openalex-w7206178233: Democratic school management sounds good on paper; this study asks how to make it real. Reviewing books, articles, and dissertations on the topic, the authors examine how participatory planning, where teachers, families, and staff help set a school's direction, can strengthen democratic governance in public schools. It is a literature-based analysis aimed at educators who want decision-making to be shared rather than handed down from above.
openalex-w7212422433:
Cristiane Raquel Woszezenki leads a team that ran code shops for gifted school kids in Turvo, Santa Catarina. Gifted kids in plain class can drift: the work is too slow, and their spark goes dull. The shops gave them Scratch, Python, small boards, and smart tech with no screen at all. The group was small, so the team asked the kids how the tasks felt, in forms filled in as they went.

The frame joins two big ideas: that gift shows in rings of skill, zeal, and new thought, and that deep joy comes when task and skill match. Hard tasks, pitched right, can wake that joy. The kids' own takes on their thought are the core of the study. For schools, the point is plain. Gifted minds need work that can bite back, or the gift goes to sleep in the back row.
openalex-w7213408233:
Maria Flavia Nascimento Guimarães presents fractal geometry and its uses in the natural world. Fractals are complex shapes that repeat similar patterns at different scales. The 2026 article, based on library research, reviews their maths properties and applications in biology, geology, computing, and art.

Branching blood vessels, river networks, and plant growth are given as natural examples. Fractal ideas also serve image compression, computer graphics, and simulation of natural patterns. The concept is linked in the article to Benoît Mandelbrot, who developed it. The author concludes that fractal geometry helps model natural systems that smooth, regular geometry describes poorly.
openalex-w7213454633:
Débora Valim Inoch leads a team reading childhood through philosophy and education. Their 2026 theoretical article draws on Matthew Lipman, Walter Kohan, Michel Foucault, Jorge Larrosa, and Giorgio Agamben. Childhood is treated not as a simple biological stage, but as experience shaped by language and power.

Lipman's philosophy for children is set against Kohan's warning about turning philosophy into a fixed method. Foucault shows how schooling disciplines and sorts children. Larrosa presents childhood as mystery needing welcome, while Agamben links it to language and history. A tension runs throughout: efforts to control children versus childhood as openness, difference, and new beginnings.
openalex-w7213466433:
Bruna Emily Faustino Baptista returns with co-authors, now reviewing teaching practices for literacy in the first two school years. Their 2026 systematic review searches SciELO Brazil from 2015 to 2026. Sixteen studies were kept under PRISMA guidance, with a thematic synthesis.

Debate between literacy as code learning and literacy as social practice runs through the field. Recent curriculum policy, including the national common base, shapes much recent research. Sound awareness and other cognitive processes receive strong attention. A clear gap remains: few studies examine teacher mediation inside real classrooms. The authors argue that future work must watch practice closely, not only discuss policy and theory.
openalex-w7213512733:
Matheus de Souza Machado Barboza and co-workers review diagnostic strategy for pulmonary tuberculosis. Their 2026 and review follows PRISMA guidance. PubMed, SciELO, and Scopus were searched for original work, reviews, and trials from 2023 to 2026 in three languages.

Careful clinical assessment, direct sputum smear testing, and a rapid molecular test form the core trio, the review finds. Together they speed early detection and flag resistance to a key drug, rifampicin. Bacterial culture remains the reference standard, vital when few bacilli are present and during treatment monitoring. Stronger laboratory networks inside Brazil's public system are presented as essential to break community transmission.
openalex-w7213536933:
Antonio Cerino Dias Cohen Ferreira and Cleidison da Silva Santos build a teaching tool for the Archimedean solids. Their 2026 applied article uses GeoGebra Classic 5, a dynamic maths program. It addresses a shortage of interactive materials that show three-dimensional transformations step by step.

Starting from the Platonic solids, the authors model cutting, expansion, and snub processes dynamically. Sliders and vector animations give a tactile-visual feel for how the thirteen solids arise. Exact deductive calculations sit behind the animations. The aim is to cut the abstraction that makes spatial geometry hard. History of maths, rigorous proof, and computer modelling are joined to support teaching at school and university level.
openalex-w7213949233:
Ana Carolina Fontana Morgan leads a systematic review, in English, on thinking outcomes in early-onset epilepsy. Their 2026 review follows PRISMA guidance and searches PubMed for the last fifteen years, in English or Portuguese. Ten studies entered the qualitative synthesis, with quality checked by standard tools.

Early epilepsy was tied consistently to weaker executive function, attention, and memory. Language, visuo-motor skills, and mental processing speed also suffered. Worse outcomes followed earlier seizure onset and hard-to-control epilepsy, among other factors named. Age at onset, cause, seizure burden, and medication use can all shape cognition during key brain growth periods. The review maps that risk for clinicians and families.
openalex-w7214187833:
Fernanda Chicralla Siqueira and Carla Sarlo Carneiro Chrysóstomo study the gap between teaching theory and practice in Brazilian technical schooling. Their 2026 library, study adds an objective questionnaire given to trainee pupils at a state public school in Campos dos Goytacazes, Rio de Janeiro.

Supervised placement should be a field of knowledge and critical reflection, they argue, not model imitation or technique repetition. Most pupils could relate theory to practice, the data show. A significant minority, about one in six, found theory distant from placement reality. Technical course curricula need reform to fit professional training needs, they conclude. Graduates must leave ready to extend and apply what they know.
openalex-w7214445133:
Víctor Béjar Tinoco, Flor Madrigal Moreno, and Salvador Madrigal Moreno, all at a Mexican university, reviewed research on university marketing in the digital era for a 2026 article. Their review covers studies from 2020 to 2026 indexed in major databases, and asks how universities attract and keep students when most contact now happens online.

Instead of treating digital tools separately, they organize the field into six linked areas, including market strategy, branding and reputation, social media, student experience, loyalty, and artificial intelligence with analytics. These areas increasingly converge around the student journey, they find. Artificial intelligence acts mainly as a supporting layer for automation and personalization. Their closing framework ties these capacities to attraction, retention, and reputation, with responsible data use running through all of it.
openalex-w7216551833:
Cleber Nonato Macedo Costa led a 2026 review on using nanotechnology to turn turmeric's active compound, curcumin, into a better anti-inflammatory therapy. Turmeric, Curcuma longa, has long interested drug researchers, and curcumin shows anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects in experiments. Its weakness is practical: it barely melts in water, is absorbed badly, and is broken down fast, so little reaches the body in usual products.

Packing curcumin into nanoscale carriers offers a fix. Polymeric nanoparticles, liposomes, and nanoemulsions raised its spreading, stability, protection, and release in studies so far. Real blocks remain: safety and toxicity, shared standards, production cost, and scale, and lab and preclinical results cannot yet confirm a healing effect in humans. The authors judge this a promising but unfinished path for new drugs.
outlines-of-phrenology-being-also-a-manu: Outlines of Phrenology, 1833. The reference manual. This book preserves that work. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
phrenology-in-connexion-with-the-study-o: Phrenology in Connexion with the Study of Physiognomy, 1833. Another edition. This book preserves that work. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
pitcairn-ancient-criminal-trials-vol1-18:
Robert Pitcairn gathered Scotland's old criminal trials from the justiciary records, and volume one appeared in 1833. Ancient Criminal Trials in Scotland opens in 1488 and runs to 1596. Among its cases stand the North Berwick witch trials that gripped King James the Sixth.

Murder, treason, feud, and witchcraft fill the records in the court's own terse style. Pitcairn prints the charges and verdicts as the clerks kept them, with brief guides for the reader. The volume shows a hard land living under a hard law. It opens the great archive of Scotland's criminal past for all later study.
pitcairn-ancient-criminal-trials-vol2-18:
Pitcairn's second volume of Scottish criminal trials runs from 1596 to 1609. Printed in 1833 with the rest of the set, it carries the justiciary records into the reign of James the Sixth and First. The courts of Edinburgh sit at the center of the work.

Case follows case: killings, plots, church strife, and charges of witchcraft among them. The records speak in the dry voice of the court, which makes the violence in them strike the harder. Readers see early Stuart Scotland through its crimes and punishments. The volume keeps the long run of the archive unbroken.
pitcairn-ancient-criminal-trials-vol3-18:
The third volume of Pitcairn's Scottish trials covers 1609 to 1624 and closes the set in full. Printed in 1833, it ends a run of records that began in 1488. Three volumes thus span more than a century of Scottish criminal courts.

The last years of James the Sixth's Scottish reign supply the cases here in rich supply. Feuds, murders, and trials for hidden crimes fill the court's rolls from year to year. Pitcairn's care in printing the old records made the set a working tool for historians. Together the volumes give Scotland's criminal past in its own words, start to end.
plos-pbio-0020233:
Jyoti K. Jaiswal, Sabyasachi Chakrabarti, Norma W. Andrews, and their group studied cell dumping in PLOS Biology in 2004. Lysosomes are sacs inside cells that hold digestive enzymes. When they fuse with the cell surface, they dump their contents outside, a process called exocytosis.

A sensor protein called synaptotagmin VII controls how wide the fusion pore opens. The team shows it keeps the pore from expanding too fast or too far. That restraint may let cells release contents in a measured way, or reseal the pore. The work matters for wound repair, where lysosome dumping helps patch torn cell membranes, and for diseases where that release runs wild.
plos-pbio-0020333:
Lars I. Leichert and Ursula Jakob developed a way to see protein damage inside living cells in PLOS Biology in 2004. Many proteins carry sulfur-based groups called thiols. Oxidative stress changes those groups, and the changes can act as signals or as harm.

Their method tags the changed thiols so they can be spotted in intact cells. Before this, such changes were mostly read in ground-up samples where the living pattern was lost.
