Watching them in place shows which proteins react first when stress hits. That view helps sort helpful redox signals from plain damage, a split that matters for diseases from heart failure to neurodegeneration.
plos-pone-0000033:
Cathy Collins, Peter Azmi, Maribel Berru, and co-authors weakened a genetic switch and watched the patchwork result in a 2006 study. An enhancer is a stretch of DNA that boosts a gene's activity. Turn the enhancer down, the team found, and the gene no longer behaves evenly across cells.

Instead they got variegated expression: the gene switched fully on in some cells and off in their near-identical neighbors, like a mosaic. That patchiness is more than a curiosity. It shows how small changes in a control element can produce mixed tissues. The pattern appears in real diseases, where one cell type is split between working and silent copies of a gene.
plos-pone-0000133:
Timothy J. Crone, William S. D. Wilcock, Andrew H. Barclay, and colleagues published this ocean study in PLOS ONE in 2006. Black smokers are vents on the deep sea floor, along mid-ocean ridges, where superheated water pours out of cracks in the crust. The team recorded and analyzed the sound these vents make.

Measuring vent noise is more than a curiosity. Sound offers a way to monitor vents that are far too deep and hot to watch directly. The authors characterize what the vents sound like and what drives the noise. The results help oceanographers read deep-sea activity from a distance, using hydrophones.
plos-pone-0000233:
Sutirth Dey and Amitabh Joshi published this population ecology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. They keep laboratory populations of fruit flies arranged as metapopulations, groups of linked local populations. The authors disturbed single local populations and found, as the title says, that these local perturbations do not affect the stability of the whole metapopulation.

Whether a connected system absorbs local shocks matters for conservation, where habitats are patchy. The fly experiments suggest the wider network stays steady even when one patch is hit. Results like this test ecological theory in a system small enough to watch completely, something impossible in the wild.
plos-pone-0000333:
Daniel Goldreich published this perception theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The cutaneous rabbit is a famous tactile illusion. Taps at the wrist and elbow feel like a rabbit hopping up the arm, landing at spots never touched. The author presents a Bayesian perceptual model, a model that weighs evidence like a statistician, that reproduces this and other touch illusions.

A model that predicts where phantom taps are felt supports the idea that perception is inference, not recording. The paper extends that account across several spatiotemporal illusions of touch. It links a party-trick illusion to a serious theory of how brains build sensation.
plos-pone-0000433:
Jim Karagiannis and Mohan K. Balasubramanian described a kinase with an unexpected second job, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Cyclin-dependent kinases are famous for driving the cell cycle. This one also promotes cytokinesis, the final split of one cell into two. It does so by modulating phosphorylation of the tail of Rpb1p. Rpb1p is the largest subunit of RNA polymerase II, the enzyme that reads genes.

Phosphorylation tags on the polymerase tail coordinate how gene messages are made and processed. Linking a cell-cycle kinase to those tags during division suggests the cell syncs its split with its gene-reading machinery. The finding comes from fission yeast, where such core machinery is easiest to dissect.
plos-pone-0000533:
Peixin Zhu and colleagues tightened the control of a workhorse gene switch in neurons, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The tetracycline-controlled system lets researchers turn a chosen gene on with a drug dose. The team worked on silencing and un-silencing of tetracycline-controlled genes in neurons, where leaky expression can ruin an experiment.

Neurons are long-lived and sensitive, so a switch that truly stays off until called is valuable. Precise control lets scientists ask what a gene does in the adult brain without disturbing development. Improvements of this sort rarely make news, but they raise the reliability of a whole generation of brain gene experiments.
plos-pone-0000633:
Sergey N. Arkhipov and Ivan V. Maly modeled a positioning problem inside T cells for PLOS ONE in 2007. When a T cell meets an antigen-presenting cell, its inner parts turn toward that partner. Aimed that way, the immune response lands where it should. The mechanisms behind the orientation were largely unknown.

At the center sits the T-cell receptor, which recognizes the antigen and keeps recycling through the cell surface. The model plays receptor recycling against receptor-mediated contact to see how the two together shape orientation. Modelers get testable structure here, and immunologists get a clearer picture of how a T cell aims itself.
plos-pone-0000733:
Nagendra N. Thakur, Susanne El-Gogo, Beatrix Steer and co-authors studied repeated DNA inside a herpesvirus genome, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Gammaherpesviruses cause important infections in humans, especially in patients with weakened immune systems. Their genomes contain variable numbers of internal repeats. The precise role of those repeats in disease inside a living host was not well understood.

Using laboratory infections, the team tested what one such repeat does. The title states its contribution: the repeat helps amplify latency, the virus's dormant state. Latency is how herpesviruses persist for life. A genome feature that boosts it is a target worth knowing for any cure strategy.
plos-pone-0000833:
Gilles Crevel, Reina Hashimoto, Sharron Vass and colleagues asked how many of the cell's replication machines are truly needed, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The MCM2-7 proteins are crucial components of the pre-replication complex in eukaryotes, licensing DNA for copying. They are significantly more abundant than other components of that complex. The team wanted to determine whether the entire cellular content was necessary for DNA replication in vivo.

Working in Drosophila S2 cells, they report differential requirements for MCM proteins: not every member is needed in equal measure. Surplus licensing factors may serve as backup against replication stress. Knowing the true minimum matters for understanding replication failure in cancer cells.
plos-pone-0000933:
Sung Yon Um and Thomas McDonald studied how two small partner proteins pair with a heart channel, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The proteins, KCNE1 and KCNE2, were both proposed as helpers for the HERG channel. That channel helps reset the heart's electrical beat, so its partners matter for safe rhythm.

Using a cell system where both partners were expressed, the pair report that KCNE1 was pulled down with the channel more readily than KCNE2. Unequal pairing hints the two helpers are not interchangeable. The detail feeds into work on inherited rhythm disorders. It also shows why drug side effects on HERG are so closely watched.
plos-pone-0001033:
Jacques Zimmer, Huguette Bausinger, Emmanuel Andres and colleagues phenotyped natural killer cells in people missing a transport protein, for PLOS ONE in 2007. TAP deficiency blocks a transporter that loads antigen pieces for display. Natural killer cells from such patients respond weakly, though their surface profile looks almost normal.

The team looked closer at NK cell subsets in these patients and noticed a distinguishing feature in their makeup. Rare deficiencies are natural experiments: one missing part reveals what the whole system needs. Their close phenotyping may explain the weak response that a normal surface scan hides. It also informs care for a very small patient group.
plos-pone-0001133:
MicroRNAs are short pieces of RNA that fine-tune gene activity, and they turn up again and again in cancer. Igor Makunin and colleagues asked where the genes for these molecules sit in the genome, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They compared human and mouse data.

The authors used a public database of mapped retroviral insertion sites from mouse cancer models. They found that matching microRNA genes in the two species tend to lie in genome regions tied to cancer. That pattern hints that these regulatory genes are not placed at random. It also gives cancer researchers a clue about which genome regions deserve closer looks.
plos-pone-0001233:
Night work fights human biology: the circadian system promotes sleep at night, and the first night shift piles sleep deprivation on top of that misalignment. Nayantara Santhi and colleagues measured one cost, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They studied visual selective attention, the ability to focus on relevant sights and ignore the rest.

The authors report that acute sleep deprivation and circadian misalignment, combined as they are on a first night of work, impair that attention. Cognitive deficits from night work grow as sleep pressure mounts. Quantifying the impairment on the very first night speaks to how shifts should be scheduled.
plos-pone-0001333:
Choosing between a small reward now and a larger one later is a daily problem, and serotonin is suspected of shaping that choice. Saori Tanaka and colleagues used brain imaging to study serotonin's role in reward prediction, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Animal experiments on impulsivity had suggested serotonin matters for behaviors requiring prediction of delayed rewards.

The authors report that serotonin regulates prediction of rewards differently over short and long terms. The two zones involved are the ventral and dorsal striatum, parts of a reward-related brain region. Low and high serotonin shifted predictions over different horizons. Their results connect a single chemical to the mechanics of patience.
plos-pone-0001433:
Mathieu Marella and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on shielding brain cells in a rat model of Parkinson's disease. Faults in the cell power unit are closely tied to this disease. A toxin that blocks that unit is used to mimic the disease in rats. The team tested a yeast gene that can bypass the blocked step.

Rats given the gene were guarded against the toxin's harm to dopamine nerve cells. That guard effect backs the power unit view of the disease. It also shows that gene based bypass is at least in part feasible. More work would be needed before any use in people could be weighed.
plos-pone-0001533:
Keisuke Yonehara and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a subtype of eye nerve cell in mice. About a dozen types of these cells carry visual data to the brain. How each type grows and wires was still in its early days. The team used a marker gene that lights up just one type.

The lit cells project to a small brain hub that steers eye motion. That clean line marks the type's job in the visual web. A marker for one type lets labs trace its growth step by step. Such maps are the base for work on sight loss and repair.
plos-pone-0001633:
Stephen E. Malawista and Anne de Boisfleury Chevance filmed the Lyme disease germ in motion for a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The germ is Borrelia burgdorferi, a corkscrew-shaped bacterium spread by ticks. For the body's hunter cells to clear it, they first have to catch it, and that depends on how fast the germ can swim.

Using real-time phase-contrast video microscopy, the authors timed the spirochete. It moved back and forth across a platelet, a small blood cell fragment it had attached to. The full text gives the speeds they measured and what the films show about how the germ moves. Hard numbers on the germ's motion help explain how it slips through tissues and dodges the immune system in early Lyme disease.
plos-pone-0001733:
José Antonio Picanço Diniz and co-authors tracked brain infection by two rare viruses in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Itacaiunas and Curionópolis are Brazilian rhabdoviruses that prefer nerve tissue. Earlier reports had proposed a new genus for them and described gross brain pathology in infected newborn mice.

This study followed the time course of the encephalitis they cause, marking early and late pathogenic events. The full text gives the infection timeline, the brain lesions at each stage, and how the two viruses compare. A stage-by-stage record helps virologists place new rhabdoviruses and understand how nerve-loving viruses damage the developing brain.
plos-pone-0001833:
Travis J. Bourret, Steffen Porwollik, and Michael McClelland studied how stomach defenses attack Salmonella in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Reactive nitrogen species, derived from dietary and salivary nitrogen oxides, support the innate defenses of the acidic stomach. The mechanisms by which these species kill microbes in the gastric lumen were poorly understood.

The team reports that nitric oxide antagonizes the acid tolerance response that protects Salmonella against innate gastric defenses, leaving the bacteria exposed to acid. The full text gives the survival experiments and the response pathway data. The stomach is the gate most foodborne germs must pass, so its chemistry is a first line of food safety.
plos-pone-0001933:
Stephen Millen and co-authors studied how delays in finding tuberculosis change the path to care, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Many steps can stall a case: the patient waits, the clinic tests slowly, or results come back late. Each day of delay leaves a sick person untreated in the community, free to pass the germ to others.

The team focused on two effects of diagnostic delay: how many patients drop out before care, and how long the total wait to diagnosis grows. Work that pins down where time is lost tells health services where to act first. Faster diagnosis is one of the cheapest ways to cut spread.
plos-pone-0002033:
Alessandro Alboresi and co-authors charted the light-harvesting parts of a moss, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In green life forms, the antenna that catches light for photosynthesis is built from subunits of the light harvesting complex family. These proteins both gather light and protect the cell from too much of it.

The moss Physcomitrella patens is a land plant with a simple body, close to the first land plants. By computer and lab analysis, the team identified subunits that evolved when plants adapted to land. Such a parts list shows what dry, bright life demanded of the photosynthetic machine.
plos-pone-0002133:
Conor Doherty, Sharon Cox, Antony Fulford, and co-authors studied anemia that lingers after malaria, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Iron pills are often given to treat this anemia in places where iron shortage is also common. The problem is that malaria itself causes strong inflammation in the body, and that response locks iron away.

The authors explain how the inflamed body holds back iron from broken-down red blood cells and blocks iron taken by mouth. That makes plain why iron treatment can fail right after an attack of malaria. Their work helps doctors time iron therapy so the body can actually use the iron it is given.
plos-pone-0002233:
Jorieke Peters, Luuk Hilbrands, Hans Koenen, and co-authors grew patient-ready regulatory T cells in the lab, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Regulatory T cells calm the immune system, and therapy based on them is a hopeful route for immune disorders. In animal studies of transplantation and autoimmunity, success depended on T cells tuned to the exact target the immune system must learn to spare.

The team generated human regulatory T cells specific to a chosen alloantigen, starting from a rare blood cell group. Antigen-specific cells should work harder where they are needed and leave the rest of immunity alone. The method is a step toward cell therapy for transplant patients.
plos-pone-0002333:
Amit Dias, Michael Dewey, Jean D'Souza, and co-authors tested home care support for dementia caregivers in Goa, India, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In developing countries, families carry nearly all dementia care, often with no training or relief. The team developed a home based program to support those caregivers.

A randomised controlled trial assigned families to the program or to usual care. The team measured caregiver burden, caregiver mental health, and behavioral problems in the person with dementia. A low-cost home model that eases burden in Goa could be adapted wherever professional dementia services are thin on the ground.
plos-pone-0002433:
Djelouadji, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Zoheira Djelouadji, Catherine Arnold, Saheer Gharbia, among others. Its subject is multispacer Sequence Typing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis Genotyping. Genotyping methods developed to survey the transmission dynamics of Mycobacterium tuberculosis currently rely on the interpretation of restriction and amplification profiles.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002533:
Zafarmand and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Mohammad Hadi Zafarmand, Yvonne T. van der Schouw, Diederick E. Grobbee, among others. Its subject is the M235T Polymorphism in the AGT Gene and CHD Risk. The title goes on to note evidence of a Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium Violation and Publication Bias in a Meta-Analysis. The M235T polymorphism in the AGT gene has been related to an increased risk of hypertension.

This finding may also suggest an increased risk of coronary heart disease (CHD). The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002633:
Chana Palmer and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of systematic evaluation of candidate blood markers for detecting ovarian cancer. Authorship is credited in the record to Chana Palmer and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Epithelial ovarian cancer is a significant cause of mortality both in the United States and worldwide. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002733:
In 2008, Isabel Bäurle and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was differential interactions of the autonomous pathway RRM proteins and chromatin regulators in the silencing of arabidopsis targets. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Isabel Bäurle, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. We have recently shown that two proteins containing RRM-type RNA-binding domains, FCA and FPA. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002833:
In 2008, Barbara Jaron and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was effect of attenuation of treg during BCG immunization on Anti-Mycobacterial th1 responses and protection against mycobacterium tuberculosis. The catalog record names Barbara Jaron first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The functional equilibrium between natural regulatory T cells (Treg) and effector T cells can affect the issue of numerous infections. A further point appears in the abstract. In unvaccinated mice, the influence of Treg in the control of primary infection with mycobacteria remains controversial. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002933:
Steffen Steinert, Esther Lee, Guillaume Tresset and colleagues built a probe to trace fat traffic inside cells in 2008. Sphingolipids group into membrane microdomains and their movement is tied to viral infection, toxin entry, and storage diseases. Tools to watch that traffic live had been lacking.

Their probe is a fluorescent peptide that binds glycolipids and glows under the microscope. With it they traced pathways that depend on cholesterol-rich microdomains. Published in PLOS ONE, the probe gives cell biologists a way to follow lipid routes tied to several diseases and infections. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003033:
Koji Hase, Daisuke Takahashi, Masashi Ebisawa and co-authors studied autoimmunity in mice lacking the enzyme AID in 2008. AID works in germinal center B cells and centrally controls somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination, two ways antibodies are refined. Humans with AID faults develop a hyper-IgM syndrome.

AID deficiency also causes organ-specific autoimmune disease, the title reports. That pairing, weak antibody refinement plus autoimmunity, is the puzzle the paper explores. Published in PLOS ONE, it helps explain why some immune deficiencies come with the immune system attacking the body as well. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003133:
Claudia Scherr, Meinhard Simon, Jörg Spranger and colleagues test a duckweed bioassay in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Plants in the Lemna group are common test organisms in studies of toxins and the environment. They are small, grow fast, are easy to handle, and react strongly to many chemicals. Yet little was known about how stable the test system is over space and time.

The authors check the stability and natural variation of a Lemna gibba test. Readers learn how much results can shift for reasons other than the chemical being tested. That matters for anyone who relies on plant bioassays to judge water or chemical safety.
plos-pone-0003233:
Leigh-Ann Woolley, Joshua J. Millspaugh, Rami J. Woods and colleagues study elephants after a park fire in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In predator-free large herbivore populations, where feedbacks occur at the limit where forage can no longer support the population, environmental catastrophes may play a significant role in population regulation. Fire is one such potential event.

The team examine population and individual elephant response to a catastrophic fire in Pilanesberg National Park. Readers learn how the largest land animal copes with sudden habitat loss. That evidence matters for park managers who must decide how fire should be used or suppressed.
plos-pone-0003333:
Frank Hailer and Jennifer A. Leonard study hybridization among North American canids in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Population densities of many species throughout the world are changing due to direct persecution as well as anthropogenic habitat modification. These changes may induce or increase the frequency of hybridization among taxa. If extensive, hybridization can threaten genetic integrity of species.

The authors examine hybridization among three native North American Canis species in a region of natural sympatry, where their ranges overlap. Readers learn how wolves, coyotes and related canids mix where they meet. Hybridization complicates conservation law, which usually protects named species.
plos-pone-0003433:
Alison Wringe, Paul E. M. Fine, and Roland W. Sutter estimated a rare polio risk in this 2008 paper. The oral polio vaccine uses a weakened live virus. In rare cases, that virus changes and regains the power to spread. Such vaccine-derived virus can infect people much like wild polio.

The authors set out to estimate how much of that infection occurs. Their numbers feed into the endgame plan for eradicating polio. Stopping vaccine use at the right time depends on this risk. Too early or too late, the plan could seed new outbreaks.
plos-pone-0003533:
Yan Ding and co-authors found selection marks near a cancer-linked gene in this 2008 paper. A study of brothers with prostate cancer pointed to one locus. That spot sits inside FHIT, a tumor suppressor gene. FHIT can trigger death in faulty cells.

Within an intron of the gene, the team found a strong signature of natural selection. Introns are the non-coding stretches inside genes. Selection there hints the region does more than sit idle. The finding ties prostate cancer risk to deeper evolutionary history. Prostate cancer is among the most common cancers in men worldwide.
plos-pone-0003633:
Mats Dehlin, Maria Bokarewa, Robert Rottapel, and colleagues published this arthritis study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Rheumatoid arthritis swells the tissue lining the joints and fills it with immune cells. The team studied Flt3 ligand, a signal that helps blood and immune cells grow.

The authors found this signal inside the joint itself, where it helps drive the disease. Its local presence pushed both the start of arthritis and its later worsening in their tests. The work points to a target within the joint for drugs meant to calm this inflammation at its source.
plos-pone-0003733:
Jörg Fröbisch published this paleontology paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. The end-Permian crisis, about 252.5 million years ago, was the most severe extinction in Earth's history. Anomodonts were plant-eating relatives of early mammals that lived through that event.

Fröbisch tracked the group's global taxonomic diversity through time and across the Permian-Triassic boundary. He set those curves against the terrestrial rock record, which can bias what fossils are found. The survey shows which anomodonts made it through the Great Dying and where they held on. Such records help judge how the rock record itself skews the tale.
plos-pone-0003833:
Sanna P. Seitsonen, Päivi Onkamo, Gang Peng, and colleagues published this eye genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Age-related macular degeneration is the most common cause of visual impairment in industrialized countries. Variants in complement genes and in the LOC387715 region are widely reported to raise its risk.

The team investigated whether two variants, CFH Y402H and LOC387715 A69S, interact. They report combined effects beyond what each variant does alone. Such interaction refines estimates of who faces the highest odds of losing central vision to this disease. Such joint effects matter when clinics weigh a patient's risk.
plos-pone-0003933:
Rongzhong Jin, Zhengbing Lv, Qin Chen, and co-authors built a bird flu vaccine in silkworms in 2008. The H5N1 virus has caused severe infections in people. It also carries the risk of becoming a wider pandemic threat. Workable vaccines against it were urgently needed.

Their PLOS ONE article reports a vaccine built on a baculovirus display system. The virus grows in the silkworm Bombyx mori and shows flu proteins on its surface. The team tested safety and the immune response it raised. Silkworm-based output could offer a cheap way to make vaccine in bulk. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004033:
Ian C. Grieve, Nicholas J. Dickens, Michal Pravenec, and co-authors analyzed gene co-expression across tissues in 2008. Some DNA regions govern how strongly nearby genes are expressed. Others exert control from far away in the genome. Evidence also suggested genes in clusters get co-regulated.

Their PLOS ONE article runs a genome-wide co-expression analysis across tissues. Coordinated activity can reveal shared control points. It also helps assign function to genes by the company they keep. Multi-tissue data make the resulting networks broader and sturdier. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004133:
Su Wang and colleagues published this heart study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The team used mice bred to make extra copies of a calcium channel part called alpha-1C in the heart. By four months of age these mice had enlarged hearts and swollen heart muscle cells. They also had stronger calcium currents, yet a normal store of calcium inside the cells.

As the mice aged to eight to eleven months, some went on to develop dilated cardiomyopathy, a stretched and weak heart. The study traces the order of events: an over-contracting state and failure of the heart to relax came before the later calcium overload. That sequence helps explain how this kind of heart failure builds over time.
plos-pone-0004233:
Vinca Icard and colleagues published this hepatitis C study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hepatitis C virus particles in the blood of long-term patients vary widely in density. The lightest particles owe their buoyancy to riding on apolipoprotein B positive lipoproteins, the fat-carrying particles rich in triglycerides.

The team asked whether the virus's envelope glycoproteins, its outer coat proteins, can be secreted without that lipid system. They report that secretion depends on building apoB-positive lipoproteins. The virus, in effect, ships itself out inside the liver's fat-export system. It cannot leave the cell well without that fat machinery.
plos-pone-0004333:
Dan Arking and colleagues published this heart genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Extremes of the electrocardiographic QT interval, a measure of the heart's electrical reset, are associated with increased risk of sudden cardiac death. Identifying the genetic variants that modulate the QT interval may reveal the underlying causes of that risk. Earlier studies had already pointed to the gene region NOS1AP.

In a multi-ethnic population, the team report multiple independent genetic factors at NOS1AP that modulate the QT interval. Several separate variants in one region each nudge the heartbeat's timing, and together they shape risk.
plos-pone-0004433:
Many proteins have loose, floppy regions with no fixed shape, and Avner Schlessinger, Marco Punta, Guy Yachdav, and co-authors improved computer prediction of those regions in PLOS ONE in 2009. Such disordered proteins are common in jobs like gene control and cell signaling. Different prediction tools tend to be good at different kinds of disorder.

The team combined several separate approaches into one predictor, which they call MD, for META-Disorder. By pooling methods that see the problem from unlike angles, the combined tool judges disorder better than single tools. Better maps of floppy regions help biologists guess what a new protein does. They also matter for drug design, since loose regions can form pockets that medicines might grip.
plos-pone-0004533:
Compounds that jam a step in gene splicing can protect against retroviruses, report Anne Keriel, Florence Mahuteau-Betzer, Chantal Jacquet, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The compounds are indole derivatives, a new class of splicing inhibitors. They act selectively on the splicing help given by proteins called SR proteins, which guide how gene messages are cut and joined.

Some of these molecules had already been shown to compromise the assembly of HIV, blocking the virus from building new copies. This work extends that protection against retrovirus pathogenesis more broadly. Splicing is a step the virus cannot skip and cannot easily change. Targeting the cell's own splicing helpers, rather than the virus, may also make drug resistance harder for the virus to evolve.
plos-pone-0004633:
A pondweed that grows three kinds of leaves shows adaptation written into a key photosynthesis gene, report Satoko Iida, Atsuko Miyagi, Seishiro Aoki, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Heterophyllous aquatic plants adapt to environmental changes by producing different leaf types: submerged, floating, and terrestrial leaves. Homophyllous plants, by contrast, produce only submerged leaves and grow entirely underwater.

The gene studied is rbcL, which encodes part of Rubisco, the enzyme that captures carbon dioxide. The team examined molecular adaptation of that gene in the heterophyllous genus Potamogeton. A plant that must photosynthesize in air and water faces two different worlds. Changes in its core carbon gene record how evolution tuned it for both.
plos-pone-0004733:
Uli Broedl and colleagues reported that low levels of a fat hormone predict soft, risky artery plaques, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Blocked heart arteries are the main cause of heart artery disease. What a plaque is made of matters more for sudden harm than how big it is, doctors now know.

Soft plaques with little calcium are more prone to burst and cause attacks. The team found low hormone levels linked on their own to such plaques. A simple blood test could help flag patients at higher risk. Those patients could then get closer watch and stronger care.
plos-pone-0004833:
Joseph Gillespie led a team that mapped an odd secretion system in Rickettsia bacteria for PLOS ONE in 2009. Such systems move DNA or proteins from one cell to a new host cell. Most bacteria use them to swap genes or to inject proteins into host cells during infection of plants, animals, or people.

The Rickettsia form stands out as odd, yet it is kept in all strains the team checked. These bacteria live inside host cells and cause spotted fevers and typhus. A system kept by all of them is apt to do a key job. That job may be to push proteins into host cells. If so, the system is a good target for new drugs.
plos-pone-0004933:
Interferons are alarm proteins that help the body fight viruses. The interferon-lambda family is one of their less understood branches. Brian Fox, Paul Sheppard and Patrick O'Hara studied its origins. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They used genomic data to annotate the family and trace its history.

Lambda proteins fold much like type-I interferons and the IL-10 family. Yet their sequences have drifted far. The kinship is hard to see from sequence alone. Genome-level evidence let the authors recover it. The study shows how genome maps can rescue relationships that sequences hide.
plos-pone-0005033:
Tiny RNAs called microRNAs steer development. Many work only in specific tissues. Tali Avnit-Sagi and colleagues found a switch behind one such case. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The microRNA is miR-375. Its gene's promoter was the subject of the study.

The promoter directs expression selectively to the endocrine pancreas. That is the hormone-making part of the pancreas. The switch explains the microRNA's tissue loyalty. It also gives researchers a precise tool. They can now drive chosen genes in the endocrine pancreas alone. Such tools are gold for diabetes research. They let scientists test gene functions in exactly the right cells.
plos-pone-0005133:
Metastatic lung cancer has grim survival with standard chemotherapy. A small fraction of tumors carry EGFR mutations. Those respond better to targeted drugs like gefitinib. Rafael Rosell and colleagues customized treatment in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used EGFR mutation status to assign therapy. They also measured BRCA1 message levels in tumors.

Treatment was tailored to each patient's markers. The customized approach aimed to beat one-size-fits-all chemo. BRCA1 levels helped choose among chemotherapy options. The study is a step toward matching lung cancers to their best drugs. It treats molecular testing as a treatment guide, not a curiosity. Such personalization is now central to oncology. This trial was an early proof of the principle.
plos-pone-0005233:
Some tumors, such as bone cancers and bone metastases, harden with calcium and depend on new blood vessels to grow. Treating them is an urgent unmet need. Segal and colleagues built a combined polymer therapy aimed at those tumors in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Polymers can carry drugs through the body and release them at a chosen target. The team combined polymer-bound agents to strike the vessel-dependent, calcified growths together. A guided, combined attack could hit bone tumors harder than single drugs while sparing the rest of the body.
plos-pone-0005333:
Predatory fish are thinning out on Caribbean reefs, but catch records can mislead about how badly. Stallings used fishery-independent data, surveys not based on catches, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The data reveal an effect of human population density on reef predators.

Region-wide assessments are hard because data are often thin in developing areas. Survey data showed denser human populations go with weaker predatory fish communities. Unbiased numbers like these give reef managers a firmer basis for fishing rules and marine reserves. Reef fish counts made by divers do not depend on what boats choose to land. So they show the true state of a reef even where catch logs are thin or not kept at all.
plos-pone-0005433:
Raheleh Salari and co-authors built a computer tool for finding hidden genes in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Some RNA strands do not make proteins but still do key jobs, such as turning genes up or down. Finding the genes for these RNAs in a genome is hard, since they leave few clear marks.

Their tool, called smyRNA, searches DNA for patterns in the shape and order of the code that hint at such genes. It works from the code alone, without needing a known example first. Tools like it help complete the map of what genomes contain and what those parts do.
plos-pone-0005533:
Jun Gao, Mari Davidson, and Wayne Wahls studied gene swapping in fission yeast for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Stress-sensing enzymes help cells react to hard conditions inside and outside. One such system works through a protein called Atf1, which binds DNA at set sites and can boost gene swapping nearby.

The team found that Atf1 boosts swapping during the making of sex cells even when the stress enzyme's usual tag is missing. That means the protein has a second way to act. The detail refines how cells link stress to the mixing of genes in offspring.
plos-pone-0005633:
Konstantinos Xanthopoulos and co-authors studied sugar patterns on prion proteins in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Prion diseases, such as mad cow disease, begin when a normal protein refolds into a harmful form. Both forms carry sugar chains at two sites.

The team compared the sugar patterns of the harmful form across species and strains. The patterns differed in ways that may help tell strains apart. Sugar fingerprints could improve tests that must distinguish prion strains for food safety and diagnosis. Strains differ in which species they infect and how fast they act, so telling them apart is more than a naming exercise.
plos-pone-0005733:
João Wanderley and colleagues showed in 2009 that dead-looking parasites help live ones cause leishmaniasis. Some Leishmania parasites copy the surface marks of dying human cells, a trick called apoptotic mimicry. Those marks tell host cells to stand down rather than attack.

The team found that the mimics and the normal live parasites work as a team. Together they infect more strongly than either group alone. The mimics quiet the host, letting the live parasites settle in. That teamwork helps explain why this disease can be so hard to clear, and suggests blocking the quiet signal as a tactic.
plos-pone-0005833:
Jason Rasgon proposed in 2009 a genetic scheme to spread engineered traits through mosquito populations, or to erase them. Replacing wild mosquitoes with modified ones that cannot spread disease is a serious control idea. But engineered mosquitoes are usually less fit, so their genes fade out.

His multi-locus assortment plan uses several gene sites to drive the trait in and keep it in. Multiple loci make the drive harder for the population to shed. The paper works through the logic before any field release. Such planning is essential, since released gene drives cannot easily be recalled.
plos-pone-0005933:
Some cancer drugs work better as a pair than alone. Hwang-Phill Kim, Young-Kwang Yoon, Jin-Won Kim and colleagues asked in 2009 why lapatinib pairs well with a class of chemotherapy drugs. Lapatinib blocks two growth receptors, EGFR and HER2. The PLOS ONE paper traces its effect on thymidylate synthase, an enzyme tumors often make in excess.

The drug lowers that enzyme by keeping EGFR and HER2 out of the cell nucleus, the team reports. With less of the enzyme, cancer cells grow weaker and the partner drug hits harder. Naming this chain of events gives doctors a clear reason for the pairing and a lead for picking patients most likely to gain.
plos-pone-0006033:
People with Alzheimer's disease suffer heart attacks and heart failure at high rates. Subat Turdi, Rui Guo, Anna Huff and colleagues asked in 2009 whether the disease itself weakens the heart. Their PLOS ONE paper uses a mouse model carrying Alzheimer's genes, called APPswe/PS1dE9, and tests heart muscle cells for faulty contraction.

The title confirms the fault: heart muscle contraction is impaired in these mice. The team also checked the cells' calcium handling and the proteins that govern it. A brain disease with a heart shadow widens what Alzheimer's care should watch, and the mouse gives researchers a way to learn where the two organs' troubles meet.
plos-pone-0006133:
Some genomes are patchworks, stitched from borrowed parts. Paul Morris, Laura Schlosser, Katherine Onasch and colleagues read the patchwork of an oomycete in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper analyzes the genome of Phytophthora sojae, a water mold that rots soybean roots, using strict criteria to find complex proteins built from fused domains.

Multiple horizontal gene transfers and domain fusions built novel regulatory and metabolic networks in this genome, the title reports, including hundreds of new multifunctional proteins. Borrowed genes let a pathogen reinvent its chemistry quickly. The catalog gives plant disease research a map of the enemy's inventions, and evolution a worked example of novelty by theft and fusion.
plos-pone-0006233:
Human embryonic stem cells could supply fresh tissue for many diseases, but lab recipes often rely on animal products. Andrzej Swistowski and colleagues report cleaner culture conditions in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. For clinical use, cells must be grown in fully defined conditions with nothing animal-derived.

Their four-step, scalable method grows the stem cells, then neural stem cells, then dopamine neurons from them. Dopamine neurons are the cells lost in Parkinson's disease. A defined recipe makes batches more consistent and safer to consider for patients. It also eases the path from lab promise toward real cell therapy.
plos-pone-0006333:
Old World vultures are in steep decline, and the Egyptian vulture is one of them. Laura Gangoso and her team set island birds against mainland birds in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They checked how prone each group is to infection and how strong their immune defence is.

Changes in how farm animals are kept are a main cause of the mainland crash, the authors note. Germs add a second threat that acts on top of the first. Island and mainland birds face these threats in unlike ways. Knowing the gaps helps plans to save the birds aim at the right risks.
plos-pone-0006433:
José Rivera and co-authors studied a protein that holds back cancer spread in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The protein, BRMS1, cuts the number and size of secondary tumors in a mouse model of breast cancer. It does this without slowing the main tumor's growth. When BRMS1 levels fall, spread becomes more likely.

The team searched for the short sequences in BRMS1 that send it to the right place inside the cell. Place matters, because a protein can only work where it sits. Pinpointing those address tags clarifies how BRMS1 does its job. That knowledge may help efforts to block metastasis, the deadliest part of cancer.
plos-pone-0006533:
Santanu Dasgupta, Rex Yung, William Westra, and colleagues followed mitochondrial changes on the road to lung cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mitochondrial DNA mutations are reported in different tumors. However, there was no information on the temporal development of these mutations or content changes along the path to cancer. The team traced mitochondrial footprints through a long mucosal path in the airways.

Following changes step by step shows when mitochondrial damage appears. Early markers could flag tissue on its way to cancer. The airway's surface gives a map of exposure to smoke and other harms. Their approach links that exposure history to molecular change.
plos-pone-0006633:
Frank Emmert-Streib and Matthias Dehmer predicted cell cycle genes from cause-and-effect links in PLOS ONE in 2009. Modern biology stands out for tools that yield huge data sets. Those sets give deep views of how molecules act on each other. The authors used causal interaction analysis, a method that infers which gene drives which. Their aim was to predict which genes the cell cycle controls.

Genes of the cell cycle drive cell division, and their faults lie at the root of cancer. A good forecast from data alone helps pick which genes to test in the lab first. The paper adds a tool to the kit for reading large gene data sets.
plos-pone-0006733:
Jean-Christian Borel and co-authors compared blood vessel health in obesity hypoventilation syndrome in PLOS ONE in 2009. People with this syndrome breathe too shallowly, especially in sleep. The syndrome brings higher cardiovascular illness. Obesity alone inflames the body and stiffens blood vessels. What chronic under-breathing adds on top was unknown.

The team compared inflammatory status and endothelial function across groups. The endothelium is the inner lining that controls vessel behavior. They asked whether hypoventilation worsens inflammation beyond obesity itself. Separating the two effects guides treatment priorities for these patients. It clarifies whether fixing breathing should calm vessel damage too.
plos-pone-0006833:
Simona Lamba and colleagues catalogued a specific mutation across human tumors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene is GNAQ, encoding part of a signaling protein. Mutations at one position, codon 209, had just been found frequently. They appeared in blue naevi and in uveal melanoma, an eye cancer. The mutations lock the protein in an active state.

The team profiled how widely the Q209 mutation occurs across tumors. A tight tumor profile helps pathologists use the mutation as a marker. It also marks patients who might suit targeted drugs. GNAQ joined the list of genes driving uveal melanoma. The profile sharpens that cancer's genetic picture.
plos-pone-0006933:
Valeria Petkova and H. Henrik Ehrsson explored a strange touch illusion in PLOS ONE in 2009. Feeling touch on a body part normally requires stimulation of that part itself. At least, that holds for healthy people without synaesthesia. Their experiments produced a different result, a kind of phantom touch.

Participants felt touch referred between their two hands. A touch on one hand could be felt as belonging to the other. Ownership of the hands seemed to shift along with the sensation. The illusion shows that the brain builds body ownership from signals it can rearrange. That finding informs research on prosthetics and on disorders of body perception.
plos-pone-0007033:
Yijun Chen, Rob Cairns, Ioanna Papandreou, and colleagues rethought tumor metabolism in PLOS ONE in 2009. Otto Warburg long ago described the odd metabolism of tumors. Cancer cells favor glycolysis and show reduced mitochondrial activity. Yet glycolysis yields far less energy per glucose than full respiration. That waste puzzled researchers for decades.

The team argued that oxygen use itself can throttle tumor growth. Their perspective reframes the Warburg effect as a regulated choice, not a defect. If oxygen consumption gates growth, then metabolism is a lever on tumors. The view suggests fresh drug strategies aimed at cancer's fuel handling.
plos-pone-0007133:
Helena Wensman, Nils-Erik Heldin, Gunnar Pejler, and colleagues profiled dog mammary tumors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Bone morphogenetic proteins, or BMPs, are gaining attention in tumor growth. Most BMP studies covered carcinomas, the common epithelial cancers. Sarcomas were little studied by comparison. Dog mammary tumors offer several tumor types in one system.

The team measured BMP expression across those tumor phenotypes. They also checked activation of the Smad pathway, the BMP relay. Expression profiles differed clearly by tumor type. Such maps may predict behavior and suggest which tumors answer to BMP-based drugs.
plos-pone-0007233:
Kuo-Hsiang Tang, Xueyang Feng, Yinjie J. Tang, and colleagues studied carbon use in a marine bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2009. Roseobacter bacteria make up a large share of marine bacterial communities. Reports said this group can fix carbon dioxide, but the pathway involved was still unknown.

The authors present metabolic studies on Roseobacter denitrificans OCh114. They examine carbohydrate metabolism alongside carbon fixation. Their work identifies how this common ocean bacterium gains carbon and energy. Ocean scientists can use the results to model how marine microbes shape global carbon cycles.
plos-pone-0007333:
Laura P. Smith, Maik Nierstenhoefer, Sang Wook Yoo, and colleagues reported bile acid production in the human ovary in 2009. Bile acids are end products of cholesterol elimination. They are required for absorbing dietary fats and fat-soluble vitamins, and they balance cholesterol synthesis in the liver against excretion from the body.

Finding that pathway outside the liver was unexpected. The authors show the bile acid synthesis pathway is present and functional in the human ovary. Their PLOS ONE result raises new questions about local cholesterol handling in reproduction. Ovarian bile acids may influence hormone production or egg development.
plos-pone-0007433:
Sherry Flint-Garcia and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on hybrid vigor in maize, the boost seen when different corn lines are crossed. Breeders call the effect heterosis: offspring outperform both parents. It is a foundation of modern corn farming. The team measured how widespread the effect is across many traits in a broad collection of maize varieties.

They found that heterosis shows up for multiple traits at once, not just one or two. The pattern held across diverse germplasm drawn from many breeding backgrounds. That breadth matters for breeders choosing which lines to cross. It suggests the vigor gained from mixing diverse parents is a general feature of maize. The results support breeding strategies built on wide genetic diversity.
plos-pone-0007533:
Junichi Funada and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on what fuel the failing human heart actually burns. The metabolism of the failing heart has been debated for years. Indirect estimates disagreed about which substrates it prefers. The team measured directly, sampling blood as it entered and left the heart. They studied patients with heart failure, patients with type 2 diabetes, and healthy controls.

Comparing blood in and blood out gave exact uptake numbers for each fuel. That arterio-venous method settles questions that estimates could not. Knowing what the struggling heart takes up shapes ideas about feeding or treating it. Energy starvation is part of heart failure, so fuel choice is not a detail. The study replaces a controversy with direct measurements in people.
plos-pone-0007633:
Laurent Schibler and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the gene defects behind several inherited short-stature conditions. Those chondrodysplasias involve FGFR3, a receptor that controls how cartilage cells mature. Most bones form through that cartilage route, so its timing is crucial. The molecular physiology of these conditions stayed only partly clear. The team profiled gene expression in human chondrocytes, the cartilage cells themselves.

Profiling the actual human cells revealed which gene programs the faulty receptor disturbs. That view is closer to patients than animal models alone. It shows how a single receptor's misbehavior ripples through bone growth. New insight of this kind guides the search for treatments for dwarfism conditions. Few such treatments exist today. The study maps the disturbed circuitry that any future therapy must address.
plos-pone-0007733:
Daniel Cheng and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks whether a well-known gene changes how the aging body works. The gene is APOE, and one form of it, called epsilon4, is tied to illness in old age. Healthy bodies show rich, complex patterns in signals like heart rate.

That complexity tends to fade with age. The team studied robust elderly adults, people aging unusually well. Those carrying the epsilon4 form showed reduced physiological complexity. The finding hints that genes help set the pace at which the body's systems lose their flexibility.
plos-pone-0007833:
Alexander Finlayson and Kevin Freeman published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It uses a cell motility screen to find genes that drive invasion. Cells invade through the matrix around them in wound healing and immune responses. Cancer uses the same machinery to metastasize.

Their screen pushed cells through chambers coated with matrix gel. Cells that invaded well carried pro-invasive genes worth naming. One hit was the MARCKS-related protein. It helps build adherens junctions, the seams between cells, and plays a role in tumor formation. The screen offers a way to map invasion genes systematically.
plos-pone-0007933:
Massimiliano Oliveri and colleagues studied how the brain links space and time, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2009. People speak of the past as behind them and the future as ahead. The team asked whether the cerebellum, a brain part best known for movement, helps hold that map.

Their tests tied the cerebellum to the way people join time words and time ideas to places in space. The link showed up for both action and language tasks. The work suggests the movement center also helps the mind lay time out in space, a habit built deep into how we talk and think.
plos-pone-0008033:
Ju-Hee Jeong and colleagues studied the brakes on a flowering signal in a small plant for PLOS ONE in 2009. The signal gene, FLOWERING LOCUS T, tells Arabidopsis when to bloom, and its message travels through the plant. Blooming too early or late can ruin seed set.

A team of enzymes that strip marks from the gene's wrapping proteins keeps the signal gene quiet until its time. More than one enzyme can do the job, so the brake holds even if one fails. That backup design shows how much rides on blooming on schedule.
plos-pone-0008133:
Lei Zhang and colleagues built a family-based gene test that reads two traits at once in PLOS ONE in 2009. Family studies are a sturdy way to link genes to traits, since they resist some common biases. Most tests still handle one trait at a time, wasting the fact that traits travel together.

Their joint test wrings more signal from the same families by using both traits and their link. More signal means fewer families needed for the same find, or bigger finds from the same data. The method suits the paired measures common in heart, bone, and brain studies.
plos-pone-0008233:
Hallan Souza-e-Silva and his team built a math model in PLOS ONE in 2009 of how T cells grow up. T cells are born in the thymus, a small organ near the heart. As they grow there, they touch cells and stuff round them again and again. Those touches help pick which young cells live and which die. A sound set of grown T cells is a must for the body to fight germs well.

Their model is based on grids of simple cells that act by small local rules. From such plain rules, rich growth forms can spring up on their own. A grid model lets labs test views of thymus growth that are hard to check in flesh. The work joins immune science with math.
plos-pone-0008333:
Andrea Li and Qasim Zaidi studied visual suppression and shape in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Cross-orientation suppression occurs in the striate cortex, an early visual area. It has been linked to efficient encoding of visual stimuli. The authors showed that release from this suppression helps decode three-dimensional shape. Textured surfaces slanted in depth became easier to read.

When a surface slants, parts of its texture gain visibility. The brain uses that change to judge the surface's shape. The finding connects a basic cortical mechanism to real perception. It helps explain how flat images yield solid shapes.
plos-pone-0008433:
Alvaro Cervera and co-authors link a gene to stroke outcome in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The gene makes a protein called mannose-binding lectin, or MBL. MBL starts one arm of the complement system, a part of innate defense. That system can also harm brain tissue after a stroke. The team study mice and people who lack working MBL.

They find that lack of MBL guards mice after a stroke made in the lab. They also link that lack to outcome in human stroke cases. The work points to a defense path that may do harm after stroke. Blocking it could one day help limit brain damage.
plos-pone-0008533:
Ben Spycher and co-authors build a disease model for wheezing in young children in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Wheezing disorders in childhood vary widely. Children differ in symptoms and in how illness unfolds over time. Several classifications into phenotypes have been proposed for clinical use. But validation of those schemes has lagged behind. The team base a new model on clinicians' own perceptions of cases.

They ask clinicians to judge similarities between wheezing children. Statistical modeling turns those judgments into disease phenotypes. Such a model reflects how doctors actually sort cases in practice. It may guide treatment choices better than schemes built on theory alone.
plos-pone-0008633:
Yuzo Yamamoto and co-authors study smell learning in salmon in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Juvenile salmon imprint the odors of their natal stream. As adults, they use that memory to home back and spawn. Neither the odor properties of stream water nor imprinting timing were clarified. The team focus on amino acids as candidate odor cues in lacustrine sockeye salmon. Those salmon mature in lakes rather than the ocean. They run electrophysiological and behavioral experiments.

They show amino acids are imprinted as olfactory cues by the juveniles. The timing and duration of that imprinting window are defined. Homing is thus chemically specific, not a vague stream memory. The work clarifies a famous migration mystery.
plos-pone-0008733:
Nicholas Rule and Nalini Ambady asked whether politics shows on a person's face. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tested a bold claim. Faces reveal obvious traits like age and sex at a glance. They may also carry faint hints of group membership. Political leaning has no clear visual marker, which makes it a hard test case.

Volunteers viewed photos of Democratic and Republican faces. Judges sorted them at rates better than chance. The cues remain subtle and hard to name outright. Still, the result suggests faces leak social information viewers can sense without knowing how. That finding feeds debate about snap judgments of strangers.
plos-pone-0008833:
Taketoshi Kiya and Takeo Kubo recorded neuron activity in the visual brain of honeybees. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Forager bees navigate by sight with remarkable skill. Their optic lobes process what the eyes take in. Some neurons use GABA, a calming signal, while others do not. The team compared foragers with bees re-orienting after hive moves.

Activity patterns differed between the two bee groups and neuron types. Those differences hint at how experience reshapes visual circuits. Bees that relearn landmarks may rewire their optic lobes. The work links navigation behavior to brain cell activity.
plos-pone-0008933:
Joseph Sacco and colleagues measured the body size of British cancer patients for PLOS ONE in 2010. Most chemotherapy drugs are dosed by body surface area, a measure based on height and weight. Britain had no standard figures for its own patients to base doses and costs on. The team gathered records from several cancer centres across the country.

They worked out the average surface area for adults receiving chemotherapy in the United Kingdom. The figures give hospitals a firmer basis for planning drug doses and budgets. A shared average also helps when comparing treatment costs between centres. It is a simple reference study, but one that everyday cancer care depends on.
plos-pone-0009033:
Liset Elstgeest and co-authors checked IV feeding rules for babies born far too early, in PLOS ONE in 2010. New national guidelines advised less fluid but earlier total parenteral nutrition for preterm infants. Parenteral nutrition feeds the baby entirely through a vein. The first days of life are delicate for salt and water balance.

The team measured sodium, potassium, and fluid balance over the first three days. They compared babies managed under the new guidelines. Feeding early while restricting fluid could tip electrolytes either way. The audit tells neonatal units whether the new rules keep tiny patients stable.
plos-pone-0009133:
Sunita Biswas and co-authors showed that a bee's senses tune the glue between its brain cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neurexins and neuroligins are partner proteins that meet across a synapse. Their bridge helps synapses mature and pass signals cleanly between neurons. In humans, faults in these proteins are linked with autism.

The team varied what young honeybees could smell, see, and feel. Sensory input changed neuroligin and neurexin levels in the bee brain. Experience, in other words, adjusts the brain's synaptic hardware directly. A bee model may help untangle how environment meets autism-linked genes.
plos-pone-0009233:
Alma Brolund and colleagues published this antibiotic study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Resistance to trimethoprim, a common antibiotic, was rising in gut bacteria. Kronoberg County in Sweden ran a two-year push that cut trimethoprim prescriptions by 85 percent. The question was whether using less of the drug would also cut resistance.

The team examined Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae samples at the DNA level. They tracked the resistance genes, called dfr genes, that spread between bacteria. Their molecular census shows how the gene pool shifted during the intervention. Such data test a core hope of antibiotic stewardship: that restraint today preserves the drug for tomorrow.
plos-pone-0009333:
Christopher Brochu and co-authors published this fossil study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Africa's ancient crocodiles were far more varied than the few kinds alive there now. Their family ties and origins remained poorly understood. Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, famous for early human fossils, also holds crocodile remains from the Plio-Pleistocene.

The team describes a new horned crocodile from those hominid sites. Horns are unknown on any living crocodile, so the find is striking. The species adds a branch to the African crocodile family tree. It also shows that the neighbors of our early ancestors included crocodiles stranger than any alive today.
plos-pone-0009433:
Dobromir Dotov, Lin Nie, and Anthony Chemero put a famous idea from philosophy to a lab test in PLOS ONE in 2010. Martin Heidegger said a tool in smooth use feels almost part of the hand. He called that state ready to hand. When the tool fails, we notice it at once, and it turns unready to hand.

The authors ran tests designed to catch that shift as it happens. Their results support the claim that skilled tool use can break down in a clear, sudden way. The study gives hard data to an idea long used in thinking about mind and machines. It shows how smooth action and clumsy action differ.
plos-pone-0009533:
Patricia Schirmer and co-authors checked an outbreak tracking system during a flu pandemic in PLOS ONE in 2010. The system, called ESSENCE, scans electronic records from Veterans Affairs hospitals across the United States. It aims to spot disease surges early. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic gave it a real world test. The team compared its signals with the known course of the pandemic.

The system picked up the pandemic wave in the hospital network well. Its alerts matched the rise and fall of cases seen by other means. The result shows that routine electronic records can flag an outbreak as it builds. Early warning buys time for hospitals to staff and stock up.
plos-pone-0009633:
Donald Courter and co-authors dissected a cancer linked protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. Osteopontin is a protein found at high levels in many tumors. It comes in several forms whose jobs were unclear. One part of it, the RGD domain, is a short motif that binds cell surface receptors. The team used genetic methods to test what that domain does in tumors.

The RGD domain proved to drive tumor growth and spread. It works by switching on pathways that keep tumor cells alive. Narrowing the effect to one small domain sharpens the target for drug design. A blocker aimed at that domain might slow both growth and metastasis.
plos-pone-0009733:
Healthy coral reefs are often pictured as coral kingdoms. Peter Vroom and Cristi Braun mapped what actually covers a healthy reef in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. Their census appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The reef lies in a subtropical part of the Pacific.

The team recorded cover species by species across the seafloor. Algae, not coral, took the lead in this baseline. A baseline like this shows what a thriving reef looks like before damage. It gives managers a yardstick for judging reef health later. Few healthy reefs have been mapped this closely.
plos-pone-0009833:
Detecting molecules on a surface often means watching light bounce off it in special ways. Rahber Thariani and Paul Yager combined two such methods into one imaging setup. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The work comes from biosensor research, where surfaces act as detectors.

Surface plasmon resonance tracks binding by shifts in reflected light. Adding surface plasmon resonance-enhanced fluorescence makes faint signals glow brighter. Running both at once means one sample gives two kinds of readout. Combined imaging could sharpen tests that detect disease markers and other targets.
plos-pone-0009933:
Small ermine moths look almost identical, so their family tree needs DNA to draw. Hubert Turner and colleagues built that tree for the genus Yponomeuta. Their molecular phylogeny appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

A molecular phylogeny uses gene sequences to sort species by ancestry. The study covers the Palaearctic, the region spanning Europe and northern Asia. Ermine moth caterpillars are known for the webs they spin over trees. Some family members are orchard and garden pests. A clear tree settles which moths are truly close kin. The genus holds dozens of named species.
plos-pone-0010033:
The authors were Catalina March, Verónica Regueiro, Enrique Llobet, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study covered a hospital germ, Acinetobacter baumannii. The bacterium can cause pneumonia caught in hospitals. Airway cells it infects raise signals that call in immune help and make germ-fighting molecules.

The team traced which host signals switch on during that response. They focused on IL-8, a signal that draws immune cells, and beta-defensins, which attack germs. Knowing the wiring helps explain lung defense and may point to ways to support it. The work was done in infected airway cells in the laboratory.
plos-pone-0010133:
The authors were Jie Chen, Bin Tang, Hongxin Chen, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined insect genes for an enzyme called trehalase. Trehalase splits the sugar trehalose into two glucose molecules. Insects use it in many body processes, and it comes in soluble and membrane-bound forms.

By silencing each gene with RNA interference, the team compared their roles in making chitin. Chitin builds the insect outer skeleton, so its production is vital. The two forms turned out to do different jobs, a clue for pest control aimed at molting.
plos-pone-0010233:
The authors were Baosheng Ge, Feng Yang, Daoyong Yu, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study stabilized a key plant protein outside its membrane. Photosystem-I harvests light energy in plants, but membrane proteins fall apart once removed from their membrane. That instability hampers purification, crystallization, and building devices from such proteins in the lab and in industry.

The team designed short amphiphilic peptides, chains that have water-loving and water-avoiding parts. Those designer peptides raised the thermal stability of isolated photosystem-I. More stable light-harvesting protein could serve in bio-based solar devices and sensors.
plos-pone-0010333:
Angela Abbatecola, Fabrizia Lattanzio, Liana Spazzafumo and a large team followed older adults with diabetes for PLOS ONE in 2010. Memory and thinking often decline in this group, but the reasons were not clear. The team asked whether body fat, and where it sits, could forecast that decline. They tracked a large group of older people over two years.

Nearly seven hundred people took part, some with type 2 diabetes and some with normal blood sugar. Fat measures were taken at the start, then thinking skills were checked over time. Fatness did predict later decline among those with diabetes. The result hints that weight and fat placement belong in brain-health care for older patients. It also opens a path for testing whether fat loss protects the mind.
plos-pone-0010433:
Paul Janssen and a large team reported the full genome of a metal-loving bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cupriavidus metallidurans strain CH34 survives places loaded with toxic heavy metals. It was first isolated in 1976 from a metal processing site. Over thirty years, its tolerance drew steady research. The complete gene sequence now opens its survival playbook.

Reading all its genes shows the full toolkit for resisting metals. Such bacteria can clean polluted water or recover valuable metals. They also warn how germs adapt to human-made extremes. A genome is both a parts list and a history book. This one records decades of evolution beside industry. The sequence will anchor metal-resistance studies for years.
plos-pone-0010533:
Mingjun Wang, Mette Larsen and Morten Nielsen used computer prediction to find flu peptides that rouse helper T cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Vaccine design needs to know which virus fragments the immune system notices. Class I HLA molecules display fragments that usually summon killer T cells. The team predicted nine-unit fragments from influenza A that bind these molecules. They then tested whether those fragments also stirred helper CD4 responses.

Finding helpers among supposed killer targets widens vaccine options. Peptide vaccines must provoke the right mix of immune cells to work. Computer prediction narrows thousands of fragments to a testable few. That saves lab time and sharpens vaccine candidates. The study links flu immunity to a surprising cross-over effect.
plos-pone-0010633:
Alessandra Conversi and colleagues documented an abrupt change in the Mediterranean Sea, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In the late 1980s, many parts of the sea's ecosystem shifted within a few years. Water properties, plankton, and fish changed together, a pattern scientists call a regime shift.

The authors compared records from several European seas. Similar jumps appeared in the North Sea and Baltic around the same time. A broad climate swing may have pushed all of them at once. Linked shifts warn managers that whole ecosystems can flip quickly, and that single-species plans may miss the real driver.
plos-pone-0010733:
Hanna Laurén and colleagues scanned gene activity in young rat brains after seizures, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A long seizure in a child can set the stage for later epilepsy. The chain from that first event to a seizure-prone brain is called epileptogenesis, and its molecular steps are poorly known.

A drug called kainic acid triggered the seizures in juvenile rats. Gene chips then read activity in the hippocampus region CA1. Hundreds of genes shifted in the hours and days after. Some shifts point to cell stress; others to rewiring. Each cluster is a candidate place where treatment might interrupt the road to epilepsy.
plos-pone-0010833:
Henri Cohen, Patrice Voss, Franco Lepore and colleagues published this study of touch and memory in PLOS ONE in 2010. Blind people often sharpen their remaining senses, and the authors asked how working memory handles Braille, the raised-dot script read by fingertip. They compared people blind from early life, people with some residual vision, and sighted readers.

Groups took memory span tests using Braille touch or a matching visual task, sometimes while repeating a word aloud to block inner speech. Fully blind readers held Braille items in memory as well as sighted readers held visual items under the same block. Their Braille memory also looked more robust than that of readers with partial vision. Cohen and colleagues suggest that life without sight reshapes memory, and that visual experience itself can shape how touch-based memory develops.
plos-pone-0010933:
Clayton Collings, Alfonso Fernandez, Chad Pitschka and co-authors published this genome packaging study in PLOS ONE in 2010. DNA in cells is spooled around proteins called nucleosomes, and the spool positions are not random: certain letter patterns in the DNA favor a spool forming there. The authors mined a genome-wide library of yeast nucleosome DNA for those patterns.

They counted all four-letter words in the DNA and found the rhythms were driven by a small set of shared consensus patterns. Follow-up experiments showed those short motifs genuinely encourage nucleosomes to form at specific spots. Collings and colleagues distill a crowded set of periodic signals into a compact code. Reading that code helps predict where the genome is open for business and where it is wound shut.
plos-pone-0011033:
Simon Dankel, Dag Fadnes, Anne-Kristin Stavrum and co-authors published this obesity surgery study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dysfunctional fat tissue in obesity spills fat into other organs and fuels inflammation and insulin resistance, yet many genes governing fat tissue are still unknown. The authors used profound weight loss after bariatric surgery as a before-and-after window on those genes.

They profiled gene activity in belly fat from patients before surgery and a year after a major bypass operation. They compared it with fat from lean healthy people. Two measurement platforms were used, plus confirmatory tests. Body mass index fell dramatically after surgery. Gene activity shifted wholesale, away from stress response programs and toward homeobox factors, developmental regulators not usually associated with adult fat. Dankel and colleagues nominate new candidate genes for how fat tissue recovers, or fails to.
plos-pone-0011133:
Staubert, Boselt, Bohnekamp and colleagues traced smell related receptors in primates for PLOS ONE in 2010. A small family of receptors detects trace amines, chemicals tied to scent and social cues. The team compared three of these receptors across monkeys, apes and other primates.

Their analysis showed how the receptor genes changed in structure and function over time. Some lineages kept them sharp, while others let them fade. That pattern reveals how primate senses were tuned by evolution. It helps explain why species differ in the chemical world they can detect.
plos-pone-0011233:
Lee, Kim, Ahn and colleagues built social networks from web searches in PLOS ONE in 2010. Traditional network studies rely on surveys, which cannot reach millions of people. The team instead used search engine results to infer who is connected to whom at large scale.

Their method constructs plausible social networks without interviewing anyone. That scale lets researchers study social structure across whole fields or nations. The approach informs computational sociology, a field that mines digital traces for social patterns. It also raises care questions about accuracy, which the study works to test.
plos-pone-0011333:
Eric Hervouet and co-authors examined in 2010 what happens when a team of three linked proteins in brain cells stops working together. The three proteins help copy chemical marks onto DNA when cells divide, keeping gene patterns stable from one cell generation to the next. The study used both human and mouse glial cells, the support cells of the brain.

When the contact among the three proteins was broken, normal glial cells began to grow in a tumor-like way. That finding suggests the partnership acts as a guard against cancer in the brain. Losing the guard may be one step on the road to glioma, a hard-to-treat brain tumor. The work gives cancer researchers a clear mechanism to test further and a possible point where new treatments could intervene.
plos-pone-0011433:
Vijayababu Radhakrishnan and Jesse Martinez reported in 2010 that one member of a protein family can turn normal cells cancerous. The 14-3-3 proteins normally help hold growth signals in check by binding partner proteins. The team focused on the gamma form and tested what happens when it is overactive in cells.

The gamma form drove cancerous transformation by firing up two major growth pathways at once, the MAP kinase route and the PI3K route. One protein lifting two accelerators explains how a single change can push a cell far toward cancer. It also names a tempting target: blocking this one protein could cut both signals together. The study helps explain why tumors that raise this protein can grow so stubbornly, and where a future drug might intervene.
plos-pone-0011533:
Barbara Whitlock, Amanda Hale, and Paul Groff warned in 2010 that a favorite plant DNA barcode can be scrambled from within a single species. Botanists identify plants with short standard DNA stretches, and trnH-psbA is one of the most used. A barcode only works if it stays stable within a species while differing between species, and the team found a violation of the first half of that bargain.

Inversions, flipped segments of DNA, occur within species in this barcode region and can make the same species read as different, or distort comparisons. The flip-flops challenge a trusted identification tool at exactly the scale where it must be boring and reliable. Botanists are urged to check for inversions before naming a plant from this barcode alone. The caution protects everything built on plant identification, from ecology surveys to herbal product testing.
plos-pone-0011633:
Luis Hurtado, Mariana Mateos and Carlos Santamaria traced the past of shore isopods on the Pacific coast, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ligia isopods live in a thin band of rocky shore that runs from the middle of California down the Mexican coast, with the Gulf of California included. They stray very little from that band, so each stretch of coast may hold its own cut-off group.

By comparing DNA along the coast, the authors mapped how these groups split and spread over time. The pattern shows several distinct lines shaped by the shape of the shore. Their work turns a humble shore creature into a record of how coastal species split into new forms.
plos-pone-0011733:
Jennifer Van Grol and co-authors showed how HIV undermines cells it never infects, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Autophagy is the cell's recycling system, breaking down worn parts in sacs called lysosomes. Faulty autophagy is linked to poor pathogen control and brain degeneration, and many signalling pathways regulate it.

The team found HIV-1 blocks autophagy in bystander macrophage and monocytic cells, acting through the Src-Akt and STAT3 pathways.
