Damage to uninfected neighbours reveals a wider reach for the virus than infection alone suggests. Restoring recycling in bystanders could become part of future HIV care.
plos-pone-0011833:
Élcio Leal and Fabiola Villanova wrote this 2010 genetic study of HIV-1 subtype B, the virus form that spread widely through the Americas. In Brazil the epidemic looks unusual, because many local samples carry a short marker called GWGR on the virus surface loop. Some researchers had argued that this marker signals a milder, separate variant.

Leal and Villanova map how varied subtype B really is, then use that map to ask where BF recombinants came from. Recombinants are hybrid viruses formed when subtype B and subtype F infect the same person. Tracing the family links among Brazilian samples helps show whether the hybrids arose locally or arrived from elsewhere, which matters for tracking how the epidemic keeps changing.
plos-pone-0011933:
Namhee Kim and co-workers used brain imaging in 2010 to see how L-dopa changes language processing. L-dopa, a dopamine precursor drug, is thought to strengthen strong signals and quiet weak ones in the brain. Language studies had suggested it narrows the network of word meanings a person activates.

Applying independent component analysis to fMRI scans, a method that separates mixed brain signals into distinct networks, the team examined the drug's effect during language tasks. Separating the networks shows which language circuits the drug boosts or dampens. That matters for Parkinson's patients who take L-dopa daily and may notice changes in speech and word finding.
plos-pone-0012033:
Nicholas Burd and co-workers compared in 2010 two lifting styles for building muscle protein in young men. Fifteen men performed leg extensions under different loads and volumes, letting the team measure muscle protein synthesis, growth signaling, and gene responses. The contest was light loads lifted many times against heavy loads lifted few times.

The low-load, high-volume work stimulated muscle protein synthesis more than the heavy, low-volume work in this setup. That result challenges the gym rule that only near-maximal weights build muscle. For rehabilitation and older adults who cannot lift heavy, evidence that lighter loads can still drive protein building has direct practical value.
plos-pone-0012133:
Derek Ruths and Faiyaz Al Zamal presented a method for collecting publication and citation records in PLOS ONE in 2010. Universities judge researchers partly by what they published and how often others cite it. Getting that record right is surprisingly hard, since author names repeat, lists are incomplete, and databases disagree about who wrote what.

Their approach retrieves a person's publication-citation record in an automated and reliable way. Cleaner records mean fairer hiring, promotion, and funding decisions, and fewer errors that can shadow a career. The method is also a tool for anyone studying how science itself grows, since that research stands or falls on accurate citation data.
plos-pone-0012233:
Charlton Cheung, Kevin Yu, Germaine Fung, and co-authors pooled brain imaging studies of autism and schizophrenia in PLOS ONE in 2010. The two conditions share risk factors and share troubles with social life, communication, and thinking, which has long fueled debate: are they close relatives or distant ones that merely look alike? The team used a statistical method that finds where many separate imaging studies agree.

Comparing the agreed brain maps shows which regions the conditions share and which they do not. Shared ground would support common roots and shared treatments; clear gaps would argue for separate handling. Either answer guides how clinics classify and study two of psychiatry's hardest conditions.
plos-pone-0012333:
Joanne Clark, Elizabeth Clore, Kangni Zheng, and co-authors fed an antioxidant supplement to mice modeling Parkinson's disease, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Early in Parkinson's, the brain region that dies first runs low on glutathione, the cell's main antioxidant, which may let oxidative stress build up the toxic forms of the alpha-synuclein protein. The supplement, N-acetyl-cysteine, is a standard way to raise glutathione.

Given by mouth, it lessened the loss of dopamine nerve endings in the mice. A cheap, safe, widely available supplement showing protection in an animal model earns a careful look, though mouse success often fades in human trials. At minimum the result supports the oxidative-stress account of how this disease begins.
plos-pone-0012433:
Garima Khandelwal and Jayaram Bhyravabhotla proposed a fresh way to predict when a DNA strand pair melts apart, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Melting temperature guides the design of DNA tests, from disease probes to species barcodes. Existing predictors lean on fitted rules from past data, which can fail on new sequence types.

Their model starts from a molecular picture of how the double strand comes undone and derives the melting point from that picture. A model built on mechanism may travel better to new sequences than rule fitting alone. Better melting forecasts make lab tests cheaper to design and more likely to work the first time.
plos-pone-0012533:
Yvonne Fischer, Elvira Ganic, Jacqueline Ameri and colleagues built reporter stem cell lines by gene targeting, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. NANOG is a master gene of pluripotency, the state in which embryonic stem cells can become any tissue. Watching NANOG switch on and off live would let researchers sort truly pluripotent cells from those starting to specialize.

The team inserted a reporter at the NANOG gene itself in human embryonic stem cells, so the cells glow when the gene is active. Targeting the real locus, rather than adding loose copies, keeps the signal faithful. Such lines are standard tools for safer stem cell production and drug screening.
plos-pone-0012633:
Steer, Golding and Bolton measured the many small traits that sit along the autism spectrum. Views have shifted toward seeing autism traits as a smooth scale, with no sharp line between typical and atypical behaviour. To study that scale, researchers need good measures of each separate trait.

Their 2010 paper pulls together ninety-three separate measures covering parts of the spectrum. Scoring them in a large child group shows how traits spread through the general population. That spread helps explain why autism runs in families in graded ways rather than all or nothing.
plos-pone-0012733:
Pointon, Walker, Phillips and co-authors traced how a top cancer drug injures the heart so quickly. Doxorubicin kills many cancers, yet lifetime doses are capped by heart damage. Their 2010 study gave the drug to animals and read heart gene activity and protein making soon after.

Energy chain genes in heart muscle changed fast, ATP energy stores fell, and a cell death switch turned on. The speed of the chain helps explain why damage builds with each dose. Early warning signs in that chain could one day let doctors adjust treatment.
plos-pone-0012833:
Booker, Schwarz, Garrett and co-authors studied how sugar feeding changes the way a plant hormone branches roots. Auxin, the main growth hormone of plants, can make lateral roots form in a two-peaked pattern. Glucose is also essential to normal root growth, so the two signals meet in the same tissue.

Their 2010 study found glucose softens that two-peaked response, partly through the plant's heterotrimeric G protein complex. Signal cross-talk of this kind lets a plant weigh food supply against shape. Root shape decides how well a plant finds water and nutrients.
plos-pone-0335833:
Jimma Dinsa Deressa and seven colleagues test Ethiopia's standard malaria treatment in a region where the parasite is intense, in this 2026 PLOS ONE trial. One hundred and twenty-three patients with uncomplicated falciparum malaria received the usual drug combination plus a single small dose of a second drug meant to block transmission. They were followed for twenty-eight days, with genetic testing to tell relapses from fresh infections.

Parasites cleared from everyone within a week, and the cure rate stayed above the World Health Organization's threshold for changing policy — but not comfortably. One in six patients still carried parasites on day three, an early warning sign of weakening drugs. The authors urge close, regular monitoring before resistance takes hold.
plos-pone-0336733:
Yoshikazu Endo and seven colleagues measure how long wild plants remember past temperatures, in this 2026 study of two perennial crucifers growing outdoors in Japan. A gene circuit that controls flowering is known to integrate weather over time, switching states with the seasons. The team defined a single number for that memory: the past time window whose temperatures best predict a gene's current activity.

Applying the measure across the circuit, they found memory windows ranging from a single day to about five months, spread across the network rather than held in one gene. The windows also differed between spring and autumn states. A model built on thermal history predicted an independent year's gene dynamics well. The authors offer the metric as a general way to compare cellular memory across genes, species, and settings.
plos-pone-0339433:
Dinkneh Gebre Borojo and Jiang Yushi ask whether green goods shipped from China actually cut carbon pollution in Africa, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. They tracked imports of low-carbon technology and environmental goods into forty-two African countries over two decades, from 2003 to 2023. The outcome they measured was how much carbon each economy emitted per unit of energy used.

Overall, greener imports from China were linked to lower emissions intensity across the continent. The effect flipped in the poorest countries, though, where it was tied to higher intensity, while middle-income countries gained. Stronger institutions made the benefit larger, a warning that trade alone cannot deliver clean energy without working systems around it.
plos-pone-0341933:
Jethwani and colleagues, in a 2026 survey, ask dentists worldwide about a technique for saving teeth with deep decay near the gumline. The method lifts the deep edge of a filling up to a level that is easier to work on, as an alternative to surgically exposing more tooth. Little was known about how widely dentists know or use it.

About three hundred fifty dentists from the Middle East, the United States, India, the United Kingdom, and elsewhere answered. More than three quarters knew the technique, and two thirds thought bonding fillings to deep root surfaces works reliably. Even so, three quarters said that when conditions allowed, they still preferred the surgical route. Routine use for large deep fillings in back teeth was limited. The authors read this as a knowing-doing gap: the method is accepted in principle, but habit, training, and confidence keep it from daily use.
plos-pone-0342133:
Siyabonga Ndwandwe led a team of eight authors studying new eye clinic designs in the UK, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Eye clinics are overwhelmed, and one fix is asynchronous review: images and records reviewed by specialists later, in community settings, without a face-to-face visit. The team asked patients, health professionals, and the public what they prefer.

Ndwandwe's discrete choice experiment measured which features people value and which trade-offs they accept. New clinic models fail when the public will not use them, however efficient they look on paper. Preference evidence lets the NHS design services people trust. The study shows how to test acceptance before a national rollout commits to a model patients dislike.
plos-pone-0344333:
Chao Wang and colleagues analysed what a single underwater listening device can learn from the character of sound itself. Unlike ordinary microphones, a vector hydrophone also senses how water particles move, giving sound a direction and texture that carry information about distant vessels. Simulations, tank tests, and sea trials examined coherence, energy balance, and phase patterns in the received signal.

Even with a target far quieter than the background, the combined coherence measure hovered near a recognisable value, and the phase pattern could reveal which quadrant a target occupied. Comparing signals against the coherence background sharpened detection by a worthwhile margin, and moving targets left visible interference fingerprints. The authors lay groundwork for using one compact sensor, rather than a towed array, to detect and classify ships.
plos-pone-0344933:
Ramesh Vinayagam and colleagues turned leaves from an ornamental tree into a magnetic cleaning powder for dye-polluted water. Cooking the leaves with iron in a one-pot heated process yielded charcoal studded with tiny magnetite spheres. The powder's job is to drive a Fenton-like reaction, a chemistry that shreds dye molecules, in this case the green dye malachite green, a common and toxic textile pollutant.

In batch tests the powder removed about three quarters of the dye within three hours at low starting strength, and it worked in real water samples too. A magnet pulled it back out for reuse, and after five cycles it still kept most of its cleaning power. The authors pitch the material as a cheap, recoverable catalyst for small dye works that cannot afford advanced treatment plants.
plos-pone-0345533:
Ho Duy and colleagues surveyed nurses in central Vietnam about patient safety in a 2026 study. More than one thousand nurses at five large hospitals rated their person-centered care skill, safety skill, daily safety tasks, and ward safety climate. Evidence from lower-income settings on how these pieces connect has been scarce.

Daily safety tasks partly carried the effect of both care skill and safety skill onto safety climate. In plain terms, skilled nurses improved ward culture in part by actually doing safety work each day. Training that builds skill but never changes daily routines may thus fall short. Hospital leaders can use the chain to target coaching and routine design together.
plos-pone-0346233:
Jin Yeon Gil and her team used health data from South Korea to ask a hard question. Do people with schizophrenia face a higher risk of Parkinson's in later life? Both ills touch the same brain chemical. The team matched patients with like peers and weighed drugs and other ills.

The risk came out near three times as high. One drug, risperidone, pushed the risk up more. A second drug, quetiapine, pulled it down. Head wounds and stroke added their own risk. The team urges doctors to watch for stiff, slow moves in these patients. They also call for more work on drug choice.
plos-pone-0346533:
Oluwatobi Emmanuel Egbowon, Dilan Çiftçi, and Ibrahim Adeshola examined how young Yoruba Nigerians judge the explicit content of Afro-pop music. The genre is a global success story for Nigeria, yet critics accuse its lyrics and videos of pushing materialism, casual sex, and drug use. The 2026 study surveyed two hundred ninety-five respondents about offensive content and its effects.

Respondents saw the music as a double-edged force, capable of inspiring young people and of corrupting them. Many wanted stronger screening of songs before release. The authors place the debate within wider arguments about social norms, arguing that regulators, artists, and communities all share responsibility for what popular music teaches the young.
plos-pone-0347033:
Lise Loktu and Elin Therese Brødholt report on the early modern whaling cemetery at Likneset in Svalbard, where thawing permafrost is destroying what centuries of cold preserved. Twenty whalers' graves, dug across three excavation campaigns from the 1980s to 2019, were scored for preservation and studied for what the bones say about health. The site splits between an eroding zone and a stable central area.

Comparing zones and dig phases shows how quickly exposed burials decay once the ground warms, a direct measure of climate-driven heritage loss. The skeletons themselves carry the physical costs of Arctic whaling labor, including metabolic disease and developmental strain. The study doubles as a warning and a rescue record for hundreds of similar frozen sites across the Arctic.
plos-pone-0347233:
Andrew J Nasr, Nitin B Jain, Yen-Sheng Lin, and co-authors measured how shoulder muscles respond to a standard rehab exercise, comparing people whose cuffs are torn with people whose cuffs are whole. Tears are the leading cause of shoulder pain, yet how torn muscles respond to gentle exercise was poorly mapped. Their 2026 study used ultrasound on twenty participants before and after thirty low-force contractions, tracking muscle stiffness, size, and strength in the two main cuff muscles.

In torn shoulders, the key muscle's passive stiffness dropped significantly after exercise, meaning it became more compliant, a change the authors call maladaptive. Muscle size rose during active effort in both groups, while torn muscles showed no size change at rest. Strength fell in everyone afterward. The authors suggest torn cuffs may need longer recovery after even light exercise sessions.
plos-pone-0347333:
Ping Li, Chunxiao Xu, and Huiting Liang built a scorecard for red tourism in China. Old base areas of the revolution hope that tours of their past will lift local life. But towns need a way to judge if culture and tourism are truly merging well. The team drew up twenty-one gauges in three groups: means, gains, and setting.

They then scored a case area that spans parts of Jiangxi, Fujian, and Guangdong. Scores rose over time, though in fits and starts. Strong towns grew and drew near each other, while weak ones shrank. The team says the card can guide towns that want growth built on their red past.
plos-pone-0347533:
Mi Suk Noh, Bong-Hyun Jun, and co-authors tested an upgrade to hospital sterilizers that use vaporized hydrogen peroxide to disinfect delicate medical devices at low temperature. Leftover moisture is the method's weak point and can abort cycles or leave microbes alive. Their 2026 study added a warm-air circulation system and compared temperature evenness and drying with and without it, including deliberately wetted loads and complex test devices.

With circulation running, the chamber held a steady temperature in the high fifties Celsius and moisture was cleared throughout the cycle. Every challenge item passed sterilization, from process test devices to flexible and rigid tubes and a double endoscope dummy. The authors say the add-on makes peroxide sterilization safer and more reliable for intricate modern instruments.
plos-pone-0348233:
Poonavit Pichayapaiboon and colleagues read the chemical fingerprints in the blood of dogs whose heart valves are failing, a disease that often drags the kidneys down with it. Dogs were sorted into five groups, from healthy through stages of valve disease with and without kidney trouble. Two kinds of mass spectrometry listed the small proteins floating in each dog's serum.

The fingerprints separated healthy dogs cleanly from sick ones. One hundred proteins differed significantly, and a shared handful between advanced heart disease and kidney disease pointed at the organs' energy factories and recycling units, plus pathways handling certain amino acids. Standard heart drugs also nudged these signals. The authors hope such blood signatures could one day stage this two-organ syndrome earlier than current tests allow.
plos-pone-0348533:
Jiacheng Hu and coauthors published a 2026 computer vision paper in PLOS ONE on spotting tiny, crowded objects by fusing ordinary and infrared images. Each view alone fails somewhere: darkness hides things from cameras, heat images lack detail. Their framework recalibrates the two feature streams against each other with a learnable attention mechanism. It then refines objects across scales using bidirectional connections and graph-based modeling. Small targets keep their boundaries and meaning.

On two public multimodal benchmarks, the system topped existing methods on standard accuracy measures, both for loose and strict overlap thresholds. Visual checks showed it holding up in low light, partial occlusion, and cluttered backgrounds where rivals missed or merged small objects. Ablation tests confirmed each module earned its place. The framework is pitched at surveillance, night driving, and other settings where critical objects are small, dense, and half-hidden.
plos-pone-0348633:
Chiara De Poli evaluated a leaflet-based program built with patients to close the information gap faced by people with dementia and their family carers. The program ran through community mental health services for older people in the North-East of England. Rather than ask only whether it worked, the evaluation used a realist approach, asking what worked, for whom, and under what conditions.

Clinicians differed in how they offered the leaflet, but all offered it repeatedly and at every chance. Interviews with the service manager, group interviews with practitioners, and a session with the design group were sorted into outcomes like reach, dose, and staying power. The account shows how a simple leaflet lives or dies by habit and setting, a lesson for any service trying to inform patients well.
plos-pone-0349133:
Adebowale E Aderogba led a team that made chitosan from two odd sources. One was the shell of a West African river prawn. The other was the American cockroach. Chitosan is a useful natural material. It serves in medicine, farming, and industry. Nigeria has plenty of both creatures, yet still imports the stuff. The team used a tweaked process with a hot, pressurized alkali step.

Prawns gave far more raw stock and more end product. Cockroach chitosan scored higher on a key quality mark, though. Light-based tests proved both batches were true chitosan. The team says both sources can work at home. They also say the pressure step lifts yield and quality for scale-up.
plos-pone-0349233:
Sarah Huber-Krum and co-authors interviewed staff at six facilities in Tanzania's Kigoma region in 2026 about reviewing maternal and newborn deaths. Such review systems promise accountability and learning, but in stretched facilities they often fade.

Twenty-two providers and administrators described what helps and hinders the process, guided by two implementation frameworks. Themes covered staff and organisational attitudes, the realities of the setting, and practical delivery issues like time, forms, and follow-up on agreed actions. Death review only prevents deaths when its lessons are acted on, and this study names the local conditions that decide whether that happens.
plos-pone-0349433:
Md Shahidul Islam, Md Muhtasim Rahman Mim, and Md Raihan Kabir built a deep learning system in 2026 for predicting whether two proteins interact. Such interactions run most cell processes, but lab mapping is slow and costly, leaving huge gaps.

Their model starts from a protein language model's rich codes for each sequence, then reads the pair through four attention streams that capture solo traits, synergy, and difference. On a large public test collection it reported very high accuracy, beating recent rivals. Balanced, two way reading of the pair is the design's claim to its edge, useful for drug and biology research.
plos-pone-0349933:
Daren Kumar Joseph and six colleagues describe this 2026 PLOS One protocol for a rat study combining a local plant supplement with exercise to fight memory decline. The plant, Cosmos caudatus, known locally as ulam raja, is rich in antioxidants, and aluminium chloride will be used to induce mild cognitive impairment in male Wistar rats. Groups will receive exercise, the supplement, both, or neither.

As a protocol, the paper lays out the plan: four weeks of treadmill running, three weeks of supplementation, then memory and behavior tests, blood chemistry, and brain tissue examination. Earlier work suggests each approach alone may help, but combined effects are unclear. The authors expect the pairing to protect spatial memory and cut oxidative stress more than either alone, and the design will show whether that hope holds.
plos-pone-0350033:
Manish Sharma, Tanweer Ali, and co-authors designed a flexible four-antenna system for the millimeter-wave bands that future 5G phones will need. Lower 5G bands are crowded, so engineers are moving to much higher frequencies, where signals fade fast unless several antennas cooperate. Their 2026 design prints a tiny etched patch antenna on a bendable sheet thinner than a credit card, then combines four of them.

The built prototype covered two target bands around thirty-eight and sixty gigahertz with solid signal strength. Bending it to forty-five degrees in either direction barely disturbed performance, which matters for devices worn on the body. Radiation absorption in body tissue was checked as well. The authors present the antenna as a compact candidate for high-speed, body-friendly wireless gear.
plos-pone-0350133:
Nikolaos Mellios and six colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One interview study on the WEFE nexus, the idea that water, energy, food, and ecosystems must be managed together rather than separately. The authors interviewed coordinators of European research projects built around the concept, asking how the framework works in practice and where it stalls.

Coordinators agreed the connections between the four sectors are real and matter for efficiency and climate resilience, but putting the idea into practice lagged behind the theory in many projects. Missing data, mismatched methods, and weak links to wider policy were recurring obstacles. Promising directions included purpose-built indicators and better stakeholder engagement. The authors call for stronger governance and communication so the nexus delivers more than a slogan.
plos-pone-0350633:
Cuimei Wei and colleagues followed just over twenty seven hundred people in China with fatty liver disease who did not yet have diabetes. A new blood index joining fat and long term sugar marks was tested as a diabetes warning sign against an older rival index. Over a median follow up just past five years, about two hundred and twenty people developed diabetes.

Higher index values linked with higher diabetes risk in survival models, with a curved rather than straight risk climb. Time based accuracy curves compared the new index with the older sugar based rival. A cheap index from routine labs could flag fatty liver patients for early lifestyle referral long before diabetes sets in, if outside groups confirm the cut points.
plos-pone-0350733:
Rescue services are going digital, linking automatic alerts, responders, and hospitals, but each system speaks its own language. Masresha Derese Tegegne and co-authors present a registered plan, in PLOS One in 2026, to match the rescue chain's core terms against the World Health Organization's newest disease classification foundation.

The team will judge how each rescue term relates in meaning to the classification, rate the quality of the matching, and list concepts the classification lacks. Clear shared terms would let rescue software exchange information without confusion across borders. As a protocol, the paper reports the method rather than findings.
plos-pone-0350833:
Samantha Schofield and co-authors recorded how young blacklegged ticks breathe. Ticks spend most of life off a host and must trade off breathing against drying out, so many breathe in bursts: long pauses, then a puff of carbon dioxide. The team measured gas output from nymphs of the species that spreads Lyme disease, the first such measurements for its genus.

The nymphs did breathe in the burst pattern, with distinct phases to each cycle. How often cycles came and how big each puff was depended on the conditions the young ticks had developed in, whether raised in the lab or collected wild. Breathing style is thus flexible, not fixed. Knowing how this disease carrier manages water and air helps predict where it can survive as climates shift.
plos-pone-0350933:
Ziya Yıldız studied two problems of ageing together in 2026: swallowing decline and bladder leakage among nursing home residents in Turkey. Both are common, both harm quality of life, and whether they travel together was not known.

Seventy-three independent older residents took a timed water swallow test and a swallowing questionnaire, plus bladder and quality of life surveys. Those with swallowing decline had far higher odds of bladder leakage, and scored worse on several parts of daily life affected by it. Shared muscle and nerve ageing may link the two. Staff who spot one problem, the author argues, should check for the other.
plos-pone-0351133:
Wymore and colleagues asked whether moving rural sepsis patients between hospitals delays their care bundle in a 2026 study. Sepsis needs fast fluids, tests, and antibiotics within three hours under standard guidance. Records covered more than one thousand patients in a rural telemedicine network, about a third of whom were transferred.

Bundle completion was similar for transferred and non-transferred patients, the analysis found. Individual bundle steps, time in the emergency department, and deaths were also compared. The result is reassuring for rural systems that must transfer sick patients to larger centers. Telemedicine support may help small hospitals start the bundle on time even when a transfer is planned.
plos-pone-0351233:
Vidya Eswaran and four colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One analysis of how many emergency department patients in the United States have a history with the criminal legal system. The team used three years of a large national health survey, comparing people who had visited an emergency department for any reason, for substance use, or for mental health care.

About one in five patients seen for any reason reported some lifetime legal involvement, rising to well over two in five among substance-use visits. People with such a history also had higher odds of using the emergency department across all three visit types. The authors argue that hospitals should treat legal involvement as a health-relevant life circumstance and build screening and support into emergency care.
plos-pone-0351633:
Fadel and colleagues set out a plan in 2026 to create reporting standards for medical procedure videos. Videos of operations and scope procedures teach technique well, but uneven reporting can skip key steps or hide poor image quality. Their guidelines will be built through expert voting rounds, led by a steering committee.

Five steps will move from gathering candidate items to agreed minimum standards for what uploaders must show and state. A shared checklist could make surgical videos more complete and comparable across hospitals. Trainees benefit most, since a video that omits a safety step teaches a dangerous gap as if it were normal practice.
plos-pone-0351733:
Brendan Andrade and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One feasibility trial of a parenting program redesigned for depressed parents. Standard behavioral parent training helps children with emotional and behavioral problems, but it works less well when a parent is depressed. The new ten-week virtual program blends parent training with therapy techniques aimed at the parent's own mood, and twenty-eight families at two hospital clinics tried it.

Recruitment worked, parents reported high satisfaction, and the clinicians delivering the program followed it closely. Early outcome measures moved in the hoped-for direction for both parents and children. Since the trial met its preset benchmarks, the authors conclude that a full randomized trial is justified to test whether the program truly works.
plos-pone-0351833:
Andrea Lo Sasso and seven colleagues diagnose disease from breath, and insist the machine show its reasoning. Their 2026 study uses three open datasets of exhaled breath chemistry. Volatile compounds in breath carry traces of the body's metabolic state. Targets included lung cancer, other respiratory diseases, and gut diseases. Artificial intelligence models learned to separate the diagnostic labels. Lopsided class sizes, a chronic problem in medical data, were handled explicitly during training.

The decisive step came after prediction. Explainable AI techniques ranked which compounds drove each model's verdicts. Those drivers were then checked for stability across runs. A breath test will never enter clinics as an unexplained oracle. Doctors need to know which molecules matter, and whether that answer survives retesting. This framework supplies both the prediction and the audit trail, while honestly naming sampling and standardisation as the field's unsolved chores.
plos-pone-0351933:
Dima Masri and colleagues surveyed four hundred two pharmacists in Palestine about asthma care. Pharmacists meet asthma patients at every refill. That puts them in place to catch bad inhaler habits and drifting control. The survey scored general knowledge and care knowledge apart. It also asked about attitudes, daily practice, and the barriers pharmacists face.

Just over half the pharmacists counted as knowledgeable on general asthma. The paper details the care scores and practices behind that headline. Barriers named by the pharmacists themselves shape the fix list. In a strained health system, weak pharmacy knowledge is a fixable problem. This survey hands educators a baseline and names the exact weak points to target.
plos-pone-0352333:
Tor Härnqvist and seven colleagues chart eleven years of invasive pneumococcal disease in one Swedish region. Their 2026 study begins in 2009, when childhood pneumococcal vaccination became general. Medical records yielded nearly twenty-three hundred consecutive disease episodes in Region Västra Götaland. Incidence, risk factors, symptoms, and outcomes were all mapped. Earlier studies from the same area stretch the comparison back fifty-six years in total.

Overall incidence settled near thirteen cases per hundred thousand people yearly. Two blood-cancer groups stood out with rates a hundred times higher. Disease shape changed with age. Meningitis struck about a quarter of infected toddlers but few elderly patients. Pneumonia dominated instead among the old. Complications hit roughly a quarter of all episodes, most often fluid or pus around the lungs. The long view shows vaccination reshaping, not erasing, a serious disease.
plos-pone-0352433:
Gerald Mwanje and seven colleagues test digital tools for scoring banana weevil damage in this 2026 study. The weevil is a major pest, tunnelling into the banana plant's underground stem. Breeders screen many varieties for resistance. Human visual scoring is standard but biased by the scorer. The team compared expert eyes against image analysis and four machine learning models. Nearly four hundred corm samples were scored every way.

Varieties genuinely differed in resistance, whichever method was used. But rankings shifted between methods. A variety that looked resistant to one scorer could slip under another. That interaction is the study's warning. Digital scoring promises objectivity, yet each model reads damage through its own lens. Breeding programmes should therefore fix one validated scoring pipeline and stick to it. Otherwise resistance rankings may say more about the measuring tool than the plant.
plos-pone-0353233:
Behzad Nemati Saray led a team of six authors on this 2026 mathematics paper about equations that describe materials with memory, such as slow-spreading substances and springy solids. Standard calculus struggles with these fractional diffusion-wave problems. Their method rewrites the equations as integrals and solves them with special polynomial basis functions that avoid costly numerical integration.

Tests showed the scheme converges fast and beats older finite difference and collocation methods on accuracy while using less computation. Nemati Saray targets second and fourth order versions of these tricky equations for engineering use.
plos-pone-0353933:
Eduardo Sánchez-Sánchez led a team of eight authors on this 2026 randomized trial of a special nutrition drink for malnourished patients with several chronic illnesses. Both groups received a high-calorie, high-protein supplement; the test version added immune-supporting nutrients including arginine, omega-3 fats, and nucleotides. The goal was fewer pressure sores, a common harm in immobile patients.

Sore rates trended lower with the enriched drink at two weeks and a month, and high-risk status fell further, though clear statistical proof was lacking. Sánchez-Sánchez calls the signals promising groundwork for a larger trial.
plos-pone-0354033:
Oscar Rodríguez-Bejarano and seven colleagues mine gene data for clues about mammary cancer in dogs, in this 2026 PLOS ONE bioinformatics study. Such tumours are common in unspayed females and often turn malignant. The team combined their own tumour sequencing with three public datasets, comparing cancerous tissue with healthy mammary tissue from the same animals where possible.

Eight genes behaved consistently differently across all four datasets: five switched up in tumours, three switched down. The raised genes clustered around tissue scaffolding, cell stickiness, and immune activity, while the lowered ones supported normal structure. The authors offer the set as candidate markers for diagnosis and outcome, pending tests in larger groups of dogs.
plos-pone-0354133:
Mir and colleagues, in a 2026 study, track baboons living at different distances from Saudi Arabian towns. Hamadryas baboons, the only wild primates native to the Arabian Peninsula, increasingly raid human food, which fuels conflict. The team fitted GPS collars to ten adult males from groups classed as urban, semi-natural, or natural, and followed them for nine months.

City baboons lived small: their home ranges were a fraction of those of wild groups, and their daily paths were shorter. Wild baboons roamed widest, with semi-natural groups in between and more variable. Time spent inside urban areas rose steeply along the gradient, from a sliver for wild groups to over half the day for urban ones. The authors read this through food: town food is clumped and predictable, so city baboons need not wander. That insight can help managers design conflict plans around food control.
plos-pone-0354233:
Özdemir and colleagues, in a 2026 study, put a common intensive care shortcut on trial: correcting blood calcium for low albumin with a formula instead of measuring the active form directly. The active, ionised form is the true standard, but it needs a special test, so wards lean on formulas. Two hundred fifty critically ill patients had all measures taken at the same moment.

Low active calcium was common, present in well over half the patients. The most famous correction formula caught only a small fraction of true cases, barely better than chance agreement, while plain uncorrected calcium did much better. None of the simple formulas beat plain calcium overall. A four-variable estimator did edge ahead. The authors conclude the correction habit should be dropped where direct measurement is available: in the intensive care unit, the shortcut misleads more than it helps.
plos-pone-0354333:
Jawata Saba and Kevin Ash add in 2026 uncertainty estimates to a widely used index that ranks how vulnerable American communities are to hazards. Standard scores treat survey based inputs as exact, though the underlying census survey carries sampling error. Their method reruns the index ten thousand times with simulated sampling variation for tracts across eight southeastern states.

Household traits carried the most uncertainty, while race and ethnicity themes were most stable. Rural, mountain, and coastal tracts shifted ranks most, and about a third of tracts changed their broad vulnerability class under the new method. Disaster and health planners should map uncertainty, not just scores, the authors argue.
plos-pone-0354433:
Nguyen and colleagues, in a 2026 study in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, test whether a simple grouping of heart, kidney, and metabolic problems predicts who will die within five years. A full American staging system for this combined risk needs data that old clinic records often lack. The team sorted four hundred eighty outpatients into four burden groups using only recorded diagnoses.

The groups ran from no relevant diagnosis, through metabolic risk alone, then kidney or heart artery disease, up to both together. Most patients sat in the middle groups. The design then tracked deaths over five years with survival curves and adjusted models, using age bands rather than exact ages to protect privacy. The authors present the grouping as a pragmatic stand-in for clinics with thin records, and a rare outcome test of the combined-risk idea in Southeast Asia.
plos-pone-0354633:
Christel T A J Derks leads a cross-sectional check of two sleep questionnaires translated for Dutch hospital wards. Hospital sleep is often poor, yet wards lacked trusted local tools to measure quality or name what ruins it. Patients on medical and surgical wards in six teaching hospitals completed the translated scales, which had passed through forward and back translation and formal validation steps.

Several hundred patients answered, most staying in shared rooms for several nights, and over half said they slept worse than at home. Complaints included uncomfortable beds among other ward factors gathered by the survey. Derks and colleagues report the scales' measurement quality and use the answers to show where ward sleep breaks down, giving hospitals targets for quieter, more restful nights.
plos-pone-0354733:
Eghosa Ekhaese, Kingsley Dimuna, and Aniefon Essien study in 2026 how far green city principles have been put into practice in Lagos, Nigeria, and what that means for residents' well-being. Lagos is among the world's largest cities and faces fast growth, climate strain, and pollution. In depth interviews, site observation, and a checklist scored how fully the principles were applied.

Several obstacles blocked practical use, from weak enforcement to strained infrastructure, in the authors' account. Where green steps did land, links to better daily life appeared. Policy makers and planners are urged to fund and follow through on green plans rather than adopt them on paper alone.
plos-pone-0355233:
Dan Kambayashi, Shota Suzuki, and Masayoshi Hirohara published this 2026 scoping review on pharmacists working with veterinarians. Pharmacists often help animal care teams, yet their roles differ widely by place. The reviewers searched English and Japanese sources through August 2025 to map what these partnerships look like and how each profession views the other.

Most reports describe pharmacists mixing or handing out drugs for animals and answering drug questions. Evidence stays limited and uneven across regions. Kambayashi and colleagues call for better mutual understanding, animal-specific training for pharmacists, and stronger studies before such teamwork can grow into standard practice everywhere.
plos-pone-0355733:
Chayanis Som-On and co-authors translate in 2026 a brief mood screening tool into Thai and test whether it can flag bipolar disorder among people seen for depression. Mistaking bipolar illness for plain depression can lead to wrong treatment. Clinic patients with depression or with bipolar illness completed the new version, which was checked against a standard interview and an older Thai tool.

The short screener held together acceptably for its size, gave stable scores over time, and separated bipolar cases about as well as the older tool. A cut point of four or more gave a useful balance. The authors call it practical for busy clinics.
plos-pone-0355833:
Katharine Gurski, Yeona Kang, and Yanping Ma model a subtle risk of long-acting HIV prevention in this 2026 paper. Injections given every two months protect against HIV, but if someone is infected around the time of an injection, the slowly fading drug could give resistant virus strains room to evolve. The team built a mathematical model of early infection that treats viral evolution as a game shaped by changing drug levels.

Their model follows two routes of spread inside the body, direct cell-to-cell transfer and free virus, each with its own trade-offs between infectivity and drug resistance. Because drug pressure rises and falls between injections, strains compete in shifting conditions. The model shows threshold behavior: depending on starting conditions, outcomes ranged from full control to escape and delayed detection. The work helps explain why infections on this prevention method can be hard to spot early.
plos-pone-0355933:
Jessie Harney ran a survey experiment during the 2024 United States presidential campaign. She tested whether attack ads carry collateral damage. Her 2026 study showed more than sixteen hundred Democratic voters a real party ad, or no ad. The ad branded Donald Trump a convicted criminal. She then measured views of ordinary people with criminal records. She also measured their sense of political representation.

Voters who saw the ad judged people with records more harshly. It was a spillover from one famous target to a whole stigmatized group. Yet the same voters felt better represented by their party. A hopeful counterweight also worked. Hearing first from a state representative who had himself been through the justice system largely erased the damage. Campaigns, Harney argues, face a real trade-off in such language.
plos-pone-0356233:
Costanza Di Chiara and seven colleagues survey pediatricians in southern Europe about new ways to protect babies from RSV, a common virus that can severely infect infants, in this 2026 study. Spain had already rolled out a long-acting antibody injection for infants, while Italy and Cyprus and Greece had not. Nearly six hundred pediatricians answered questions on the older antibody, the new injection, and a vaccine given in pregnancy.

Awareness of the disease's risk factors was solid everywhere, but self-rated knowledge of the new injection was middling and of the maternal vaccine poor, with differences between countries. Despite that, the great majority were willing to give the injection and backed it for all infants; a fifth cited barriers such as unfamiliarity and logistics. Nearly half leaned toward preferring the maternal vaccine. The authors say education, not persuasion, is the immediate bottleneck for rollout.
plos-pone-0356533:
Atsushi Yamada, Kana Unuma, and Osamu Kitamura measure a tissue-repair protein in the blood of autopsy cases, in this 2026 forensic study. They test whether it can help confirm heart attacks after death. Diagnosing a heart attack at autopsy can be hard when tissue changes are still subtle. The team compared eighty cases: deaths from heart attack, from fatal asthma, and from trauma, measuring a protein called periostin that rises with cardiac injury and remodeling.

Periostin levels were significantly higher in the heart attack group than in either comparison group. Levels did not drift with the time elapsed since death and were barely swayed by patients' characteristics or other illnesses, two properties a forensic marker needs. The authors offer the measurements as baseline data and suggest periostin could assist postmortem evaluation when classic findings are inconclusive, rather than replace them.
plos-pone-0357033:
Projestine Muganyizi and a large trial team examine whether living at moderate height changes birth outcomes for anemic mothers. Most altitude research concerns very high places, yet nearly everyone lives below that band. Their data come from a major trial of bleeding after birth, covering anemic women who delivered in hospitals across four countries in Africa and Asia.

The analysis compares women living at mid heights with those near lowlands, using blood loss after birth as the main measure, plus rates of heavy bleeding and other birth details. Muganyizi and colleagues aim to fill a practical gap: clinics at moderate height serve huge populations, and even small altitude effects on already anemic mothers could change how staff prepare for delivery.
plos-pone-0357233:
Florent Amiot and colleagues study aging in a small brain structure that makes the fluid bathing the brain, using the gray mouse lemur, a primate whose brain ages much like ours. The structure helps regulate thinking and movement, but its aging story was sketchy. Lemurs of different ages took behavior tests, after which the team read gene activity and protein levels in the tissue.

Older lemurs moved less surely and explored less, while memory and sight tasks held up, and the tissue's basic architecture stayed intact. Thousands of genes shifted with age, immune and transport pathways rising while signaling pathways fell, and animals differed more from each other with age. One water-channel protein dropped and tracked motor decline. Amiot and colleagues describe reorganization, not simple decay.
plos-pone-0357633:
Carla Treloar and colleagues published a 2026 qualitative study in PLOS ONE on attacking stigma in Australian health care at the structural level, not just by training individual workers. Stigma keeps stigmatized patients from care and worsens their outcomes, but most anti-stigma programs stop at education and skills. The authors interviewed twenty senior stakeholders and asked which existing quality and governance machinery could carry stigma reduction, focusing on the outer setting around services.

One lever towered over the rest: accreditation against national standards. What accreditation demands gets leadership attention and resources, so writing stigma into those standards could pull whole systems along. Participants also saw openings in general workplace laws, such as industrial relations rules, to force attention where patient-focused arguments stall. The authors frame structural tools as the underused frontier of stigma work and propose trials of these macro mechanisms inside real quality programs.
plos-pone-0357733:
Saori Miura and colleagues measure what happens during a single guided forest walk in Saikai City, Japan, offered through a public health program. About ninety adults joined certified health walking courses over one year, and staff checked blood pressure, pulse, heart rhythm patterns, and mood before and after each session. The program follows a German spa tradition that treats paced walking in nature as preventive care.

Blood pressure fell after the walks, and mood shifted in the right direction: tension and anxiety eased while energy, friendliness, and calm rose. Heart rhythm measures tied to stress balance did not change. Miura and colleagues note there was no comparison group, so the forest itself cannot be credited apart from the walking, the group, and the break from routine.
plos-pone-0358233:
Takashi Teramoto studied street ranking in Kyoto in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Ranking streets sounds simple until the comparisons are incomplete, with many pairs never directly judged. Teramoto used intersection names as a route into ranking the city's streets and compared methods for handling the missing pairs.

The comparison shows which ranking methods stay reliable when preference data are patchy. That question reaches far beyond one Japanese city: product rankings, sports tables, and peer review all face partial data. A method that stays fair with gaps is worth having. Teramoto's test on real city structure gives ranking designers a grounded case to check their tools against.
plos-pone-0358333: Ahmadi-hamedani and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on blood clues in dogs and cats. Young platelets, the cell bits that help blood clot, can signal how hard the bone marrow is working. The review gathers studies on immature platelet measures in pets. As a scoping review, it maps the field's reach. Vets could use such measures to judge marrow health without invasive tests.
plos-pone-0358433:
Xian Pan and three colleagues design a flight controller that holds a drone on course despite unknown forces, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The mathematical problem is broader than drones: steer a chain of uncertain systems while disturbances change over time. Their scheme watches each link of the chain with a disturbance observer that estimates the push in real time and feeds the estimate into the control law, canceling it as it happens. Neural networks approximate the dynamics nobody can write down exactly.

Two engineering choices keep the design practical. Estimated parameters are bundled together, shrinking the number the system must tune live. A surface technique avoids the exploding algebra that plagues step by step controller design. In simulations of drone longitudinal motion, the scheme tracked its path more accurately and shrugged off disturbances better than a comparable controller lacking observers. The observers, more than the networks, earn the credit.
plos-pone-0358533: Chen and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on signaling proteins in kidney cancer. Cytokines are small proteins that carry messages between cells and shape immune responses. The team looked for a pattern of these proteins that is specific to renal cell carcinoma tumors. A tumor-specific pattern could aid diagnosis or point to how the cancer evades the immune system.
plos-pone-0359833:
Sinan Karageçili, Deniz Inan, and Nouman Ali published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a computational study searching for natural compounds that bind CXCR4, a protein receptor on cell surfaces. The work is framed as relevant to endometriosis and to ovarian cancer progression.

Computer screening can test many natural substances for fit against a target before any lab work begins. CXCR4 helps cells move and signal, roles that feed both conditions named in the title. Drug discovery researchers use such candidate lists to choose which compounds deserve costly laboratory testing next.
pmc-12967033: Published in 2026, Short communication: performance of beef cows fe tackled an open problem. The solution advanced knowledge. Writers of history may cite it later. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
pmc-13236833:
Wegner, von Wirén, and Kunze review how to engineer a family of enzymes called omega-transaminases. Drug makers prize these enzymes because they build chiral amines, mirror-image molecules that many medicines need in just one form. Yet the enzymes still stumble: some react too slowly, refuse certain starting materials, stall at chemical balance points, or wilt in industrial solvents.

The field, the authors show, has shifted from hunting new enzymes in nature to redesigning known ones on purpose. Protein engineering now targets each weakness directly. Their review maps those strategies, giving chemists a guide to enzymes that could replace harsher, metal-based routes to the same drugs.
pmc-13240933:
Angelis and colleagues in Copenhagen tuned a U-Net network to outline the epidermis in optical coherence tomography scans of actinic keratosis. Manual tracing of these precancerous lesions is slow and inconsistent. The team varied image size, batch size, and training length systematically. Expert annotations served as the reference standard.

A modest setup won: small images, tiny batches, and fifty training rounds. It reached a Dice score of 0.86 against expert tracings. Bigger images and longer training added compute without accuracy, sometimes overfitting. A lean network, carefully tuned, proved enough for this segmentation task.
pmc-13241433:
Fujiwara's team in Osaka modeled artery walls as sponges rather than sealed, incompressible tubes. Tests show artery volume can shift by a tenth or more under load. Their biphasic framework couples a stretchy solid skeleton with moving tissue fluid. Cut to one radial dimension, the model ran as finite blocks.

Modeled warps matched test averages within two percent. Fluid pressure inside the wall explained the seeming squash on its own. That pressure also builds hidden outward tension in the solid frame. The authors offer the framework for settings where fluid-solid interplay matters.
pmc-13241533:
Xue and colleagues in Shanghai etched grid patterns into MEMS cantilever actuators to break a stubborn trade-off. In these tiny beams, faster vibration normally means smaller bending at the tip. Their design carves a flexible grid zone near the free end. The root segment stays stiff, preserving the resonant frequency.

Fabricated cantilevers more than doubled their tip tilt angle while vibrating faster than plain beams. Tip travel also rose by about half. Built into a two-axis micromirror, the design more than tripled the optical scan angle. The mirror reached a twenty-five degree field of view, showing the approach suits other MEMS actuators too.
pmc-13242133:
Koziar and colleagues at Surrey hunted tuberculosis in blood drawn years before symptoms, using UK Biobank plasma. Nearly three thousand proteins were profiled in a cohort of half a million. Forty-two people developed TB around the sampling window. Matched control participants had never had the disease.

Several proteins differed sharply between cases and controls, including CDCP1 and a gut hormone marker. The altered signature appeared before diagnosis and lingered years after treatment. Immune and inflammatory pathways dominated the changed proteins. Koziar proposes plasma panels for bedside point-of-care TB risk screening.
pmc-13242433:
E. E. Hartman and colleagues checked whether having a parent nearby changes how young children rate their own quality of life. Their study appeared in Quality of Life Research in 2026. It covered 303 children aged five to seven at primary schools, each with a parent also taking part. Some children answered the PedsQL questionnaire at school with a research assistant, while others answered at home with a parent reading the items aloud.

Children scored their quality of life higher when a parent was present, which shrank the gap with parent ratings and raised parent-child agreement. Parent ratings themselves did not differ between the two settings, and the pattern held for both mothers and fathers. The authors read this as gentle parental help with understanding and recall, not coaching. They caution against self-reports taken without a parent nearby and call for clear rules on giving these questionnaires.
pmc-13244133:
Javier Ottaviani led this 2026 nutrition study asking whether simply following healthy eating advice gives people enough flavanols, plant compounds linked to heart benefits. A large trial called COSMOS had found benefits at 500 milligrams per day.

The team measured flavanol intake with blood and urine markers in two studies: COSMOS in the United States, with 6,509 people, and EPIC-Norfolk in Britain, with 24,154 people. Eating more fruit and vegetables did raise flavanol levels. Yet fewer than one in four people who met the eating guidelines reached the 500 milligram level. The authors say set intake targets for flavanols may still be needed.
pmc-13246533:
Yoon, Ma, Kanke, and co-authors mapped, hour by hour, how gut lining cells respond when inflammatory signals break their barrier, in this 2026 Inflammation Research paper. A leaky gut barrier contributes to inflammatory bowel disease, yet most drugs target the immune system rather than the lining itself. Using cultured intestinal cells injured by cytokines, the team tracked gene activity over time with RNA sequencing.

The response unfolded in phases, switching on programs for cell junctions, tissue remodeling, and stress defense. Computer analysis nominated several control points, and blocking some of them, including JAK2 and gasdermin D, reduced the barrier damage. One regulator, HNF4A, stood out as a hub, and its target gene SLC26A3 was sharply reduced in patient colon tissue.
pmc-13250233:
McDonough and a wide team test whether a walking program for people with severe mental illness can work in real services. Their 2026 BMJ Open feasibility trial, called Walking fOR Health, ran in four community mental health teams in the United Kingdom and Ireland. Participants received thirteen weeks of education, activity tracking, and health coaching, or a single education session.

Fifty-four adults took part, and the study hit ninety percent of its recruitment target. Nearly all participants gave follow-up data, and engagement with the program's parts stayed high throughout. Trackers showed a modest daily rise in brisk activity for the coached group compared with controls. Feedback was strongly positive, so the authors judge a full trial worthwhile, with some design refinements first.
pmc-13250633:
Yang Nan and co-authors map the future home of a medicinal shrub in this 2026 study. Acanthopanax sessiliflorus grows in East Asian temperate forests and is valued in herbal medicine, but how climate change will shift its range was not well measured.

A computer model trained on climate, soil, and land shape found its current good habitat covers a large area of northern China, centred near Beijing and the Changbai Mountains. The yearly swing of temperature mattered most. Under all four future climate paths, the best habitat shrank by 2100, most steeply under high emissions, and the range centre drifted northwest. The authors offer the maps for planting and conservation plans.
pmc-13250833:
Laila Almufleh follows a repaired tooth root for two years in this 2026 dental case report. A 34-year-old man suffered an accidental hole through the middle of a lower molar root during root canal work, a mishap that can doom a tooth.

The hole, about three and a half millimetres wide, was sealed at once with a premixed ceramic-like repair material. Some material squeezed out past the root, which often raises concern. Two years on, detailed 3D scans showed the old bone lesion fully healed, and the tooth worked with no pain and healthy gums. The author argues that spilled repair material need not spoil the outcome.
pmc-13251833:
Feng Zhan and co-authors build a record-setting green display pixel in this 2026 paper. Ultra-sharp screens need green light that is pure in colour and stays bright for years, a pair of goals that usually fight each other.

The team designed platinum-based glowing molecules with a stiff three-dimensional shape and bulky guards, which narrowed their glow sharply. Placed in a top-emitting device tuned like a tiny echo chamber, the colour narrowed further and hit the green point of the BT.2020 broadcast standard. Efficiency was high, and the projected lifetime to 90 percent brightness passed 540,000 hours at standard brightness, far beyond commercial display norms.
pmc-13252833:
Elena Palmieri and colleagues design a vaccine platform against a drug-resistant germ in this 2026 study. Klebsiella pneumoniae is a leading cause of newborn sepsis in poorer countries and no vaccine exists, so flexible platforms that mix sugar coats with proteins are in demand.

Using a binding system that snaps vaccine parts together, the team paired a model sugar coat with a bacterial surface protein. Longer sugar chains and higher protein shares drew stronger immune responses in rabbits. The choice of carrier protein also shifted results. Serum from rabbits given the best design protected mice against a real clinical strain. The work guides the recipe for a future maternal vaccine.
pmc-13257633:
Georgios Christou and Dimitrios Kiortsis measured blood flow speed in the descending aorta of healthy athletes. A fast reading can raise suspicion of aortic narrowing, even in fit people with no such problem. Their 2026 study sets a normal range so athletes are not misjudged.

The team examined five hundred fifty-nine athletes aged twelve and older, using ultrasound and exercise testing. Flow speed topped out at two meters per second, and younger athletes ran fastest. More endurance training nudged values upward, while a wider aorta lowered them. Forty athletes rechecked years later showed little change beyond what aging predicts.
pmc-13258333:
Haiping Liu and co-authors built a tiny electronic nose meant to warn before a lithium-ion battery overheats dangerously. Failing batteries leak telltale gases before thermal runaway, so sniffing them early can prevent fires. Their 2026 work combines custom microchip sensors with commercial ones.

Simulations first shaped the sensors' micro-hotplates, which were then coated with zinc oxide, plain or gold-dusted. Fed twenty seconds of sensor responses, the combined nose sorted six gases, including hydrogen, methane, and carbon monoxide. It named the right gas in over ninety-nine of a hundred trials. The authors offer the device as an early-warning solution for battery packs.
pmc-13258733:
Katie H Long leads a 2026 study of how precisely women can locate a touch on the breast. Touch localization means naming where on the skin a touch landed. The team compared the breast with the hand and the back, body parts known for sharp and poor touch precision. They also tested the areola and nipple, and checked whether breast size changes, such as expansion, affected accuracy.

Breast precision was even lower than that of the back, until now the standard example of poor precision. Precision was lower in breasts that had expanded more, which fits the idea that nerve supply does not grow with body size. Touches to different parts of the nipple were largely indistinguishable, suggesting sparse nerve density there. Errors were also systematically biased toward the nipple, as if touches were pulled toward it.
pmc-13260533:
Miriam Jacobs leads a 2026 prospective study of disease burden in German patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis, a group of diseases in which immune attack inflames small blood vessels. The team used a disease-specific patient form, AAV-PRO, alongside established measures of quality of life, fatigue, participation in daily life, physical function, depression, and optimism. Doctors separately scored disease activity, built-up damage, and steroid side effects. Seventy patients took part.

Most patients had one subtype called GPA, at 64.3 percent, with a mean disease duration of 10.5 years at enrollment. Patients with active disease scored higher on every AAV-PRO domain, meaning worse burden. Strong correlations appeared between form domains and physical function, social role functioning, and taking-part measures, with several coefficients between 0.7 in the weakest case and 0.88 in the strongest case. The authors argue these links help doctors read the form in routine practice.
pmc-13261133:
Xiaonan Liu and co-authors report a 2026 study of how an epigenetic enzyme helps tendon healing. Tendon repair involves inflammation, cell reprogramming, and rebuilding of the matrix between cells. The protein p16INK4a marks stressed and aging cells. Removing such cells helps age-related tendon disease, but their role during regeneration was unclear.

In a mouse Achilles tendon puncture model, injury-induced p16INK4a-positive cells promoted structural and functional recovery. Single-cell RNA sequencing identified them as mainly mesenchymal cells with high matrix gene expression. These cells showed increased activity of JMJD3, an enzyme that removes a repressive chemical mark, and higher expression of collagen genes Col1a1 and Col3a1. Deleting or blocking JMJD3 disrupted collagen organization and reduced tendon strength. Lowering the repressive mark pharmacologically sped repair. The findings show these cells can help, depending on context.
pmc-13261333:
Hua Luo reviews the peacekeepers turned traitors of prostate cancer: regulatory T cells. These cells normally prevent friendly fire, but inside tumors they shield cancer from immune attack. Luo's 2026 review draws on single-cell and spatial studies to map where they sit and what they do.

Where Tregs cluster in tumor stroma, and how activated they are, predicts relapse better than their raw count. A dense stromal presence more than doubled biochemical recurrence risk. Antibody drugs against one brake, CTLA-4, flopped in big trials, but engineered versions emptied tumor Tregs in animals. Luo argues for subset-specific targeting paired with hormone or radiation therapy.
pmc-13262433:
Bo Zhu leads a team mapping gene control in rice pollen formation in a 2026 journal article. Making male reproductive cells, the cells that form sperm, requires deep resetting of chemical marks on DNA and its packing proteins. The team profiled these marks and gene activity cell by cell, from early dividing cells through to sperm cells.

Gene programs in later cells were largely set up by packing states laid down earlier, they found. One activating mark placed during the key division stayed in place, while a repressive mark faded over time. DNA methylation, a silencing chemical tag, stayed mostly stable, with one brief dip. Blocking the enzyme that places the activating mark disrupted later gene activity and pollen growth.
pmc-13262633:
Zhaofan He leads a team giving soft robots a sense of their own shape in a 2026 journal article. Soft robots bend freely, which makes their form hard to track, especially in tight spaces like surgery. The team's sensor is a single optical fiber attached at one end. Bending scrambles the light pattern inside it, and a learning program reads shape from that pattern.

The same fiber setup served three test tasks with different decoders. On soft grippers it confirmed grip states with over 99 percent accuracy. On a bionic hand it tracked shape with about five times finer detail than before. On a soft surgical robot it rebuilt the 3D form with strong overlap scores above 0.93.
pmc-13263233:
Shinichi Harada and co-authors report two anesthesia cases that led to a dangerous heart rhythm in a 2026 case report. In both patients, the inhaled anesthetic desflurane lengthened the QT interval, a measure of the heart's electrical reset time. Then a dose of ephedrine, a drug used to raise blood pressure, triggered extra heartbeats that spiraled into torsades de pointes and fibrillation.

One case was a 21-year-old man having a brain tumor biopsy; the other a 50-year-old woman having womb cancer surgery. Heart tracings showed the sequence step by step in both cases, and the QT length settled within two days. Blood mineral levels were largely normal. The authors warn that ephedrine needs care when desflurane has stretched the QT interval.
pmc-13263333:
Essam Menshawy and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on feed additives for Nile tilapia, a widely farmed fish. A total of 120 young fish were split into four groups for sixty days. Groups received a plain diet, lactic acid, rosemary leaf meal, or both additives together.

All supplemented groups grew better than the control group, and the combined diet worked best. Blood markers of liver and kidney strain fell, while total protein and albumin rose in the combined group. Gut tissue showed taller villi, the tiny folds that absorb food, and more mucus-making cells. Genes tied to growth, immunity, and antioxidant defense were also switched on more strongly.
pmc-13263533:
Mahdi Norouzi and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of a newer mesh material in pelvic organ prolapse surgery. In prolapse, pelvic organs slip down and bulge through the vagina. Sacrocolpopexy fixes this by anchoring tissue to the spine with mesh. The review compared polyvinylidene fluoride mesh with standard polypropylene.

From 319 screened studies, twelve were included, covering 1,093 women. Rates of mesh exposure, recurrence, sexual problems, and reoperation with the new material were all near zero, though small samples left wide uncertainty. New urge incontinence appeared in a third of women. No outcome differed significantly between the two meshes, so the authors call for stronger trials.
pmc-13263933:

Project Blue Book was the United States Air Force program that logged reports of unidentified flying objects. Special Report No. 14, prepared with the Battelle Memorial Institute and issued in 1955, took thousands of cases and tested them with statistics rather than opinion.

Analysts sorted sightings into known and unknown and asked whether the two groups truly differed. On qualities like shape, color, and motion, they found the unknowns did stand apart, a result quoted ever since. The prose is dry and methodical. Skeptics and believers both cite the study, which makes it a rare shared piece of ground in a loud debate.
