King Chandakapali asks the sage Gheranda how a person can master the body and reach liberation, and the Gheranda Samhita records the answer. Gheranda lays out a sevenfold path, broader than the limbs of Patanjali. The teaching proceeds as a calm dialogue between king and sage.

Purification rites come first, then postures, then breath work, withdrawal of the senses, meditation, and final absorption. Each stage gets practical detail meant for use, not mere theory. The Samhita stands with the Hatha Yoga Pradipika among the root manuals of hatha yoga. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-10033:
After the Metamorphoses, Ovid turned to the Roman calendar and wrote the Fasti, a poem that moves month by month through the year. Frazer's translation is the version named here. Ovid finished only January through June before exile cut the work short.

For each festival he gives the rite, its origin story, and the gods and heroes tied to the day. Readers learn why Romans honored strange old gods and how myth explained custom. The poem is a rich store of Roman religion and folk practice, told with the same wit and speed that mark all of Ovid's verse.
tob-10233:
Four hundred twenty-three short verses, in F. Max Müller's translation tradition, gather sayings attributed to the Buddha in the Dhammapada. Buddhism's most beloved scripture, it has been memorized by monks and householders for two thousand years. No single story carries it; each verse stands as counsel that can be recalled in daily life.

Verses are arranged by theme, including anger, craving, folly, wisdom, and the awakened person. The teaching is practical: master the mind, speak truthfully, harm no living thing, and watch where desire leads. Because the language is brief and concrete, readers can enter anywhere, though the cumulative picture is a full discipline of attention and kindness.
tob-10333:
Heinrich Kramer, with Jacob Sprenger named as co-author, published the Malleus Maleficarum, the Hammer of Witches, in 1486. Kramer was a Dominican inquisitor whose witch trials had met resistance. He wrote the manual to win backing and guide other judges.

Three parts argue that witchcraft is real and mostly women's work, list the harms witches were said to do, and set out trial steps, torture, and sentencing. Print spread the manual across Europe, and it fueled witch hunts for two centuries. Historians read it today as key proof of how fear, law, and print fed a persecution.
tob-13333:
James George Frazer reshaped the study of myth and religion with The Golden Bough, his vast study of magic and religion. The title comes from the golden bough at Nemi, where a priest ruled until a challenger killed him. Frazer ranged across the whole world to explain that rite. He returned to the riddle again and again as his evidence grew.

Frazer argues that magic came first, that religion grew from its failure, and that science later grew from both. He piles up cases of taboo, sacred kings, and dying gods. Later scholars corrected much, but the book's sweep still stuns readers.
tob-4214-10833:
Two friends argue about faith in Religion: A Dialogue, the best-known piece in Saunders's Schopenhauer selection. Philalethes, the lover of truth, presses the case against natural religion. Demopheles defends faith as a useful cloak for truths the crowd cannot bear directly.

Around the dialogue stand essays on government, free will, ethics, and the emptiness of worldly striving. Schopenhauer writes with unusual wit for a German thinker of his weight. He mocks cant, praises honesty, and returns always to his core claim that will drives the world. Readers meet the atheist at his most combative and most entertaining here.
tob-4333:
Volume two of Augustine's Confessions, in William Watts's translation of 1631 as reprinted in the Loeb series, carries the autobiography into its searching later books. The stolen pears and the Milan garden lie behind; what remains is harder. Augustine turns his mind on memory itself, and on the riddle of time.

What is time, he asks, if no one asks me, I know; if I must explain, I cannot. The final book reads Genesis as a figure of the church and the soul's rest. Verified from the 1919 edition record, Watts's old English suits the old bishop. The restless heart's inquiry completes itself here.
un-ga-res-33: How long should the first members of UN councils serve? Resolution 33, passed on 13 February 1946, settles the point for the men and women picked in January of that year under stopgap rules. They would hold office for twelve months. Fresh votes for their successors would fall at the second part of the first regular session, and the Secretary-General had to report any rule changes needed to make that work.
un-ga-res-a-69-33:
Small arms kill on a vast scale in the Sahel and Sahara lands. Resolution A/69/33, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, deals with help for states that fight their spread. The text recalls the vote of the year before on the same aid. It voices deep worry at the toll of such arms, above all among children, and at the harm they do to the fight against poverty.

African states had set a shared stand on the illicit flow of small arms at Bamako in the year 2000. World reports had warned that states must fight small arms as hard as the great arms of war. The vote backs aid to Sahel-Saharan states to curb the trade and to gather the arms in.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 33, adopted on 13 February 1946 at the thirty-second plenary meeting, is a short ruling on terms of office. The Assembly stated its sense that members of councils elected in January 1946 under the provisional rules should serve twelve months. Votes for their successors would come at the second part of the first regular session. It asked the Secretary-General to report what rule changes that would need.

General Assembly resolution 69/33 (2014) supports help for states trying to curb the illicit traffic in small arms and light weapons and to collect such weapons. The text stresses the human cost of illicit small-arms spread, especially in the Sahelo-Saharan region. It backs the Economic Community of West African States convention on small arms. The Assembly encourages the Secretary-General's advisory missions, national commissions against illicit proliferation, and civil-society work. It invites continued technical and financial assistance to affected states that request it.
un-sc-res-1033: Catalogue data places Resolution 1033, a United Nations Security Council text, in the year 1995. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-133: Cameroun sought a seat at the United Nations. Resolution 133 records the Council's reply. The Council adopted it on 26 January 1960. No member dissented. The meeting was the Council's 850th. The record states that the Council examined the application. It recommends that the General Assembly admit the Republic of Cameroun. The text is one formal sentence. It is kept in the official record.
un-sc-res-1333:
Resolution 1333 addressed Afghanistan under the Taliban when the Council adopted it on 19 December 2000. The Taliban still sheltered Usama bin Laden and let his network run training camps. Opium taxes paid for much of that activity. The Taliban had ignored earlier demands to hand him over for trial.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council sets an arms embargo on Taliban-held territory. States must close all Taliban offices and all offices of Ariana Afghan Airlines. Funds of bin Laden and his associates, including Al-Qaida, are frozen at once. Flights to Taliban areas are barred unless cleared for aid or peace talks. The Taliban must close the camps and halt the drug trade.
un-sc-res-1433: Under number 1433, the catalog lists a Security Council resolution dated to 2002 in the official UN record. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-1533:
Congo's arms embargo gained its own watchdog committee on 12 March 2004. Armed groups and militias still held ground in North and South Kivu and in Ituri. Weapons kept flowing in against the ban set by resolution 1493 (2003). Experts had tied the war to the illegal mining and sale of Congo's natural wealth.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council restated the demand that all states block arms supplies to the eastern groups. MONUC was told to keep seizing weapons found in breach of the embargo, within its means. All parties had to give MONUC staff free and instant access. The Council set up a sanctions committee of all its members to watch the embargo. States, above all in the region, were urged to end illegal resource trading, using courts where needed. The machinery here became the base of the Congo sanctions regime for years after.
un-sc-res-1633:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1633, adopted on 21 October 2005. The crisis dragged on and conditions kept getting worse. Elections set for 30 October 2005 could not be held. The African Union had ruled that President Laurent Gbagbo could stay on for at most twelve more months.

The Council backs the African Union plan in full. A new prime minister, accepted by all sides, must be named by 31 October 2005. The prime minister gets full power over the cabinet, defense, and election work. An international working group will draft a road map toward free elections by 31 October 2006. Militias must disarm at once, and anyone blocking peace faces targeted sanctions.
un-sc-res-1733: Resolution 1733, a 2006 Security Council text, is preserved in this collection through a Wikisource copy of the official record. Its number fixes its place among the year's decisions, between its neighbors 1732 and 1736. The entry holds the complete act at that address: findings, decisions, and the reporting instructions that typically bring the text to a close.
un-sc-res-1833: Kept under number 1833, a formal Security Council resolution is preserved through a Wikisource transcription of the official record. The Council's fifteen members, five permanent and ten elected, stand behind the text. What they jointly decided is the entry's content: findings stated in order, then operative paragraphs that put the decision into effect.
un-sc-res-1933:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1933, adopted on 30 June 2010. The last presidential election had taken place in October 2000. The vote promised under the Ouagadougou peace deal kept slipping, with no date set. Unrest in February 2010 showed how fragile the calm remained.

The Council renews the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire until 31 December 2010. Ivorian leaders must publish the final voters list and name the election date without more delay. The Secretary-General's envoy will certify each stage of the vote. The mission guards civilians, watches the arms embargo, and backs reunification and disarmament. Hate speech in the media could draw targeted sanctions.
un-sc-res-233:
War broke out in the Near East at the start of June 1967. On 6 June, one day into the fighting of the Six-Day War, the Security Council acted. The Secretary-General had briefed the Council on the situation. Members had heard statements from the parties. The Council said it was concerned at the outbreak and at the danger in the region.

Its demand was short and direct. It called on the governments concerned to stop all military activity at once. That halt was meant as a first step, not a settlement. The Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed without delay. The fighting in fact ran on for four more days.
un-sc-res-33: The Council settled a point of procedure with the General Assembly in 1947. The issue was how membership applications would be handled under the two bodies' rules. On 27 August 1947 the Council accepted its experts' advice. A sub-committee would negotiate matching changes to the Assembly's rules. Some Assembly proposals on the Council's own rules were accepted as well. The dry text aligned the paperwork of admissions between the two organs.
un-sc-res-333:
Rhodesia's sanctions net was tightened on 22 May 1973. The sanctions committee's second special report lay before the Council. Measures so far had not ended the illegal regime. Some states had failed to stop trade with it, against resolutions 232 (1966) and 253 (1968). South Africa and Portugal refused to help apply the sanctions at all.

The Council approved the committee's recommendations and pressed for urgent action on them. States whose laws allowed imports of Rhodesian minerals and goods had to repeal those laws at once. All states were called to pass laws with harsh fines and jail for sanctions breakers. Contracts with South Africa and Portugal had to carry clauses barring Rhodesian goods from the deal. Insurance firms were to be barred from covering flights into and out of Rhodesia. Marine insurance contracts had to state plainly that no Rhodesian cargo was covered.
un-sc-res-433: At number 433 in its series, the Security Council decision is catalogued here as a 1978 record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-733:
Somalia collapsed into civil war at the start of 1992, and Somalia itself asked the Council to take up its case. The fighting was taking a heavy toll in lives and property. The Council was gravely alarmed at how fast the situation was getting worse. It treated the collapse as a threat to peace and security in the region. Resolution 733 was adopted unanimously on 23 January 1992.

All parties in Somalia were strongly urged to stop fighting at once. They had to agree a cease-fire and work for reconciliation and a political settlement. The Secretary-General was asked to expand aid to the people affected. Working with African and Arab partners, he also had to press the factions to end hostilities and let relief supplies through. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council imposed a general and complete arms embargo. All deliveries of weapons and military equipment to Somalia were banned.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1033, adopted unanimously on 19 December 1995, concerns Western Sahara and the stalled identification of voters for its self-determination referendum. The Council repeats its commitment to holding the referendum without further delay, under the Settlement Plan accepted by Morocco and the Polisario Front. It notes both parties' responses to the Secretary-General's proposal for moving the identification process forward.

The Council stresses that the Identification Commission can work only if both parties trust its judgement and integrity. It welcomes the Secretary-General's decision to intensify consultations aimed at an agreed plan. It asks him to report urgently. If those consultations fail, he is to give the Council options. They include a programme for the orderly withdrawal of MINURSO, the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara.

Cameroun's path into the United Nations runs through this short text of 26 January 1960. The Council had looked at the new Republic of Cameroun's request to join. Its answer was yes: it told the General Assembly that Cameroun should be admitted. Under the Charter, that step by the Council is the required step before the Assembly can vote a new country in. This brief text is the formal gate through which Cameroun's membership passed.

Sanctions on the Taliban are sharply widened by Resolution 1333, adopted unanimously on 19 December 2000. The Taliban still sheltered Usama bin Laden, indicted for the 1998 embassy bombings in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam. The Taliban let terrorist training camps operate on Afghan soil despite the demands of Resolution 1267 (1999). Opium taxes helped pay for it.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands the Taliban hand over bin Laden for trial, close all terrorist camps, and end sanctuary for terrorists. It imposes an arms embargo on Taliban-controlled territory and bans military advice to the Taliban. It orders states to freeze the funds of bin Laden and those associated with him, including the Al-Qaida organization, as listed by the Sanctions Committee. Taliban offices and Ariana Afghan Airlines offices must close, flights to Taliban territory are banned, and sales of the heroin-making chemical acetic anhydride to that territory are banned.

Angola's long civil war had ended months earlier when, on 15 August 2002, the United Nations Office in Angola was replaced with a fuller mission. The peace rested on the Lusaka Protocol and its addendum. A stronger United Nations presence, the Council judged, could help lock in the peace while the remaining steps were completed.

The new United Nations Mission in Angola, UNMA, is set up for six months, until 15 February 2003. Its work spans political, military, human rights, humanitarian, and economic goals, and its staffing includes a Child Protection Adviser. Whether the mission would be extended, changed, or ended was to turn on an assessment of progress in finishing the Lusaka Protocol.

Resolution 1533, adopted unanimously on 12 March 2004, gives Congo's arms embargo a referee. Militias still roamed the east, in North and South Kivu and Ituri, and weapons kept flowing into the Democratic Republic of the Congo despite the embargo imposed in July 2003. The Council also tied the fighting to the illegal stripping of Congo's natural resources, which an expert panel had documented the year before.

The Council created a sanctions committee of its own members to oversee the embargo. It further set up a group of experts to gather and analyze information on arms flows, name violators, and suggest ways to make the embargo work. That committee-and-experts pairing became the template for modern UN sanctions.

Côte d'Ivoire's transition is restructured by Resolution 1633, adopted on 21 October 2005. Elections due on 30 October could not be held. The African Union Peace and Security Council had decided on 6 October that the president's mandate had ended. It decided he should stay as head of state for at most 12 more months.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council endorses the AU decision and demands all Ivorian parties implement it at once. A new prime minister acceptable to all signatory parties must be appointed by 31 October 2005. He will have full authority over security, defence, disarmament, and elections. Ministers will be accountable to him. A new International Working Group must draw up a road map for elections by 31 October 2006 and report any obstruction of the prime minister. Militias must disarm at once, and sanctions stay ready against spoilers.

A tribute closes the year on 22 December 2006. The text honours Kofi Annan at the end of his time as Secretary-General of the United Nations. The central role he had played in guiding the organization is recognized, along with his sustained work toward just and lasting settlements of disputes and conflicts around the world. The reforms he launched and his proposals for strengthening the United Nations system are commended, and deep appreciation is expressed for his service to peace, development, and human rights.

The International Security Assistance Force in Afghanistan, ISAF, is extended for another year on 22 September 2008. Afghan authorities hold the main duty for security across the country, with ISAF assisting the government. The force's work is linked to the broader world effort in Afghanistan, including the United Nations mission.

ISAF's authorization is extended, and the states taking part may use all necessary measures to carry out its mandate. ISAF is told to work in close consultation with the Afghan government and the United Nations mission's head. Its leadership is to report regularly through the Secretary-General. More trainers and resources for the Afghan army and police are also pressed for, so Afghans can take over security themselves.

Côte d'Ivoire's election clock is pressed in Resolution 1933, adopted on 30 June 2010. The last presidential election had been in October 2000. The provisional voters list of November 2009 was still not final, and no first-round date was set. The February 2010 unrest showed how fragile the Ouagadougou peace process remained. Sexual violence and other abuses continued with impunity.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council gives UNOCI a mandate to 31 December 2010 focused on stability, protection of civilians under imminent threat, monitoring the arms embargo, and election support. It urges the Ivorian parties to publish the final voters list, certified by the Secretary-General's Special Representative, without further delay. It urges them to announce the election date, holding them fully accountable. It reaffirms the certification role for every stage of the vote and warns it is ready to impose targeted sanctions, including on media actors inciting violence.

Resolution 233 is the UN Security Council's first ceasefire call of the Six-Day War, adopted unanimously on 6 June 1967, the war's second day. The Secretary-General had given an oral report, the Council had heard statements, and it recorded its concern at the outbreak of fighting and the menacing situation in the Near East.

The resolution calls on the governments concerned to stop all military action in the area at once, as a first step. It asks the Secretary-General to keep the Council swiftly and steadily informed. The fighting ran its course before diplomacy caught up, and the war's outcome set up Resolution 242 five months later.

Rulebooks, not wars, fill this early text. In 1947 the Council and the Assembly were still shaping how they worked. Their rule drafts clashed in spots. Rule 58 dealt with bids by new states to join. A team of the Council's own rule experts had views on the text. Resolution 33 passed on 27 August 1947 by ten votes to none. Australia held back.

The rule team was told to treat with the Assembly's match body. It could deal on the Council's revised rule 58. Side shifts in the Assembly's rules were part of the pact. One word fight is spelled out: the Assembly's bid to swap decide for consider was turned down. Other tweaks got a yes. The text is dry as dust. It still shows two young bodies learning to mesh their gears.

Resolution 333, adopted on 22 May 1973 by twelve votes to none with three abstentions, tries to make Rhodesia sanctions work better. Earlier measures since 1966 had not ended the illegal regime, the Council admitted, and some states were still trading with it in breach of the Charter. South Africa and Portugal were condemned for refusing to cooperate with the sanctions effort at all.

The Council approved the recommendations in the sanctions committee's second special report, a list of tightening steps. It asked the committee to keep working on ways to close the gaps. The Assembly's decolonization committee had also written in support. Sanctions were the Council's chosen weapon against Rhodesia, and this is a maintenance order for that weapon.

A Pacific island state, newly independent from Britain, sought a seat at the United Nations in the summer of 1978. Resolution 433, adopted unanimously on 17 August 1978, deals with the application of Solomon Islands. The Council examined the application. It then recommended to the General Assembly that Solomon Islands be admitted to membership in the United Nations. That single recommendation is the whole text of the resolution.

Resolution 733 is the UN Security Council's first response to Somalia's collapse into civil war, adopted unanimously on 23 January 1992. Somalia had asked the Council to take up its situation, and the Secretary-General reported rapid deterioration, heavy loss of life, and widespread damage after the state fell apart.

The resolution asks the Secretary-General to expand humanitarian aid and appoint a coordinator, presses him and regional leaders to contact all factions to end hostilities, and strongly urges an immediate ceasefire. Acting under Chapter VII, it also slaps a total ban on shipments of weapons and military gear into Somalia. It was the opening move of the UN's Somalia involvement of the 1990s.
villon-oeuvres-marot-1533:
Pierre Jannet prepared this French edition of Villon's complete works, with notes and a glossary. The preface admits that little is known of Villon's life beyond what he says himself. His poems, it argues, take Villon himself as their true subject.

Thief, brawler, and the greatest French poet of the 1400s, Villon wrote from Paris taverns and prisons. The Testament and the Ballad of the Hanged Men mix street slang with piercing beauty. Lamants for lost youth run through the work beside sharp satire. An added choice of poems by his followers rounds out the book, and his voice still sounds startlingly alive today.
voltaire-letters-on-the-english-1733: Letters on the English, Voltaire's 1733 portrait of England. The Frenchman's admiration. This book preserves that classic. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. Its place in history is secure. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
zadkiel-grammar-of-astrology-1833:
Zadkiel was the pen name of Richard James Morrison, a former naval officer turned London astrologer. His Grammar of Astrology, published in 1833, presents the art's rules in the form of a school grammar. Morrison was Raphael's Victorian rival, and the two men's almanacs fought for the same readers.

The Grammar drills the student in signs, houses, aspects, and the steps of judging a chart, point by numbered point. Morrison claims for astrology a weather-wise certainty, and his forecasts made his name a household word. His work carried the revival Raphael began into the middle of the Victorian age.
